articles.title_orig: Gaorong closes $486M fund as industrial capital floods China's VCs
articles.title_zh: Gaorong closes $486M fund as industrial capital floods China's VCs
articles.content_orig:
What's the deal? Gaorong Ventures has completed fundraising for its Tianjin Gaorong Changying Fund, securing 3.261 billion CNY (about $486 million) in committed capital. The venture fund drew heavily from China's traditional industrial sectors rather than the usual tech-focused backers.
Who's backing it? Junzheng Group and its wholly-owned subsidiary committed 1 billion CNY, more than 30% of the total. Pig farmer Muyuan Industrial added 350 million CNY, Zijin Mining entities 300 million CNY, Jiahua Energy 200 million CNY, and Newland Digital Technology 100 million CNY — capital from chemicals, agriculture, and mining pooled into one market-oriented fund.
Why now? Gaorong's close lands amid a broader rebound. Fundraising in China's primary market is recovering, with 3,981 new funds raised in the first half of 2026 totalling 1,049.464 billion CNY — up 95.8% and 49.6% year-on-year, respectively.
The bigger shift: State-owned capital has anchored the market for years, but industrial capital's move into market-oriented funds is newer. Wuyuan , Matrix Partners China , and Lisi have all advanced new offerings with similar backers.
Who else is in? Wuyuan's new fund drew 100 million CNY from Xiaomi -linked Hanxing Venture Capital , plus entities tied to Liu Qiangdong and TAL Education . Zhihu plans to put 1.5 billion CNY into Lisi's Xingshen Fund. Matrix Partners' Chuangyi Future Fund targets 7 billion CNY and has secured 3.72123 billion CNY so far, with SF Express , East Money , and Vipshop among its backers.
The signal: Industrial giants — once cautious — are now writing large cheques to tech investors, reshaping who funds China's startups. GPs that pair strong track records with deal-sourcing strength are winning the new money.

articles.title_orig: China is Watching Us. Is the U.S. Air Force Still Watching China?
articles.title_zh: China is Watching Us. Is the U.S. Air Force Still Watching China?
articles.content_orig:
A Rockwell B1 Lancer heavy bomber takes off to depart for home at RAF Fairford on Sunday
The US has withdrawn all of its bombers from RAF Fairford, the UK military base at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.
A statement from a Pentagon official confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.
The US did not give a reason for the withdrawal, but it follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences near the base and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
Whitehall sources have not disputed the decision from Washington was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.
The BBC has also been told it was a military rather than a political decision - taken at an operational level - and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts.
The UK's Ministry of Defence has not commented.
Tracking websites showed B-1 bombers flying out of RAF Fairford on Sunday.
The New York Times reported US commanders had received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against RAF Fairford according to two US officials.
The newspaper wrote the new information was part of the same threat warnings from three weeks ago, but officials acted quickly after specific details emerged in the past 24 hours.
The planes reportedly took off while aerial refueling aircraft were still being scrambled to support their flights to the US.
Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but did not provide further details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.
Initially, five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF). All five were UK nationals from London.
They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".
The sixth man, aged 25, was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts. Counter terror police confirmed on Saturday he had also been released on bail.
RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
The withdrawal of the bombers comes as the US tries to recover from the damage inflicted on its aircraft by Iranian precision strikes.
It is technically possible for the US to conduct precision strikes directly from the US without a UK base - like in Operation Midnight Hammer last year.
But the removal of the bombers from RAF Fairford will remove a foothold for the country outside of continental Europe.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
Days after the incident, and before the arrest of the sixth man, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Fox News that it "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor".
Rubio did not provide further details - saying at the time he was limited on what he could say on air.
US President Donald Trump separately said he was "surprised" the five men had been released on bail.
"We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this.
Many B-1 bombers flown from the UK were armed with precision-guided "bunker busting" bombs, with thicker casings to penetrate hardened or buried targets such as weapons stores.
They also carried air-to-surface missiles used against more heavily defended targets deeper inside Iran.
Each bombing mission, depending on the location of the target, would likely have taken around 12 to 15 hours in total there and back, with air-to-air refuelling both ways.
The Pentagon has stressed its bombing aircraft remain able to conduct missions "anywhere, anytime", including through "operations that launch and recover from the continental United States".
Additional reporting by Chris Partridge.

articles.title_orig: FBI arrests ‘Chinese foreign agent’ for spying on Taiwan president’s son
articles.title_zh: FBI arrests ‘Chinese foreign agent’ for spying on Taiwan president’s son
articles.content_orig:
The FBI has arrested a “Chinese foreign agent” at Los Angeles International Airport accused of spying on the Taiwanese president’s son.
Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, was arrested on Sunday before her planned departure to China, the first assistant US attorney for the Central District of California, Bill Essayli, said in a post on X.
Authorities charged Zhang, 34, of Irvine, California, with acting as an unregistered foreign agent.
Zhang surveilled Taiwanese President William Lai Ching-te’s son, the FBI said. The agency did not directly name Zhang’s alleged target, but later shared a news article identifying him as Lai Ting-yu.
The US Justice Department said Zhang travelled to Seattle in 2025 at the behest of Chinese officials. She sent photos, video and license plate information of the Taiwanese leader’s son and his family to China.
Essayli called Zhang a “Chinese foreign agent” and said she “used tradecraft to avoid detection”.
“She never notified the Attorney General she was acting for a foreign government, a federal offense,” he added.
Essayli said Zhang will appear in a Los Angeles federal court on Monday.
William Lai Ching-te and his Democratic Progressive Party say that Taiwan is already an independent country separate from China. Beijing views the island as Chinese territory.
Washington does not have ⁠formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but the US is bound by law to provide the island with the means to ‌defend itself.
Earlier this week, the US delivered two F-16V ⁠Block 70 fighter jets to Taiwan as the island seeks to build its defence capabilities to deter a feared attack by China .
In January, Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged to achieve the “reunification” of China and Taiwan, calling Beijing’s long-held goal “unstoppable”.

articles.title_orig: Crowds gather in Spain for world's biggest human tower contest
articles.title_zh: Crowds gather in Spain for world's biggest human tower contest
articles.content_orig:
Published: 18:43 EDT, 4 October 2026 | Updated: 21:03 EDT, 4 October 2026
Thousands have gathered at a Spanish arena to watch a near-century-old competition which sees teams battle to build the tallest human tower.
Held every two years in an ancient bullfighting ring in Tarragona, the castells competition sees human tower groups from across Catalonia gather to face off.
Some teams built towers of eight human storeys over the weekend, with the Marrecs de Salt team winning Saturday's competition in the Tarraco Arena.
Teams of up to 500 men, women and children compete to build the tallest tower in the exhibition - which can be as many as ten levels tall.
The highest and most complicated tower is dubbed the winner, with some reaching over 40ft tall in recent years.
This year's edition was the competition's 30th outing since its first staging in 1932.
Teams competed in Catalonia's Castells event, which challenged competitors to build the tallest human towers
Held every two years, the competition has been staged 30 times since its inaugural outing in 1932. Pictured: the Castellers de Barcelona team forming a tower
But the Castellers de Barcelona tower collapsed into itself as the red-shirted participants tumbled over
Castells are human towers, which can reach up to ten people tall or over 40ft high
Thousands gathered at the Tarraco Arena, west of Barcelona, to witness the face off
Towers rose out of the crowded arena floor as teams vied to produce the tallest castell
Members of one pink-clad team, the Castellers Joves de Valls, collapsed as their tower failed on Sunday
But others were more successful in the near-century-old Catalonian competition
Members of Castellers Colla Vella wearing red uniforms banded together to form a human tower
Crumbling towers are not uncommon in the competition, as the Castellers Joves de Valls showed
A sea of blue-clad members of the Colla Castellera de Sant Pere i Sant Pau team begin to form a tower
Members of the Castellers Joves de Valls reacted to another team's effort to form a tower this weekend
Originating at the end of the 18th century, castells can be spotted outside the competition in Catalonia's cities and town squares.
In 1867 the choral tune Els Xiquets de Valls by Josep Anselm Clave said 'strength, balance, courage and good judgment' were the key ingredients for a successful tower.
Generally teams work outside competitive spaces to push their own limits, with the Tarragona contest a rare exception.
Castells need a minimum of six levels to be considered as such and each level has its own name.
At the top is the crowner, who signals the tower's completion by raising their arm at the end of its construction.
According to Europeana teams can have any number of members from 100 to 1,000.
Teams are recognisable by their uniforms and are often named for their place of origin, for example Xiquets de Valls, Marrecs de Salt and Castellers de Barcelona.

articles.title_orig: Spain's prime minister calls early elections as pressure mounts over housing crisis
articles.title_zh: Spain's prime minister calls early elections as pressure mounts over housing crisis
articles.content_orig:
PM says vote will take place on 29 November after parliament rejected two of his government’s emergency relief measures
Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez has called a snap election for 29 November, just days after rightwing parties blocked his minority government’s emergency measures on housing amid widespread protests ( 9:10 ).
The election will take place on Sunday, 29 November, the earliest possible date procedurally.
In a fierce address, Sánchez framed the election as choice between “regressing” under a “far-right coalition” or “keeping moving forward” with his progressive administration ( 9:04 , 9:09 , 9:17 ).
He said the election will be about who will guide Spain through a period of disruption amid high political tensions, global instability, climate emergency, and uncertainty posed by the rise of AI ( 9:13 ).
Sam Jones and Ashifa Kassam in Madrid
The government’s efforts to address the housing crisis were set out in two decrees that contained a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.
But the decrees were voted down in congress on Friday by the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence party Junts.
The PP, which is leading the polls but which may need to rely on Vox’s support to form a government, said it had rejected the government’s plans as it believed that construction, and not regulation, was the best way to tackle the crisis.
The rejection of the decrees met with an angry response from the crowds who had gathered outside congress, eliciting boos and cries of “shame” and “Your profits; our misery”.
Long-brewing fury over the high cost of renting and the precarious nature of many tenancies exploded late last month following the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal , an 87-year-old woman who was removed from the home in Madrid where she had lived for 70 years. Abascal said she could not possibly afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.
Her plight prompted tens of thousands of people to take to the streets to protest, and saw a huge tent camp reminiscent of the 2011 indignados movement spring up in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square.
Over the weekend, large demonstrations were held across the country as protesters stepped up their demands for urgent action on the housing crisis. Authorities said 70,000 people had taken part in a protest in Madrid on Saturday, while organisers put the figure at 500,000.
Although polls consistently place the PP well ahead of Sánchez’s Spanish Socialist Workers’ party – and show that support for Vox is growing – the prime minister may be hoping that the focus on housing, and the right’s rejection of his government’s plans to address the crisis, will mobilise leftwing voters.
The housing issue has also served to deflect attention from the government’s much-criticised handling of the continuing crisis in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta , which was sparked when around 70,000 people crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours.
Pedro Sánchez is clearly hoping to mobilise voters around the housing crisis and the broader message of home, with opinion polls suggesting his left-wing government might otherwise struggle to retain power.
The conservative People’s Party (PP) looks most likely to take first place and could be take power alongside the far-right Vox party. Polling currently puts the PP on roughly 32-34%, well clear of Sánchez’s Socialists (PSOE) on 26-27%. Vox sits in third place on 18-19%, comfortably ahead of smaller left-wing rivals Sumar (5-6%) and Podemos (2-3%).
Vox’s potential entry into a governing coalition would mark the first time a far-right party has held power in Spain since the end of the Franco dictatorship in 1975.
A defeat for Sánchez would bring down one of western Europe’s few remaining left-leaning administrations at a time when populist and conservative parties are making gains across the continent.
Sánchez’s decision also brings forward one of Europe’s most closely watched electoral contests – originally slated for 2027 alongside major votes in France , Italy, and Poland.
The conservative People’s Party is very pleased with the announcement.
“At last,” they say on their X, with a slick election video – set to the EU’s anthem “Ode to Joy” – to go along with it.
Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez has called a snap election for 29 November, just days after rightwing parties blocked his minority government’s emergency measures on housing amid widespread protests ( 9:10 ).
The election will take place on Sunday, 29 November, the earliest possible date procedurally.
In a fierce address, Sánchez framed the election as choice between “regressing” under a “far-right coalition” or “keeping moving forward” with his progressive administration ( 9:04 , 9:09 , 9:17 ).
He said the election will be about who will guide Spain through a period of disruption amid high political tensions, global instability, climate emergency, and uncertainty posed by the rise of AI ( 9:13 ).
In a very political conclusion of his speech, Sánchez says the voters will have to decide whether they want the country to “regress or keep moving forward,” as he paints the opposition as “a far-right coalition that offers no proposals,” but only wants to “repeal and curtail the rights and freedoms of the last eight years.”
“I have faith in my fellow citizens because I know you are a brave and compassionate people who rise to meet challenges and are unafraid to be the first, or the only ones, to step up and stand on the right side of history. We will work to earn your trust, to inspire hope, and to win again. ”
Sánchez says “to do more, we need to renew and expand public support” for the “deep reforms” required.
“We must mobilise and secure a much broader progressive majority in parliament – one that allows us to overcome the elites … and continue transforming Spain ,” he says.
“ The time has come for the Spanish people to decide what future you want for yourselves and for your country, ” he says. “It’s now up to you.”
He says the world is facing “a highly complex era” with “great tensions,” climate emergency, and social and technological changes, brought about by the rise of AI.
But, he says, it can also be a great opportunity.
“You, the Spanish people, must decide what role you wish to play in this era, and what role you want Spain to play,” he says.
Sánchez calls snap election for 29 November.
Sánchez says his government had to deal with “a highly contentious” parliament where “many confuse reaching agreements with betrayal,” and deal with “powerful economic and social elites” who want to influence Spain’s future without being ever elected.
He says his government had to deal with “the worst opposition in history,” as he says they never wanted to show any responsibility for the state, but kept challenging and questioning the legitimacy of the government.
He sums up what he says are his government’s achievements with Spain becoming the fastest-growing economy in the EU, recording a purchasing power increase “at three times” of France and Germany , but also with social and energy reforms.
“We have done everything in our power to defend the interests of the Spanish people,” he says.
He also points to his government’s decisions on foreign policy, with continued support for Ukraine , and work in the EU and at the UN, “fighting tyrants, oligarchs and speculators.”
He says it all transformed Spain into “a global example.”
Sánchez opens by saying that just over three years ago the electorate chose a progressive government following “the path of transformative ambition and social justice” that his government has been on since 2018 – despite various “unprecedented” emergencies and international challenges.

articles.title_orig: Monday is World Teachers’ Day, honoring educators and marking 60-year milestone
articles.title_zh: Monday is World Teachers’ Day, honoring educators and marking 60-year milestone
articles.content_orig:
BEND, Ore. (KTVZ) -- Students and families across Central Oregon can join people around the world Monday in recognizing the educators who help children learn, grow, and prepare for their futures.
World Teachers’ Day is observed each year on October 5th to celebrate teachers and draw attention to the support, training, and working conditions they need to succeed.
The date commemorates the adoption of the 1966 International Labour Organization and UNESCO Recommendation Concerning the Status of Teachers. The landmark document established international standards related to teacher preparation, recruitment, employment, professional development, rights, and responsibilities.
This year’s observance marks the recommendation’s 60th anniversary. The 2026 theme is “Standing with teachers: 60 years of protecting the profession, advancing its status and shaping our futures.”
UNESCO says this year’s events will examine challenges affecting the status of teachers and call on communities and policymakers to protect, promote, and elevate the profession.
Teachers’ influence often extends well beyond lessons in reading, writing, math, and science. Educators also help students build confidence, explore career paths, solve problems, and navigate important stages of their lives.
For Central Oregon families, Monday offers a simple opportunity to thank a teacher, counselor, or other school employee who has made a difference.

articles.title_orig: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
articles.title_zh: Ethiopian rebel forces withdraw from Tigray regional capital
articles.content_orig:
Rebel forces in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region have said they have temporarily withdrawn from the regional capital, Mekelle, as fighting with the national army moves towards the city.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has been running the region, said its decision to relocate was made because of concerns about risks to civilians.
Two residents in Mekelle told the BBC that pro-government forces now control the city and TPLF fighters have abandoned it. One resident also said mobile phone services appear to have resumed in parts of the city.
Fighting has erupted in recent weeks between the TPLF and allied groups and government forces in parts of the northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.
The development marks a major shift in the conflict and raises concerns among observers that the fighting could further destabilise the Horn of Africa, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries.
The US Department of State called for "restraint" and "dialogue" on all sides ahead of a diplomatic meeting about the conflict in Egypt on Sunday with leaders from some of Ethiopia's neighbours.
The presidents of Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan - which all have strained relations with Ethiopia - met on Sunday in the Egyptian coastal city of El-Alamein.
They called for "respecting the sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity of states" and the resolution of disputes through "peaceful means".
Ethiopia accuses Egypt, Eritrea and Sudan of supporting the Tigray rebels, which they deny.
Tigray residents have been trying to recover from a devastating two-year civil war that ended in 2022 when the African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides.
However, in the last six months there has been a worsening of relations, with both sides accusing each other of violating the agreement.
Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.
The civil war was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
On Friday, neighbours Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations with each other after Addis Ababa accused Asmara of supporting a new rebel alliance - an allegation that it denied.
Ethiopia has also accused Egypt of supporting the rebels, leading to the expulsion of an Egyptian diplomat, which Cairo responded to by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period.
The United Nations has warned that the deteriorating security situation in northern Ethiopia is severely disrupting humanitarian work and has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.
Ethiopia and Egypt have been embroiled in a longer dispute over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam built on the River Nile, which Cairo fears could reduce its share of water from the river.
On Sunday, the four leaders meeting in Egypt affirmed respect sovereignty and non-interference in the internal affairs of the regional states, while calling for adherence to international law over the usage of Nile waters.
In a joint statement, they rejected "unilateral measures" that could harm downstream countries, in an apparent reference to tensions over Ethiopia's dam.

articles.title_orig: Athens World War II soldier laid to rest 82 years after death
articles.title_zh: Athens World War II soldier laid to rest 82 years after death
articles.content_orig:
MARIETTA - When Spencer Rutter got the call that after more than eight decades, his uncle's remains had been identified, it didn't take him long to tell the Army where they should end up.
"They belong at Maplewood Cemetery in Glouster, with his parents," Rutter, an 83-year-old Marietta resident, said.
According to the federal Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency, Army Air Forces Sgt. Myron Lee Yaw, an Athens County native, was identified on June 25. He served in the 828th Bombardment Squadron, 485th Bombardment Group, and was killed the day after Christmas in 1944 when the B-24J Liberator on which he was the ball turret gunner was struck by anti-aircraft fire and crashed near the village of Korzonek, Poland.
It's not the homecoming Rutter's grandparents envisioned when their son went overseas to serve in the Army Air Forces. But it's one his mother, Betty Jane Rutter, Yaw's sister, hoped for as the years went on.
A DPAA release says an archaeological survey of the crash site was completed in 2018. Rutter said his mother provided a DNA sample that year. Though she passed away in 2019, her sample eventually led to the positive identification of her brother's remains.
"She knew they had remains, and they probably had his remains," Rutter said. "She would have been beside herself" to know it was confirmed.
Rutter said his mother was extremely close to his Uncle Lee, one of two brothers she lost in the war. And Lee Yaw was a doting uncle who was so excited to have a nephew that Rutter wound up being the mascot on his uncle's plane. An image painted on the plane featured a baby wearing boxing gloves and the name "Butch," his uncle's nickname for him.
"I was the inspiration for nose art on an airplane," Rutter said. "If he had survived the war, I would have been one spoiled nephew."
Yaw's remains were returned to Ohio on Sept. 25 and escorted from the airport in Columbus back to Athens County. A funeral was held on Saturday.
Evan Bevins can be reached at ebevins@newsandsentinel.com.

articles.title_orig: Asian stocks rise as weak U.S. jobs data eases Fed hike bets; Japan surges
articles.title_zh: Asian stocks rise as weak U.S. jobs data eases Fed hike bets; Japan surges
articles.content_orig:
Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved
A person walks in front of an electronic stock board showing Japan's Nikkei index at a securities firm Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, in Tokyo. (AP Photo/Eugene Hoshiko)
TOKYO – Tokyo shares advanced Monday at the start of a busy week for U.S. economic updates, while stock prices were little changed in Sydney and Hong Kong.
Investors have been encouraged by easing worries over inflation, which reduces the likelihood of another rate hike by the Federal Reserve.
Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 jumped 2.3% in afternoon trading to 69,901.70. Earlier in the day, it marked its first foray above 70,000 points in three months.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was little changed, edging up less than 0.1% to 8,686.40. Hong Kong's Hang Seng was virtually unchanged at 23,976.15.
Trading was closed in Shanghai and South Korea for national holidays.
Interest in shares related to artificial intelligence drew buying interest. In Japan, Tokyo Electron gained 5.2% and technology investment giant SoftBank Group's shares gained 3.1%.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., or TSMC, climbed 3%.
Last week, U.S. stocks finished near an all-time high after the latest update on the U.S. job market helped to alleviate worries about higher inflation .
The S&P 500 rose 0.7% and pulled within 1% of its record set in August . The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.5%, and the Nasdaq composite gained 1.2%.
The U.S. government said employers across the country added 29,000 more jobs to their payrolls than they cut last month. That was fewer than economists expected and a slowdown from August’s net hiring rate of 133,000.
Markets took that to mean the Federal Reserve will be less likely to raise its benchmark rate. The Federal Reserve recently raised its main interest rate for the first time in three years to try to rein in the painful increases for the cost of living.
The pullback in expectations for an October rate hike helped calm the bond market.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury briefly dropped all the way below 5.17%. That was down from its peak near 5.35% on Thursday, when it and other longer-term yields neared their highest levels in two decades.
The 10-year Treasury yield bounced back to 5.28%, more than 0.10 percentage points above its bottom for the day. That in turn helped U.S. stocks pare their own gains.
In energy trading, benchmark U.S. crude lost 1.55% to $89.70 a barrel. Brent crude, the international standard, declined 0.99% to $101.24.
Oil prices have been yo-yoing lately amid uncertainty about how the war with Iran will reshape the global oil industry.
In currency trading in Asia Monday, the U.S. dollar fell to 157.76 Japanese yen from 157.83 yen. The euro cost $1.1189, down from $1.1257.

articles.title_orig: An Invitation From the Prophet to the World
articles.title_zh: An Invitation From the Prophet to the World
articles.content_orig:
In his closing remarks during the Sunday afternoon session of general conference on October 4, 2026, President Dallin H. Oaks of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints invited the world to participate in the Salt Lake Temple Celebration, either in person or virtually.
As part of his special invitation, President Oaks highlighted a new video series. “Following this session of general conference, the first episode of a dynamic video series, ‘Dedicate,’ will premiere worldwide in multiple languages,” he said. “More will come in the months ahead, including a virtual tour of the Salt Lake Temple.”
“Dedicate” follows seven young adults from Brazil, France, Ghana, Japan, Mexico, the Philippines and the United States as they explore the Salt Lake Temple, meet with Church leaders and navigate questions of faith, purpose and spiritual growth. Throughout the series, they share personal experiences as they deepen their understanding of temples and strengthen their faith in Jesus Christ.
The first episode is now available on the Church’s YouTube channel and will be added to the Gospel Library app in the coming days.
Four additional “Dedicate” episodes will be released every Sunday at 8 a.m. MDT through November 1, with the sixth and final episode set to air in spring 2027. In addition to English, episodes are available in Cantonese, Chinese (Traditional), French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish.
For the first time since 1893, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints will open the doors of the newly renovated Salt Lake Temple. The public is invited to experience the beauty of this sacred space from April 5, 2027, to October 1, 2027. This significant six-month event is for everyone, whether they participate in person on Temple Square or from elsewhere in the world through virtual experiences.
The celebration will include the open house tour, exhibits, performances, films, service opportunities, and other experiences centered on the Savior of the world. During the celebration, guests will also find opportunities to enjoy live music, exhibits, and other events. articles.title_orig: Starlight interrupted: celebrating World Space Week
articles.title_zh: Starlight interrupted: celebrating World Space Week
articles.content_orig:
5 October 2026: World Space Week
Human interest in space has been multifaceted, ranging from the deep-seated desire to seek out the origins of our existence to the search for extraterrestrial life and habitable worlds. Prior to the modern technology used to explore space today, ancient civilizations tracked the movement of stars, planets and eclipses to measure time and to create reliable calendars dictating the best time for planting crops.
However, the frontiers of human ambition would not truly be pushed until years later, during the Space Race , a 20th-century Cold War competition between the United States and the Soviet Union for global power, political dominance, and technological superiority. On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite into space, and only four years later, Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space by completing a single orbit of Earth aboard the Vostok 3KA-3, two achievements that together shocked American scientists.
In 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first man on the moon, arriving on Apollo 11, famously uttering the words “That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.” In 1999, the UN created World Space Week to celebrate the contributions of space technology towards the betterment of humanity, choosing the dates of October 4 to commemorate the launch of Sputnik 1, until October 10, which was the entry into force of the Outer Space Treaty (OST) 1967.
Humanity’s innate curiosity and hunger for knowledge have driven achievements once deemed impossible, from lunar landings to exploring the deepest corners of the cosmos. However, in recent decades, this relentless outward push has become a double-edged sword. In September 2026, Department of the Air Force Secretary Troy Meink publicly acknowledged that the US Space Force had deployed weapons into space, although he withheld specific details about the nature of the weapons.
The Carnegie Endowment for International Peace has stated that whether the US’ deployment of a weapon into space would directly contravene Article IV of the OST which prohibits the placement of nuclear weapons into space, boils down to the nature of the weapons itself. In response to the US’ acknowledgment of its deployment of weapons into space, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun condemned the US for expanding its military build-up in space, stating that China “opposed any arms race in outer space or any attempt to weaponize it and turn it into a war zone.”
The passing into law of the US Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act ( SPACE Act 2015 ) which grants US citizens and commercial entities the legal right to possess, own, transport, use, and sell any asteroid that they recover has been criticized by scholars such as Professor Stephan Hobe who state that the legislation violates Article II of the OST, which was designed to prevent any form of territorial exclusivity over celestial bodies.
The US has defended the Act, with President Trump in 2020 signing Executive Order 13914 , affirming that the country does not view outer space as “global commons” and that Americans should have the unfettered right to engage in commercial use of resources in outer space.  Although it is a private entity and not a nation, therefore making it not directly subject to the OST, both Russia and Iran have formally complained at UN meetings that Elon Musk’s Starlink’s mega-constellations violate the spirit of Article IX of the OST, which requires countries to explore space with cooperation and respect the interests of other countries in doing so.
As the world celebrates World Space Week, it is important to acknowledge how far humanity has come and how much further we have to go in ensuring that space exploration remains both equitable and ethical.
Justice Louis Brandeis died
On October 5, 1941, US Supreme Court Justice Louis Brandeis died at the age of 84.

Brandeis had become the first Jewish justice on the United States Supreme Court in 1916 after a hotly-contested nomination battle. Learn more about Louis Brandeis from Oyez.

articles.title_orig: California woman arrested and accused of spying on Taiwan president’s son for China
articles.title_zh: California woman arrested and accused of spying on Taiwan president’s son for China
articles.content_orig:
The FBI ⁠arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport before she left for China, the agency said
US authorities arrested a California ⁠woman on ​Sunday, accusing her of spying on the son of Taiwan’s president at the behest of Chinese officials, the FBI said.
The FBI ⁠arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday before her planned departure to China , the agency said in a ⁠statement. Authorities charged Zhang, 34, of Irvine, California, with acting as an unregistered foreign agent.
Zhang surveilled a ​son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, the ‌FBI alleged. The agency ‌did not directly name Zhang’s alleged target, but later shared a New York Post report ‌identifying him as Lai Ting-yu, a US resident.
Taiwan’s presidential office described Zhang’s alleged actions as a “typical case of transnational repression” and thanked the US government for protecting Taiwanese citizens.
“Our country expresses the strongest condemnation of such barbaric conduct that disregards human rights and the sovereignty of nations,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
China’s foreign ministry did not respond to ‌a request for comment.
The Justice Department alleged Zhang travelled to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese officials and sent them photos, video and licence plate information of the Taiwanese president’s son and his family.
Zhang used tradecraft to avoid detection ⁠and never notified Washington that she was acting for a foreign government, Bill Essayli, ​the first assistant US ​attorney for the Central District of ​California, alleged in a statement.
It was not immediately clear whether Zhang ​had a defence attorney. She ‌will appear on ​Monday in a ​Los Angeles federal court, Essayli said.
Lai and his Democratic Progressive Party champion Taiwan’s separate identity from China, a position that frequently angers Beijing, which views the island as ​Chinese territory. Lai says only Taiwan’s people can decide their future.
Washington does not have formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but the US is the island’s most important international backer and weapons supplier.

articles.title_orig: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
articles.title_zh: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
articles.content_orig:
Wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse and its numbers dwindled across New Zealand due to predators and habitat loss
The population of New Zealand’s endemic wētāpunga – believed to be the world’s heaviest insect – is officially “recovering” thanks to a groundbreaking breeding programme that has overseen the release of 11,000 insects into the wild.
“The future of wētāpunga is looking bright,” said Dr Chris Green, an honorary researcher at the department of conservation, who documented the success of the project for the New Zealand Journal of Zoology. Green co-authored a report released on 2 October that outlines the success of the breeding programme.
“Eleven thousand individuals for release is extraordinary and outstanding.”
A female wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse. Its body can grow up to 10cm long (nearly 4in) and its leg span can be as wide as 20cm.
It is the largest of 70 wētā species and was once found across parts of the North Island before predation from introduced species and habitat loss contributed to their decline. By the 1990s, they were considered “endangered” and are now presumed extinct in the wild on New Zealand’s mainland. The insects reside primarily on a smattering of predator-free islands in Auckland’s Hauraki Gulf and off the coast of Northland.
But their fortune is starting to change. Over the past 15 years, tens of thousands of wētāpunga have been bred at Butterfly Creek, a wildlife facility, and Auckland zoo, enabling the release of wētāpunga across new predator-free islands and some mainland reserves north of Auckland.
Butterfly Creek and Auckland zoo established husbandry techniques that, over time, have been scaled up to rear large numbers of wētāpunga in communal creches. The young wētāpunga – or nymphs – are fed a three-part diet of fresh foliage, fish flake protein and leaf litter. The protein is “critical” to the survival of the youngest nymphs, Green said.
Once big enough to protect themselves, the insects are transferred to their new habitat. The efforts have led to 45 separate translocations to wild habitats, which is “a very high number in any recovery of a species”, Green said.
Monitoring on two islands has shown wētāpunga have established self-sustaining populations, with fourth and fifth generations born there, in what Green said was a marker of success. As a result, the species’ conservation status has improved from “nationally endangered” to “nationally recovering”.
“It’s so exciting, because we are unable to report that for so many of our other threatened species,” Green said.
New Zealand is particularly vulnerable to species decline because of its high rates of endemism and problems with introduced pests.
Green said the country was at the forefront of invertebrate recovery work and he was not aware of any other examples of breeding programmes working to this scale, or with such success.
By documenting the project’s work, he hopes other institutions will feel encouraged to develop their own programmes.
“That’s the extraordinary aspect of it – that we’ve been successful,” he said. “If other institutions can get into that sort of position, then there can be huge benefit for threatened species in New Zealand.”

articles.title_orig: The Return of Middle East Oil
articles.title_zh: The Return of Middle East Oil
articles.content_orig:
Gulf oil producers, with considerable support from the US Navy, are jamming crude through the Strait of Hormuz, right under Iran’s nose.
Oil and petroleum product flows through the critical chokepoint averaged 13.1 million barrels per day last week, according to Kpler, a marine data tracking service. That’s just under 80% of the 17.1 million barrels that had traveled through the strait each day before the war broke out.
Total Middle Eastern crude flows – through Hormuz and around it – are even more impressive: back to 98% of prewar levels, according to JPMorgan.
“Given such a strong volume passing through the strait, it is clear Iran is losing its influence over it,” said Matt Smith, director of commodity research at Kpler.
That milestone is the product of a complex operation involving military-escorted shuttles engaging in surreptitious “dark” transits of the strait that has helped restore significant flows for Middle East oil producers over the past couple of months. Adding to the recent strait traffic is a return of oil from Saudi Arabia that had been primarily diverted to the Red Sea until Iran-allied Houthis attacked a major Saudi oil pipeline earlier this month.
The crucial question: How long can the status quo hold up? The US military is expending tremendous resources in the region just to get oil through – all while global inventories continue to shrink toward operational lows and the price of fuel remains at or near record highs.
Meanwhile, Iran, backed into a corner, is starting to fight back.
The oil market seems to have unlimited tricks up its sleeve to get oil to customers – despite the world’s biggest-ever supply shock .
Global oil inventories have tumbled by around 2 billion barrels during the course of the Iran war, according to JPMorgan, but the market has held out. It has accomplished that remarkable feat through innovative solutions like pipeline diversions and the military-aided shuttle service, but also with an increase in production from outside the Gulf. And, crucially, a significant global decline in demand.
Oil prices remain uncomfortably high, but the market’s creative solutions have prevented crude from approaching its record high set in 2008.
Nevertheless, the current situation in Hormuz simply cannot last forever.
Oil is a physical product, and eventually market forces will take over. With more crude coming out of oil inventories than going in, eventually the market will reach its long-predicted and feared tipping point, at which point stockpiles are insufficient to satisfy demand. When that happens, oil prices will need to rocket higher to sap enough demand to keep the balance in check.
No one knows exactly when that will happen.
Natasha Kaneva, JPMorgan’s head of global commodities strategy, stopped trying to bother guessing.
“For the first time since the start of the Iran conflict, we don’t have a baseline view,” Kaneva conceded two weeks ago in a note to clients. “We simply don’t know how to model the endgame.”
The key, she argues, is no more about how long the war lasts but how long the market is able to clear the physical oil customers demand. Those two may be related: Without a true resolution in the Strait of Hormuz, the world will have to hold out hope that the market’s inventories hold out.
All of these market mechanics make for interesting economic theory and supply-and-demand analysis. But, practically speaking, it has meant very little for people’s wallets.
Oil has hovered above $90 a barrel all month and spent most of September north of $100. Gas prices are near their highest price of the war. Diesel, contending with the effects of the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war, blew past its previous record earlier this month and is priced well above $6 a gallon.
And crude’s return to normalcy hasn’t flowed downstream to petroleum products yet. Refined product flows out of the Middle East remain at just 58% of prewar levels, according to JPMorgan, underlining the considerable constraints remaining for gas and diesel.
The fact that oil hasn’t gone to $150 (at least not yet) is cold comfort to Americans who have to spend $100 to fill up their tanks or businesses that have to pay high fuel surcharges to get their deliveries.
Diesel costs more than $6 a gallon for the first time. Here’s how that affects you
Without much new information to go on, the market has traded in recent months on the potential prospects for a peace deal. President Donald Trump’s frequent comments throughout the war about a supposed looming deal with Iran to reopen the strait has had an outsized impact on oil prices – far more than actual physical barrels of oil.
That changed a bit earlier this month when the Houthis bombed the Saudi East-West pipeline, temporarily shutting down roughly 7 million barrels of oil flowing to the Red Sea – more than half of which had been diverted from the Strait of Hormuz. Oil neared $110 a barrel before the Saudis found yet another trick up their sleeves, proving remarkably adaptable to the situation and shifting oil back through the Strait of Hormuz.
Meanwhile, satellite imagery from Sunday showed all seven berths open at two key ports in Yanbu and Al Muajjiz on Saudi Arabia’s West Coast, signaling that the East-West pipeline has ramped back up, according to Kpler.
So, can these volumes be sustained?
“Higher crossings should not be mistaken for improved safety – rather, they reflect the industry’s increasing ability to operate under sustained risk,” Kaneva said Tuesday.
For example, she noted that insurance costs remain astronomically high. Insurers are currently valuing the largest class of 5- to 10-year-old oil tankers at $150 million, even though it costs $135 million to build a new one.
Iran, unable to get its own oil through the strait because of a US naval blockade, and losing its key source of economic leverage, has ramped up its attacks on oil tankers transiting the Gulf.
“Not surprisingly, attacks on tankers have become more common as Iran looks to deter transits,” Smith noted. “We should expect this to persist as Iran seeks to regain its grip on the strait.”
So the oil market remains at an impasse: an increasingly taxing US military effort keeping up an unsustainable status quo that continues to keep prices high for businesses and consumers.

articles.title_orig: Brazil’s presidential race: Three key takeaways from the first round
articles.title_zh: Brazil’s presidential race: Three key takeaways from the first round
articles.content_orig:
Brazil’s closely watched presidential election is heading to a second round between leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, prolonging a deeply polarised race with major implications for the country and the wider region.
Brazil’s electoral court confirmed on Sunday that the two candidates will advance to a run-off on October 25 after neither won the majority needed to secure the presidency outright, with Bolsonaro leading at 55.8 million votes to Lula’s almost 53.2 million.
Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term after a political career spanning nearly five decades.
Bolsonaro, 45, is the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro and is trying to return his father’s right-wing movement to power, even as the former president serves a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election.
The election comes at a pivotal time for Latin America’s largest economy. Brazilians are grappling with concerns over crime and the cost of living, while the country faces an increasingly tense relationship with the United States. The vote is also being closely watched across a region that has shifted sharply to the right in a series of recent elections.
While a second round was widely expected, the first-round result did not play out quite as pollsters had predicted.
Here are some of the key takeaways from the election so far.
With nearly 99 percent of votes reported, Bolsonaro had about 47 percent of valid votes, compared with 44.9 percent for Lula. Neither reached the 50 percent threshold needed to win in the first round.
That sets up another Lula-Bolsonaro showdown, four years after Lula narrowly defeated former President Jair Bolsonaro. This time, he will face the former president’s eldest son.
The race could be extremely close, as polling ahead of Sunday’s vote suggested Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro were roughly tied in a potential run-off.
That puts voters who backed one of the other 10 candidates in the first round at the centre of the fight for the presidency over the next three weeks.
Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, who together received about 5.3 million votes, have previously said they will not endorse either candidate in the run-off.
Most polls leading up to election day predicted the race would be pushed into the second round, but had Lula finishing the first round ahead of Bolsonaro.
Instead, Bolsonaro emerged with a lead of two percentage points, raising questions about why the final polls underestimated his support.
On Sunday, Bolsonaro said the results showed that Brazilians want change.
Analysts told the Reuters news agency that Bolsonaro may have benefitted from “protest votes” from people who may have preferred another candidate but saw defeating Lula as the priority. Many had been expected to shift their support to Bolsonaro only in a second round, meaning this could have consequences for his support in three weeks.
“The protest vote foreshadows what is to come in the run-off,” political analyst Rafael Favetti told Reuters. “While this should benefit Flavio Bolsonaro now, his growth potential in the second round drops precisely because that support has already been front-loaded.”
After the results came in, Lula said the votes were “unexpected” but that he would come back stronger in the run-off.
“I admit, I was convinced I would win in the first round. The game is about to start. We are in extra time. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people,” the 80-year-old said.
Bolsonaro’s surprising performance in the first round was part of a broader show of strength for Brazil’s right.
Right-wing parties, led by Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL), were performing strongly in both houses of Congress, with the PL on track to emerge as the largest force in the Chamber of Deputies and making gains in the Senate.
This included victories for other members of the Bolsonaro family , including former First Lady Michelle Bolsonaro, Flavio’s stepmother, who won a Senate seat in the Federal District, her first elected office.
His brother, Carlos Bolsonaro, was elected to the Senate in Santa Catarina.
The results show that the political movement built around former President Jair Bolsonaro – known as “bolsonarista” – remains a powerful electoral force, even with the former president barred from running himself.
“The fact that far-right candidates for the legislature have exceeded all expectations suggests a deeper popular grounding for the bolsonarista project than many expected,” Andre Pagliarini, an assistant professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and author of a book on Lula, told Al Jazeera.
“Millions of Brazilians right now evidently feel the right best reflects their values and vision for the future,” he added.
The congressional results matter beyond election night, too. Both houses were already dominated by conservative lawmakers, and a stronger right-wing presence could make it even harder for Lula to push through his agenda if he wins another term.
A Bolsonaro victory, meanwhile, could give him more room to pursue his own priorities, including his pledge to seek an amnesty for his father.

articles.title_orig: US removes all bombers from RAF Fairford base
articles.title_zh: US removes all bombers from RAF Fairford base
articles.content_orig:
The US has withdrawn all of its bombers from RAF Fairford, the UK military base at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.
A statement from a Pentagon official confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.
The US did not give a reason for the withdrawal, but it follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences near the base and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
Whitehall sources have not disputed the decision from Washington was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.
The BBC has also been told it was a military rather than a political decision - taken at an operational level - and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts.
The UK's Ministry of Defence has not commented.
Tracking websites showed B-1 bombers flying out of RAF Fairford on Sunday.
The New York Times reported US commanders had received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against RAF Fairford according to two US officials.
The newspaper wrote the new information was part of the same threat warnings from three weeks ago, but officials acted quickly after specific details emerged in the past 24 hours.
The planes reportedly took off while aerial refueling aircraft were still being scrambled to support their flights to the US.
Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but did not provide further details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.
Initially, five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF). All five were UK nationals from London.
They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".
The sixth man, aged 25, was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts. Counter terror police confirmed on Saturday he had also been released on bail.
RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
The withdrawal of the bombers comes as the US tries to recover from the damage inflicted on its aircraft by Iranian precision strikes.
It is technically possible for the US to conduct precision strikes directly from the US without a UK base - like in Operation Midnight Hammer last year.
But the removal of the bombers from RAF Fairford will remove a foothold for the country outside of continental Europe.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
Days after the incident, and before the arrest of the sixth man, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Fox News that it "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor".
Rubio did not provide further details - saying at the time he was limited on what he could say on air.
US President Donald Trump separately said he was "surprised" the five men had been released on bail.
"We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this.
Many B-1 bombers flown from the UK were armed with precision-guided "bunker busting" bombs, with thicker casings to penetrate hardened or buried targets such as weapons stores.
They also carried air-to-surface missiles used against more heavily defended targets deeper inside Iran.
Each bombing mission, depending on the location of the target, would likely have taken around 12 to 15 hours in total there and back, with air-to-air refuelling both ways.
The Pentagon has stressed its bombing aircraft remain able to conduct missions "anywhere, anytime", including through "operations that launch and recover from the continental United States".

articles.title_orig: Spain protests flare after housing bill rejected: Will it cause snap poll?
articles.title_zh: Spain protests flare after housing bill rejected: Will it cause snap poll?
articles.content_orig:
Tens of thousands of people have rallied across Spain as protests have spread since the conservative-dominated parliament rejected a bill proposing measures to tackle a housing crisis.
Parliament on Friday voted down two decrees proposed by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s minority left-wing coalition government that were intended to address the housing crisis.
The protests erupted late last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home of 70 years in the capital, Madrid. Maria del Carmen Abascal’s eviction came after an international investment fund bought her building and hiked the rent.
Local media reports have suggested that Sanchez could call snap elections for as early as November after watching the strength of Saturday’s protests across the country. Spain’s current legislative term is set to end next summer.
Will the housing crisis trigger snap elections? Here’s what we know:
The emergency measures proposed by Spain’s leftist government to tackle the country’s housing affordability crisis failed to pass on Friday.
The government had proposed two measures to protect renters in the country. The first decree was meant to stop evictions of vulnerable people, make real estate speculation harder, impose tighter restrictions on short-term leases and provide tax incentives to encourage renting and the construction of housing.
The second decree proposed making leases automatically renew when they are set to expire, essentially making them indefinite. A property owner would have to pay a tenant 12 months of rent to break the contract.
Sanchez, who leads a coalition government composed of his Socialist Party and the far-left Sumar, ⁠appealed to lawmakers in the run-up to the vote to put aside political calculations and pressure.
“Think about ordinary people, about those who most need the protection of public institutions. Think about the millions of young people who ⁠cannot afford to ⁠move out of their parents’ homes. Think about the families living with the constant ⁠anxiety of ever-rising rents,” he said before the voting.
But his government’s proposed measures were shot down by the majority of ⁠the 350-seat lower house of parliament.
The right-wing ⁠Catalan separatist ⁠party Junts refused to back the housing decrees, saying they would ultimately tighten the housing market. The centre-right Popular Party and far-right Vox also voted against the measures.
Miriam Nogueras of Junts argued the decrees would lead only to owners removing their properties from the rental market and thus driving up prices even further.
“If they really wanted to protect people, collar the vulture funds, and reactivate housing, they would have already done it. They’ve had eight years,” she added on X, referring to Sanchez’s government.
Health Minister Monica Garcia said on X that the right-wing parties “have voted for a feudal economy in which a minority extracts the salary from a majority that works for their luxuries. And they do it against their own voters, who also suffer increasingly high rents, live in fear that the contract will end and can even be evicted.”
“Today the right has given rent-seeking a parliamentary majority that it doesn’t have on the street, but it’s going to pay for it sooner rather than later,” she added.
Before the parliamentary vote, Marta Soler Gallart, head of the Department of Sociology at the University of Barcelona, explained that neither of the two decrees addressed the housing problem in the medium or long term.
“Models such as Vienna’s with its low rents are cited in support of these decrees, but it is overlooked that the Vienna model and others have low rents because of their long history of creating and maintaining public social housing,” Soler Gallart told Al Jazeera on September 30.
“In Spain, however, public funds are invested in social housing which, after a while, the recipients sell at market price.”
Soler Gallart also said the new measures disadvantage landlords with small or few properties by extending five-year tenancy agreements by a further two years and by providing an indefinite extension of their leases.
“However, these extensions are not compulsory if the landlord can prove that they need the property for their own use,” she said.
Protests erupted across Spain in late September after 87-year-old Abascal was evicted from her home. The investment fund that bought her building hiked her rent by more than 200 percent to roughly $1,880 a month, a move aimed at pushing out the long-term tenant to make way for lucrative tourist apartments.
In recent years, Spain has seen protests against mass tourism, which has been linked to the housing crisis and soaring cost of living. Spain is the second most visited country in the world, attracting 97 million tourists last year.
While Abascal has returned to her home, according to her representatives, she has become the face of the country’s housing crisis, and people across Spain have been demanding the government address the issue.
Angered by parliament’s rejection of the government measures, tens of thousands of people took to the streets.
“It’s a shame,” Nando de Anguulo, 26, who joined Saturday’s protest in Madrid, told the Reuters news agency.
“It only proves that it is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.”
While the protests were mostly peaceful, in the southeastern city of Valencia, police fired rubber bullets and tear gas to break up demonstrations. About 30 protesters managed to get inside the City of Arts and Sciences, a landmark cultural building, before police removed them.
Meanwhile, in Madrid, Spanish police arrested three members of a far-right group and fired rubber bullets on Saturday night.
Far-right activists, some of whom performed Nazi salutes, tried to reach demonstrators camped out in the Puerta del Sol, a central square in the Spanish capital, the Spanish government said.
Valeria Racu, a spokesperson for the Tenants’ Union, said Saturday’s rallies revealed “a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time and energy that is showing that eight days of people’s power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government”.
“Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” Racu added.
Housing is a sensitive issue in Spain because it impacts how people vote. The average rent in the country has almost doubled in the past 10 years. The average price per square metre has risen from 8.20 euros (about $9.08 at the time) in 2016 to 15.1 euros ($17.15) this year, according to the real estate website Idealista.
In an October 1 article for Vanity Fair, Spanish journalist Jorge Dioni Lopez noted that after eight years in power, housing is what is causing Sanchez to lose support among educated young people, children of the middle classes.
“The government faces a difficult situation. Firstly, because most of the relevant powers lie with other levels of government. Secondly, because Spain is a nation of homeowners. Unlike in other European countries, almost all the public housing that has been built has ended up in private hands, and historically, homeownership has been more attractive than renting,” he wrote.
“Housing is our savings system and also the primary means of transmitting wealth between generations,” he added.
After Spain’s parliament rejected the government’s housing reform bills on Friday, the leader of the centre-right People’s Party, (PP) Alberto Nunez Feijoo, urged Sanchez to “call elections as soon as possible”, claiming he had the support of “neither the streets nor parliament”.
While Sanchez has not officially announced new elections, the Spanish online news site El Diario has reported that elections could take place as early as November 29. Spain’s general elections are currently scheduled for July 2027.

articles.title_orig: France closes up to 500 schools Monday over student protests
articles.title_zh: France closes up to 500 schools Monday over student protests
articles.content_orig:
Up to 500 schools across France will be partially or totally closed on Monday after clashes between riot police and student protesters in recent days, the French education minister said on Sunday.
Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some "400 to 500" high schools as security conditions "have not been fulfilled", Édouard Geffray said.
He also said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the start of the protests.
Thousands of students have been demonstrating over education standards and the protests, which started last week, have spread from Paris to other cities, including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille.
High school pupils and others have objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.
On Friday, French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been affected "one way or another" by violent protests.
The education minister warned the number of schools potentially affected on Monday could be comparable to Friday's figure but promised a "partial, progressive return to lessons".
"There are activists - particularly from the far-left - who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Édouard Geffray claimed.
"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he said. Geffray added that 78 staff members in education had been wounded, which he described as "something we have never seen before".
On Friday 1,747 people were arrested, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.
Over 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according the AFP news agency, with around 85% of them minors.
Organisers of the protests have called for the demonstrations to continue on Tuesday after accusing the government of a lack of "concrete measures", according to AFP.
On Sunday, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said his government is taking further steps to "address the difficulties faced by high school students and educational staff".
He said this includes ensuring classes continue, improving facilities, better organising school days and making the French university admissions platform more transparent.
Lecornu also said the government is accelerating the review of its "vandal-pays" bill to ensure that people responsible for damage bear the cost of their actions.

articles.title_orig: Lotus Tech to Join WasabiCard's TOKEN2049 Singapore Side Event, Spotlighting Real-World Stablecoin Applications
articles.title_zh: Lotus Tech to Join WasabiCard's TOKEN2049 Singapore Side Event, Spotlighting Real-World Stablecoin Applications
articles.content_orig:
SINGAPORE , Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- WasabiCard, a stablecoin -powered global payment infrastructure platform, announced that it will host its TOKEN2049 Singapore Side Event, " STABLECOIN & PAYMENTS: FUNDS FLOW," on October 6 at Raffles Singapore.
Lotus Technology Inc. (Nasdaq: LOT) ("Lotus Tech"), a leading global intelligent and luxury mobility provider under globally renowned automotive brand Lotus, has confirmed its participation in the event. Dr. Daxue Wang, Chief Financial Officer of Lotus Tech, will join a featured panel discussion alongside senior representatives from Visa, Circle, Nium, Plume, Safeheron, OSL, WIDTH, AWS and other leading organizations across traditional finance, stablecoins and technology, exploring how stablecoins can move beyond on-chain settlement and become more deeply integrated into the real economy and everyday global payments.
From Stablecoin Settlement to Real-World Payments
As stablecoin infrastructure continues to mature, the industry's focus is expanding beyond the efficient movement of funds on-chain toward a broader question: how can stablecoin liquidity reach business operations, consumer payments and everyday commercial activity?
The event will focus on how funds move between on-chain financial systems and the real world, with two core discussions: "Wall Street On-Chain: The Next Era of Tokenized Capital Markets" and " Stablecoins Go Mainstream: From Settlement to Real-World Payments." Spanning capital markets and real-world payment scenarios, the discussions will explore what comes next as stablecoin adoption continues to scale.
For WasabiCard, bringing stablecoins into mainstream commercial use requires more than efficient on-chain settlement. It also requires infrastructure capable of connecting digital liquidity with card networks, local banking systems and payment scenarios across global markets.
"The next stage of stablecoin payments is not just about moving funds more efficiently on-chain, but about making those funds truly usable across business operations and consumers' everyday payment scenarios," said Ray Yang, Co-Founder and CEO of WasabiCard . "Having global brands like Lotus join the conversation is important because scaling stablecoin adoption requires stronger connections between payment infrastructure, real-world industries and commercial use cases. We also look forward to exploring further opportunities with Lotus."
Through its global card issuing and global remittance capabilities, WasabiCard helps businesses connect digital asset liquidity with real-world payments, providing more integrated infrastructure for moving and using funds across borders.
Lotus Brings a Global Automotive and Premium Consumer Perspective
With seven decades of boundary-pushing heritage and a legacy of motorsport championships, Lotus continues to redefine the limits of performance in racing and building the most engaging road cars in the world in the era of electrification and intelligence for global customers. As a truly global brand, Lotus boasts worldwide manufacturing footprints, leverages a global supply‑chain ecosystem, and maintains deep‑rooted business presence across multiple international markets. As the automotive industry becomes increasingly integrated with digital services and new consumer experiences, seamless global payment infrastructure is becoming an important bridge between brands and customers worldwide.
By welcoming Lotus to the event, WasabiCard aims to extend the stablecoin payment conversation beyond financial infrastructure and into real-world business and consumer scenarios.
During the event, Dr. Daxue Wang, CFO of Lotus Tech , will join the panel " Stablecoins Go Mainstream: From Settlement to Real-World Payments," exchanging perspectives with WasabiCard and other industry leaders on how stablecoins can connect global fund flows with real-world business needs, while sharing insights and experience from the global automotive and consumer sectors.
WasabiCard and Lotus to Explore Deeper Collaboration Opportunities
The TOKEN2049 Singapore Side Event will also provide an opportunity for WasabiCard and Lotus to deepen their engagement.
Building on their shared focus on global business and next-generation payment experiences, WasabiCard and Lotus are exploring opportunities for deeper collaboration across stablecoin payments, global payment infrastructure and real-world commercial scenarios.
Going forward, the two companies aim to combine Lotus' experience across global automotive and consumer scenarios with WasabiCard's capabilities in stablecoin payments and global payment infrastructure, exploring new ways to connect stablecoin technology with real-world commerce and consumer experiences.
About STABLECOIN & PAYMENTS: FUNDS FLOW
Hosted by WasabiCard, " STABLECOIN & PAYMENTS: FUNDS FLOW" will take place on October 6, 2026, at Raffles Singapore.
The event will bring together leading representatives across traditional finance, stablecoins , cross-border payments, digital assets and cloud computing for in-depth discussions on tokenized capital markets, real-world stablecoin payments and global fund flows.
Event Details & Registration: https://luma.com/gj0iv2kk?tk=jPIHnb
WasabiCard is a global payment infrastructure platform enabling Web3 enterprises, fintechs, and internet-native businesses to issue cards, distribute payouts, and manage cross-border payments through stablecoin -powered financial infrastructure. Its platform supports global card issuing, global off-ramp, and embedded payment capabilities designed for modern global commerce. WasabiCard powers payment use cases across media buying, SaaS subscriptions, global payroll, treasury management, and digital financial applications.
Follow WasabiCard on X and LinkedIn for the latest updates on product developments, partnerships, and insights into the future of stablecoin -powered payments.

articles.title_orig: US withdraws B-1 bomber aircraft from UK’s Fairford base amid Iran fears
articles.title_zh: US withdraws B-1 bomber aircraft from UK’s Fairford base amid Iran fears
articles.content_orig:
The United States has made the abrupt decision to withdraw its bombers from the Royal Air Force (RAF) base Fairford in the western part of the United Kingdom, citing concerns about a potential attack.
Media reports emerged on Sunday that an urgent redeployment was under way, with B-1 bombers leaving RAF Fairford for the US.
Roughly a dozen such aircraft had been based at RAF Fairford prior to the sudden departure.
“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” a Pentagon spokesperson told Al Jazeera.
“The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime,” the official added.
It is unclear precisely what prompted the withdrawal, which comes as the US and Israel remain embroiled in a war against Iran.
RAF Fairford has served as a stopping point for US bombers participating in the war, which began more than seven months ago, on February 28.
But the base, located roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, has been rumoured to be the target of a “terror” plot involving Iran.
On September 27, UK authorities arrested five men on suspicion of plotting to plant explosives near the base.
Iran has denied any such scheme, and the men were released without charge a day later. Investigators discovered petrol, but no explosive devices, in their vans. Still, officials in the UK say they remain under investigation.
On Thursday, British police also announced they had arrested a 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national in London on suspicion of plotting an attack against the airbase.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested last week that “Iran played a part” in the alleged plot, though he declined to provide details.
“The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry,” Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said in a statement.
“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.”
US President Donald Trump responded to the initial arrests by accusing the men of seeking to do “big damage” to US facilities. He also praised UK authorities for their efforts.
“The arrest in the UK was fantastic. Working with Britain – it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation,” Trump said of the suspects. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them.”
Iran, meanwhile, summoned the UK ambassador to Tehran over the last week in protest of the arrests.
The US has a long history of stationing forces at RAF Fairford during its wars in the Middle East, stretching back to the Gulf War in the 1990s.
RAF Fairford has been the site of antiwar protests in the past. During one instance, in 2003, five protesters broke into the airbase in an attempt to destroy military equipment slated to be used in the US invasion of Iraq.
The UK has largely declined to participate in the ongoing war on Iran, despite pressure from the Trump administration.
Still, while the UK government was initially hesitant to let the US use its bases for the war, it granted the US “defensive” access to bases, including Fairford and RAF Diego Garcia, in March.
