articles.title_orig: US criticism of Starbucks in Xinjiang rejected
articles.title_zh: US criticism of Starbucks in Xinjiang rejected
articles.content_orig:
China has firmly rejected criticism from a US congressional committee regarding Starbucks' expansion into the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region. Beijing stressed that the move of the US consumer giant demonstrates the region's social stability and economic vitality as more domestic and international brands tap its growing consumer market.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on Saturday that claims of so-called genocide in Xinjiang are "a blatant lie", in response to a question about criticism from the US House Select Committee on China, which had described Starbucks' decision to open stores in the region as "morally bankrupt".
"Relevant US institutions are accustomed to fabricating issues and attacking and smearing China for political purposes, and have no credibility whatsoever," Guo said.
READ MORE: US blacklisting slammed as destructive bullying
"Xinjiang today enjoys social stability, economic development, ethnic unity and religious harmony," he added. "China will continue to expand high-standard opening-up and provide more opportunities for foreign companies to invest and operate in China."
Starbucks opened its first two stores in Xinjiang on Sept 29, both in Urumqi, the regional capital — one at the city's Grand Bazaar and the other at Urumqi Tianshan International Airport. The openings marked the global coffee chain's debut in the region and its latest expansion in China, its second-largest market after the US.
The Grand Bazaar flagship store incorporates local elements into its design, including Atlas silk, ethnic musical instruments and bazaar-inspired architecture.
The airport outlet adopts a "silk road station" concept to serve travelers at the regional transport hub. Both locations feature locally inspired offerings.
During the weeklong National Day holiday, a Xinjiang-inspired drink and three food items are also being offered at more than 2,700 Starbucks stores across 41 Chinese cities, bringing the region's flavors to consumers nationwide.
"Entering Xinjiang is not only about further expanding our store network, but also gives us an opportunity to go deeper into this vibrant market and build long-term connections with consumers here," said Molly Liu, CEO of Starbucks China, adding that the company would continue to deepen its presence in Xinjiang and develop stores, products and experiences tailored to local demand.
Starbucks is not alone in looking to the region for growth. Domestic giant Luckin Coffee opened its first 11 self-operated stores in Urumqi in May 2024, while Cotti Coffee had entered the Xinjiang market earlier through its franchise model.
The expansion of major coffee brands comes alongside strong growth in Xinjiang's tourism sector. The region received 323 million tourist visits in 2025, up 8 percent year-on-year, with tourism spending rising 8.4 percent in the same period to 370 billion yuan ($52 billion), according to regional government data.
ALSO READ: Services seen having bigger role in GDP
Retail sales have also returned to growth this year. Xinjiang's retail sales of consumer goods reached 263.03 billion yuan in the first eight months of 2026, up 0.3 percent year-on-year, after declining 0.3 percent in the first seven months, official data showed.
The region's broader corporate base is also expanding. Xinjiang had 2,647 registered foreign-invested enterprises by the end of June, up 6.91 percent from a year earlier, while the total number of registered market entities reached 2.73 million, according to regional market regulators.
Nationwide, China saw 35,000 newly established foreign-invested enterprises in the first half of 2026, up 7 percent year-on-year, according to the State Administration for Market Regulation. The number of newly established foreign-invested enterprises in wholesale and retail rose 11.9 percent.

articles.title_orig: Trump defiant about midterm chances as he rallies for Republicans in Ohio
articles.title_zh: Trump defiant about midterm chances as he rallies for Republicans in Ohio
articles.content_orig:
With Election Day less than a month away, President Donald Trump is touting two federal cash-payment programs already underway while renewing a much larger $5,000 check promise contingent on Republicans retaining Congress.
On Friday, Trump announced one-time $90 payments to 20.8 million Medicare beneficiaries. A day later, he revived an earlier promise to give every adult U.S. citizen $5,000 — but only if Republicans retain control of Congress in November.
"If Republicans win the House of Representatives and the Senate in the 2026 Midterm Elections, I'm going to give all Adult Citizens in the United States of America, $5,000," Trump said in a Truth Social video post Saturday. The president made a similar pledge at the Republican National Committee's first midterm convention in Dallas last month.
Trump hasn't provided any details on who would authorize the payments and where the money would come from.
Those claims came on the heels of $500 Obamacare "refund" checks that began going out last week to roughly 950,000 people who bought unsubsidized coverage through the federal marketplace.
The $90 payments to certain eligible Medicare Part B enrollees are scheduled to arrive this month, funded through the Medicare Improvement Fund. The $500 Obamacare payments are already being distributed to certain full-price HealthCare.gov customers.
A Reuters analysis found 71% of the Obamacare money — $339 million — is going to residents of 13 states with some of the country's most competitive Senate and gubernatorial races, though eligibility is based on insurance status, not voting status.
Together, the flurry of offers of direct cash payments comes as Republicans head into the final stretch of a midterm campaign dominated by concerns about prices and the economy .
But the $5,000 "Trump dividend" remains just a promise and Trump has been extremely light on details, particularly on where the money would come from and who would need to authorize it. Sending $5,000 to every adult citizen would cost roughly $1.2 trillion and require congressional approval.
Some Republicans have also raised concerns about its effect on the deficit and inflation.
Rep. David Schweikert, R-Ariz., told Reuters last month he would "throw everything of my heart and soul" into stopping the proposal, warning it could push interest rates higher. And Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., called the plan a "political bribe" in a Sept. 10 interview with CNN , and said Congress controls federal spending.
The White House and offices of Reps. David Schweikert, R-Ariz., and Jamie Raskin, D-Md., did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Polling suggests the idea isn't a sure-fire political winner.
A Rasmussen Reports survey found likely voters essentially split, 47% to 48%, on the proposal. Just 15% said it would affect their vote. A Marquette Law School poll in Wisconsin found 70% opposed the payments, while an Economist/YouGov survey found 57% of registered voters doubted Trump would actually deliver them even if Republicans retained Congress.
In the past, Trump has made several promises to send cash payments to Americans — and didn't deliver.
In February 2025, the Trump administration floated a $5,000 "DOGE dividend" check, claiming the money would come from savings from the cuts enacted by the now-defunct, Elon Musk -led "Department of Government Efficiency." Those payments never materialized.
Then, in November, Trump proposed a reciprocal tariff -funded dividend payment of at least $2,000 per person . The Supreme Court struck down the tariffs in February of this year, and no checks were ever issued.
The pattern of offering cash payments directly to voters stretches back to Trump's first term. Six weeks before the 2020 election, Trump promised 33 million Medicare beneficiaries $200 prescription-drug cards "in coming weeks" — but the cards never went out .
Still, the Trump administration delivered a $1,776 " Warrior Dividend " to roughly 1.5 million service members last year, and Congress approved pandemic stimulus payments during his first term.

articles.title_orig: UK Weighs Higher Tariffs on Chinese EVs Under EU Pressure
articles.title_zh: UK Weighs Higher Tariffs on Chinese EVs Under EU Pressure
articles.content_orig:
Britain under pressure to put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicle imports ahead of protectionist trade measures
Britain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China and Europe , as manufacturers struggle to balance the benefits of both markets ahead of looming trade measures that could restrict UK exports to the EU.
The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely , and the EU imposes duties of up to 45% .
EU officials reportedly warned Andy Burnham last month that the UK must put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicles otherwise Brussels would impose protectionist “made in Europe” barriers on British exports to the bloc, hitting British carmakers in their largest market.
Ministers have so far resisted such calls, with Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, arguing any levies would “probably be reciprocated” – costing UK manufacturers sales in China .
Tariffs would also raise prices for British drivers, who have flocked to cheaper Chinese models , and could deter brands such as Chery, which is in talks to build cars at Nissan’s Sunderland plant , from investing further in the UK.
“There is a difficult trade-off,” said Emily Sawicz, of the consultancy RSM UK, adding that the UK “cannot afford to drift between the two indefinitely”. Chinese investment could be a “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers.
“Being excluded risks UK suppliers becoming increasingly shut out of those European opportunities,” she added. “Manufacturers need clarity on which direction the government intends to take so they can make long-term investment decisions.”
Ian Plummer, commercial director at Autotrader, said competition from Chinese brands had made cars more affordable and “is encouraging more people to go and buy a new car”.
Brands such as BYD, Omoda and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in the first eight months of 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to industry figures.
Figures released on Friday showed that British new car ⁠registrations rose 12% in the year to September, the best month for annual growth since 2017. The preliminary data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) showed the boom was powered by a demand for electric vehicles and Chinese brands, with the Jaecoo 7 and BYD’s ​Sealion ‌7 among the top sellers.
The trade body said on Wednesday that the European Commission’s made in Europe rules, which restrict subsidies, tax breaks and public procurement contracts to vehicles built within the EU, pose an existential threat to British car production. The EU accounted for 58% of UK car exports in the first half of the year, compared with about 4% for China.
Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The UK and EU automotive industries are deeply integrated, so effectively excluding British-produced vehicles from their largest market would assure mutual damage.”
Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s chair in Europe, said last month: “Europe cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market through the UK.”
after newsletter promotion
Victor Zhang, the deputy UK chief of Chery, which owns the Jaecoo and Omoda brands, rejected that claim, saying: “Most of what we sell are super-hybrids, not the cars that those tariffs are about, and the cars we sell here stay here.”
He added: “Tariffs can come and go, but we won’t change our ongoing investment in the UK.”
Brussels raised its own tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024, triggering a decline in what was then an accelerating sales trajectory. It is now facing calls for fresh barriers to be imposed on importing hybrid electric vehicles, potentially quotas or price floors.
Imports of plug-in and battery hybrid cars rocketed after the EU tariffs were imposed on EVs, underlining China’s ability to pivot its export efforts when hit by trade barriers.
Others in the industry believe tariffs could help protect the UK’s manufacturers, whose market share in Britain continues to be eroded Chinese firms.
Tim Tozer, a former chair of Vauxhall, said that tariffs were “vital” to stop Britain’s car sector “atrophying”. He said: “We are at last knockings now, trying to save the industry.”
He added that Reynolds was “whistling in the wind” with hopes of continuing to export to China en masse, arguing the market had become “fiercely nationalistic,” with buyers increasingly loyal to domestic brands “because they’re bloody good”.

articles.title_orig: Russia hospitalizes almost 200 people after researcher's death from plague: reports
articles.title_zh: Russia hospitalizes almost 200 people after researcher's death from plague: reports
articles.content_orig:
Nearly 200 people have been placed under medical observation in Russia's Irkutsk region in eastern Siberia over suspected exposure to plague, according to local media reports.
The report said 189 people were being monitored following the illness of an employee at an anti-plague research institute in Irkutsk. Alexei Tsydenov, head of the nearby Republic of Buryatia, said the woman had died from an unspecified form of plague.
Russia's public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said Sunday that the employee had been diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region and the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov remained stable.
The agency said expanded testing had not detected microorganisms linked to the employee's work.
The update follows local media reports on Friday that a 27-year-old employee at an anti-plague institute had fallen ill with suspected pneumonic plague after returning from a work trip to Buryatia, where an outbreak had been reported near the border with Mongolia, citing Russian Telegram channel Mash.
The White House is monitoring reports of the suspected case and related quarantines in Russia, Axios reported Sunday, citing a Trump administration official. The official said the administration was "aware, monitoring the outbreak, and assessing options," the report said.
The Russian and Moscow ministries of health, the World Health Organization and the U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.

articles.title_orig: All passengers presumed dead after plane went missing off US coast
articles.title_zh: All passengers presumed dead after plane went missing off US coast
articles.content_orig:
Six people aboard a medical transport aircraft that went missing on Saturday while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston are presumed dead, according to a statement from the flight's operator.
On Sunday evening, the United States Coast Guard said it was ending its search for survivors off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island.
"We must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died," Latitude Air Ambulance said in a statement shortly thereafter.
"Our thoughts are first and foremost with their families, loved ones, friends, and colleagues."
The Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Saturday morning.
On Saturday evening, authorities located a "debris field" confirmed to be from the aircraft.
The plane had departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time on Friday night, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT).
Four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals were onboard.
"This is an unimaginable loss for our Latitude family and for everyone who loved the six people aboard Heartbeat 104," said Peter Byl, President of Latitude Air Ambulance, on Sunday evening.
"Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities. We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day."
Latitude Air Ambulance is a Canadian company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home.
Two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, had flown to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News.
FlightAware's tracker shows that the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft).
Radio transmissions show trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported, based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net.
"You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?"
The pilot's response was inaudible.
"You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe.
The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency.
An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue".
The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar".
Latitude said in its statement on Sunday evening that it would continue to cooperate with relevant authorities during ongoing recovery efforts and investigations.
"Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred," the company said.

articles.title_orig: Preparing the Next Generation for Economic Mobility in an AI-Driven World
articles.title_zh: Preparing the Next Generation for Economic Mobility in an AI-Driven World
articles.content_orig:
(Feature Impact) Within only a few years, AI has already changed many things about the world and workforce. Entry-level jobs, particularly the ones relying on routine and predictable tasks, are increasingly disappearing to automation, leaving young people wondering how to launch their careers and futures.
Access to economic mobility - the ability to change your income or wealth - doesn't just rely on technical knowledge and skills but on leaning into humanity. Being able to think outside the box, collaborate, solve problems and grow as a person can open doors in life and at work. AI may be changing the world, but in change lies opportunity. The students who can adapt quickly are more likely to prosper as the economy continues to reshape itself.
To learn what preparing students for the future may look like in practice, consider these tips from the economic and career experts at Junior Achievement.
Young people facing AI as their competition can get a boost from cultivating the uniquely human skills technology can't replicate. Educators, parents and other adults in kids' lives can help them develop increasingly important soft skills like critical thinking, communication, teamwork and leadership, which can translate to many different careers. Hands-on skills can fit into this category as well, like the kinds required in entrepreneurship and the trades.
When young people have the chance to test themselves in a real-world setting, it lets them hone their interests, skills and confidence before the time comes to make major decisions about their futures. As early as elementary school, experiential learning activities like Junior Achievement's Biztown allow students to operate businesses, work with others, manage finances and solve problems, combining in-class learning with hands-on simulations. As kids grow up, other options can include job shadowing, internships and entrepreneurship experiments - all ways to build durable social and professional skills that can help them succeed.
Earning money is only part of the equation for a healthy financial future; equally important is understanding how to manage it. As kids prepare to earn their first sources of income, make sure they're also equipped with practical financial skills like budgeting, saving, investing, using credit wisely and planning for future goals. Giving them these tools early helps them make informed decisions about their long-term economic advancement.
Sometimes, all a student needs to succeed is someone who's willing to give them a chance. Young people in a position to meet business professionals in (and beyond) their communities may be able to turn those connections into future opportunities. This can happen naturally as they seek real-world experiences through apprenticeships, mentorship programs, career fairs and more.
Programs like Junior Achievement's 3DE puts students in authentic business challenges, connecting them with educators, business partners and volunteers as they work in teams to complete case experiences. This not only gives young people the opportunity to meet potential employers or mentors, it also lets them demonstrate critical thinking, social skills and real-world competence.
Visit jausa.ja.org for more ideas to help young people gain the confidence and connections needed to achieve economic mobility in a changing world.

articles.title_orig: MFK Fisher – still the greatest food writer in the world
articles.title_zh: MFK Fisher – still the greatest food writer in the world
articles.content_orig:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
It was Simon Schama who got me on to MFK Fisher. He called her “the greatest food writer who ever lived”. Born Mary Frances Kennedy in Michigan in 1908, the author of 35 books was best known for her Art of Eating series – which was revelatory because it took food writing beyond preparation, taste and appearance to encompass the “very human, psychological, moral and creative dramas that accompany it”, says Picador senior editor Rohan Kamicheril. These five gastronomical works, including Consider the Oyster (1941) and How to Cook a Wolf (1942), are now being reissued by Picador US with new introductions by contributors including Alison Roman, Ruby Tandoh and Bryan Washington.
Consider the Oyster (Daunt, 2018)
The Art of Eating (Knopf, 1976)
All covers in the new series feature sections of a giant lino-cut by artist Allie Webb that depicts a table full of bounty. “The lino-cut feels warm and is handmade, but it’s also a little unruly and funny, which seemed right for Fisher,” says Picador art director Alex Merto of the writer, who was known for her wry, offbeat reflections. Take her thoughts on the potato (“a poor thing, poorly treated”) or oyster (“a moping, debauched mollusc”). Each volume in the series can be purchased separately. But the design encourages you to consume them as one, taking bites of each.
An Alphabet for Gourmets (1949) is my favourite. Based on a series of columns that ran in Gourmet magazine from 1948 to 1949, the entries cover everything from solo dining (“A is for Alone”) to aphrodisiacal foods (“W is for Wanton”). I particularly admire the batty ingenuity with which she covers off the final letters. There is a chapter on marital disharmony and how it ruins one’s appetite called “X is for Xanthippe”, after Socrates’s shrewish wife. A chapter on exotic meats is called “Y is for Yak”, while “Z is for Zakuski”, named after the Russian term for a cold spread, is the title for a chapter on hors d’oeuvres.
An Alphabet for Gourmets (The Viking Press, 1949)
How to Cook a Wolf (Duell, Sloan and Pearce, 1942)
The Gastronomical Me (North Point, 1989)
Serve It Forth (Harper & Brothers, 1937)
For Schama (and others), the ultimate work is “Borderland”, an essay from Serve It Forth (1937). In it, Fisher finds herself in Strasbourg, cooped up inside during winter, feeling sorry for herself. She finds solace, while her husband is away, peeling “little dried sections of tangerine” and leaving them on sheets of newspaper on the radiator to grow “even plumper, hot and full” before chilling them in packed snow on her sill.
“I cannot tell you why they are so magical,” writes Fisher of the frozen tangerine slices. “Perhaps it is that little shell, thin as one layer of enamel on a Chinese bowl, that crackles so tinily, so ultimately under your teeth. Or the rush of cold pulp just after it. Or the perfume.” The passage captures “the muscular grace” of her prose (as Tandoh puts it), and ranks among her most “indelible” descriptions of food (to use Washington’s word). It also conjures up the manifold emotions that we attach to food. As Fisher noted in her introduction to The Gastronomical Me (1943): “When I write about hunger, I am really writing about love and the hunger for it.”
How to Cook a Wolf, An Alphabet for Gourmets and The Gastronomical Me publish on October 27 2026, followed by Serve It Forth and Consider the Oyster on November 3, at Picador . Each book will have a new introduction by Tamar Adler, Ruby Tandoh, Alison Roman, Bryan Washington and Anne Fadiman, respectively

articles.title_orig: To cull or not to cull: Greenland debates fate of world’s slowest shark
articles.title_zh: To cull or not to cull: Greenland debates fate of world’s slowest shark
articles.content_orig:
As trawlers compete with Greenland sharks for halibut and cod, conservationists and fishers clash over what to do about misunderstood species
‘W hen I accidentally catch a shark, I bring it to my dogs,” Henrik Jensen, a 27-year-old from Greenland’s west coast, says casually. “I don’t let it back down because [the sharks] bully me and cut my lines.”
Jensen has fished for halibut in Ilulissat, Greenland’s third largest town, for a decade. He works an hour north of the town’s main iceberg-laden fishery, which sustains the livelihood of nearly 400 fishers. There, the halibut are bigger and more plentiful, but so are the Greenland sharks.
“This year I’ve lost around 6,000 hooks in total. Sometimes we lose 30,000 Danish krone [£3,440] a day,” says Jensen.
The Greenland shark is one of the least understood species on the planet. As well as being the world’s slowest shark, it is the second-largest carnivorous species, after the white shark, according to the Shark Trust . Reaching about six to seven metres in length, they can live for more than 400 years. For a long time they were thought to be completely blind, although scientists have recently discovered this may not be true .
The sharks inhabit a vast range across the deep and cold waters of the north and west Atlantic, but their attempts to feed on the northern fisheries’ main catch – Greenland halibut and Atlantic cod – often see them tangled in gear and brought in as bycatch.
This acrimonious coexistence has been documented ever since targeted fishing for the sharks’ liver oil ceased in the 1960s, but it came to a head earlier this year. The Avannaata municipality, of which Ilulissat is the administrative seat, approved a controversial plan to cull 1,000 sharks, offering 300 krone for every heart of a Greenland shark.
Lars Erik Gabrielsen, mayor of the municipality, says: “We need to safeguard the income of fishermen and the catch so that we can continue to eat the foods that we have relied on for generations.”
For many fishing inshore, working in small teams on dinghies, it brought a longstanding issue to a head. Timotheus Petersen, chair of the fishing association in Kullorsuaq, says: “Our longlines are expensive – one costs 1,599 krone. When the sharks cut our lines, we cannot finish fishing. We have to spend more money and buy new gear.”
The plan was eventually dropped after the government questioned its legality, but the prospect of a future cull remains.
In its decision to approve the cull, Avannaata council cited a similar scheme from the early 2000s in the former Aasiaat municipality, where a bounty of 200 krone was offered. According to a 2007 report from the Danish Technical University, another scheme between 1986 and 2001 in the former Uummannaq municipality brought in 19,697 hearts.
But the marine conservation group Oceans North Kalaallit Nunaat (ONKN) argues that culls do not resolve the issue, highlighting the migratory nature of the species, which can swim up to 1,200 miles (2,000km) a year. “Sharks removed in north-west Greenland would quickly be replaced by individuals arriving from other regions,” ONKN warned .
Many fishers also do not consider 300 krone worth the effort of hauling a shark onboard. “It’s difficult to catch them,” Jensen says. “You need bigger hooks and chains for the lines, so I don’t think anyone wants to try.”
But the debate around a possible cull is alarming conservationists. “If somebody says, ‘I’m going to cull a couple of thousand Greenland sharks’, that’s a disaster in my opinion,” says Prof Nick Dulvy, a marine conservationist at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia.
The Greenland shark is believed to become sexually mature at 150, which means the species replaces itself extremely slowly and will not rebound from a cull quickly. It is still recovering from targeted fishing throughout the 19th and mid-20th centuries, when, at its peak in 1948, 58,000 were landed .
“They are probably – biologically – the most sensitive species in the ocean to overfishing,” Dulvy says. Globally, it is estimated that 3,500 sharks are caught every year as bycatch and the population remains in decline.
Greenland’s fishing community highlight their longstanding problem with the sharks, but do not say why it has suddenly escalated. Jenseeraq Poulsen, the director of ONKN, suggests it is due to mounting pressures within a fishing industry that accounts for about 25% of Greenland’s GDP .
“If every Greenland shark in Baffin Bay vanished tomorrow, the inshore fishery in Avannaata would still face too many boats working a quota under pressure, rising costs and no alternative employment,” he says. “When margins are narrow, a longstanding nuisance becomes intolerable.”
Even though the price of halibut continues to rise, according to the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources, the average size of the fish is decreasing annually. While Jensen maintains he can still make a good living from fishing, he describes putting fewer hooks out and bringing in fewer fish, suggesting this is due to overfishing by offshore trawlers.
For some of those fishing these waters, however, the shark is not the leading cause of losing gear. “There are more and more ‘ghost lines’ and they are too heavy to pull up by the machine we use,” Jensen says. Ghost lines are discarded or lost gear that can get entangled with new lines, breaking equipment and trapping marine life.
Halibut Greenland, a cooperatively owned fish-processing company in Ilulissat, provides funds to clean up ghost gear in the area, which ONKN views as more effective than a shark cull. Poulsen also proposes a gear-loss compensation scheme, as well as funded trials of acoustic shark deterrents.
Rebekka Nygård Bak, an adviser to Greenland’s Ministry of Fisheries, Hunting, Agriculture and Self Sufficiency, suggests new bycatch-friendly equipment regulations could be a solution. She says a campaign for better bycatch reporting will also be key to any next steps.
For Poulsen, the sharks and those fishing these waters are two components of the same ecosystem, facing growing pressures in changing seas. “The shark is the visible, tangible version of a problem whose real drivers are structural,” he says.

Company will share lessons learned from customer pilots and production deployments as life sciences organizations move AI from experimentation to practical GxP use
SANTA CLARA, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- #AIinGxP --ValGenesis Inc., the leader in enterprise digital validation, will explore real-world insights into the practical application of AI-assisted validation at KENX Europe 2026: Harnessing the Power of AI in GxP, taking place Oct. 14–15, 2026, at the Four Elements Hotel Amsterdam in Amsterdam, the Netherlands.
As life sciences organizations move from exploring AI’s potential to applying it in regulated environments, questions around performance, governance, and human oversight are becoming increasingly important. ValGenesis is addressing these challenges through AI-native digital validation and VAL™ (ValGenesis AI), the governed AI natively built into the ValGenesis Smart GxP™ platform. VAL applies AI throughout the validation lifecycle while keeping humans in control of oversight, approval, and critical decisions. Its capabilities include generating validation documents, identifying potential compliance and test-coverage gaps, interpreting execution evidence, detecting anomalies, and analyzing document changes.
“AI is moving beyond theory and into practical use in GxP environments,” said David Medina, chief marketing officer at ValGenesis. “The challenge now is understanding where it adds meaningful value, how to evaluate the results, and how to maintain appropriate control. At KENX Europe, we’ll share what we’re learning from practical applications of AI in validation and the considerations organizations should address as they expand its use.”
Kenneth Pierce, Ph.D., director of product growth at ValGenesis, will lead two sessions focused on evaluating AI performance and building trust in its use in GxP environments. “How Would You Know It Worked? Measuring AI-Assisted Validation in Practice” will draw on customer pilot studies, implementation lessons, and measurable performance outcomes to examine how organizations can evaluate AI-assisted validation. “Pacing the Frontier: AI in GxP Life Sciences Operations” will introduce an AI maturity model for building trust in AI-supported processes and expanding adoption through clearly defined intended-use frameworks.
ValGenesis is a Platinum Sponsor of KENX Europe 2026 and will host an exhibit booth and sponsor the event’s cocktail reception.
ValGenesis, Inc. is the global leader in enterprise digital validation. Serving the life sciences industry for nearly two decades, ValGenesis enables companies to digitize their commissioning, qualification, and validation processes through its AI-enabled ValGenesis Smart GxP™ platform, which includes solutions for risk management, cleaning validation, continued process verification, and CMC development. ValGenesis helps customers worldwide reduce costs, improve compliance, and accelerate innovation. For more information, visit valgenesis.com .

articles.title_orig: Trump unveils 'Super Intelligence Force' to oversee AI policy
articles.title_zh: Trump unveils 'Super Intelligence Force' to oversee AI policy
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump says he has created a new taskforce focused on artificial intelligence, which will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.
The "Super Intelligence Force" will work to ensure that the US continues to lead in the technology's development and will coordinate the government's engagement with the public, Trump posted on Sunday.
It comes after the president signed an executive order on 29 September to rename AI as Super Intelligence, after previously saying the word artificial made it sound "fake".
Trump also said last week that he would set up a board to oversee AI safety after top tech bosses signed what he described as a "morally binding" pact.
"The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies," Trump wrote.
Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Undersecretary of Defense for Research,  Engineering Emil Michael and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor will also be part of the taskforce.
It will report directly to the president and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.
The taskforce's chief, Clayton, took office as the US national intelligence director in August after Trump's original choice, Bill Pulte, was rejected by lawmakers.
On AI, Clayton has previously said: "When something's both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it."
Clayton previously served as US attorney for the Southern District of New York, overseeing several prominent cases, including the drug trafficking case against former Venezuelan President Nicholas Maduro.
The announcement of the taskforce follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry, including executives of OpenAI and Anthropic, to tighten regulation of the technology.
In an interview published on 4 October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of AI justify accepting some of its risks and argued that the technology should remain accessible to the public.
"The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this ‌technology and people having the agency," Altman told Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded.
Trump has dismissed calls for stronger oversight and largely left it to AI companies to regulate themselves.
The pact signed on 29 September includes the signatures of executives from top tech firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Google.
On the same day, the president signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence.
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.
Some experts have questioned the logic of the rebranding , arguing that the use of "super intelligence" could cause confusion as it refers to more advanced systems.
Some top tech leaders have already started to use the new name, including multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who said on social media on Sunday that he will rename his firm's AI platform SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI.
"SpaceX is a super intelligence company", Musk wrote.
The Tesla boss has recently been brought back into the US government to be part of a project to study the future of war.
Musk previously served in the Trump administration, heading the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, before his tenure ended in a public spat with Trump .

articles.title_orig: DP World Research: Supply Chain Chiefs Shift from Cost to Choice
articles.title_zh: DP World Research: Supply Chain Chiefs Shift from Cost to Choice
articles.content_orig:
Published
					Oct 4, 2026 11:12 PM        		by The Maritime Executive
DUBAI, UNITED ARAB EMIRATES – 5 October 2026: Supply chain leaders are redesigning their networks around greater choice and flexibility, as resilience increasingly becomes a source of competitive advantage and growth, according to new research from DP World’s Global Trade Observatory.
The Chief Supply Chain Officer (CSCO) Pulse Report, based on a survey in August of 103 CSCOs across 14 markets and nine industries, finds that 84% say resilience and optionality have overtaken cost reduction as the primary drivers of supply-chain strategy.
The shift is already changing how businesses design their networks. 71% plan to diversify their supplier base over the next 12 months, with CSCOs also considering changes across inventory, production locations and sourcing as they seek to preserve room to manoeuvre when conditions change.
The report describes this shift as a move from optimisation to optionality: away from designing supply chains primarily around cost and efficiency, towards creating viable alternatives that businesses can call upon as trade rules, tariffs, demand and geopolitical conditions change.
Yuvraj Narayan, Group CEO of DP World, said: “Global trade is not standing still, and neither are the supply chains that underpin it. Businesses are responding to uncertainty not by retreating from growth, but by creating more choices about where they source, how they move goods and how they reach customers.
“The role of the Chief Supply Chain Officer is changing with that environment. Supply-chain decisions increasingly shape where a business can grow, how quickly it can enter new markets and how effectively it can respond when circumstances change. The opportunity is to build networks that combine efficiency with flexibility - giving businesses the options, visibility and connectivity they need to keep growing through uncertainty.”
The report finds that this changing operating model is being accompanied by a broader transformation in the role of supply-chain leadership.
93% of CSCOs say their role in driving business growth has become more central over the past three years, while the research shows supply-chain leaders increasingly contributing to decisions around market entry, investment and risk.
Optionality is also moving beyond protection against disruption to become a tool for growth. 86% say access to alternative and multimodal trade routes is becoming a competitive advantage, giving businesses greater ability to adapt how goods move as conditions change and new opportunities emerge.
The CSCO Pulse Report 2026 explores three major shifts shaping the future of supply-chain leadership: the CSCO's expanding role as an enabler of business growth; the move from optimisation towards greater optionality; and the capabilities – including digital integration, visibility and lower-carbon supply chains – expected to become increasingly important for future growth.

articles.title_zh: Exclusive | New AI Czar Unveils Goals, Members of White House Task Force
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Sunday announced the leadership and duties of a “Super Intelligence Force,” which he said will “ensure that America continues to lead the world” when it comes to artificial intelligence.
The president said in his announcement on Truth Social that the task force will “protect the interests” and “improve the lives” of Americans. He said it will coordinate the government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, infrastructure providers and AI companies.
The group will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor. The task force will report to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, the president said.
Trump announced last month that he was planning to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the technology’s rapid development. CNN reported Friday that Trump was expected to tap Clayton to lead the group.
The announcement detailing the task force comes in the wake of episodes that have raised widespread safety concerns tied to AI, including AI agents going rogue and attempting to hack into federal databases.
The president has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns, and previously referred to fears over AI as being a “hoax.” His support for the technology comes amid widespread frustrations over the data centers used to support it, which are shaking up midterm races.
The president hosted top AI executives at the White House last week. The group signed a new commitment aimed at better “self-policing” their companies’ AI models, arguing that the light-touch approach represents the best way to balance safety concerns with the president’s desire to accelerate a technology he’s dubbed “Super Intelligence.”
“I’m seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters. “These models are very complex and, again, I believe they’re going to be used for the good.”
When asked about AI during his confirmation hearing to lead the US intelligence community, Clayton said the technology is a “game changer.”
“When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton said.
Kupor said Sunday on X that “the U.S. will continue to lead in SI to enhance the well-being of all Americans.”
Michael wrote on X that the Pentagon “has seen what is possible when red tape is removed and America’s best technology is rapidly put into action.”
“Working alongside America’s leading technology companies, we are putting the most advanced SI capabilities into the hands of our warfighters at speed and scale,” he said.
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Hadas Gold, Alayna Treene and Adam Cancryn contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Vienna shooting leaves two dead at party
articles.title_zh: Vienna shooting leaves two dead at party
articles.content_orig:
Two people died and at least 35 others suffered injuries after gunfire erupted during a homecoming gathering in Vienna, prompting a Georgia Bureau of Investigation probe in Dooly County.
VIENNA, Ga. - A late-night homecoming celebration ended in tragedy Sunday when gunfire erupted across a four-block span in a historic small South Georgia city.
Two men were killed and 35 others injured.
Emergency crews and law enforcement officers from multiple counties rushed to secure the scene as victims were taken to regional hospitals.
A crowd of more than 1,000 people gathered for an unofficial homecoming block party near West Palm and the Dooly County Recreation Department gym in the 900 block of Pine Street. Around 1:25 a.m. Sunday, gunfire broke out while deputies were stationed at both ends of the street to manage traffic.
Deputies rushed toward the gunfire and located two deceased men, identified as 21-year-old Ja’Quavion Aderious Jackson of Cordele and 23-year-old Macaleb Malik Jackson of Hawkinsville. Authorities said 35 additional victims, ranging in age from 14 to 51, suffered injuries that ranged from critical to stable condition.
Dooly County Coroner Brett Walls called the scene horrific after the two men died from fatal gunshot wounds. Most of the 35 injured victims suffered gunshot wounds, while others were hit by cars as crowds ran from the area.
Early Sunday gunfire at an unpermitted homecoming block party in Vienna left two dead and 35 wounded as state agents search for suspects.
Traffic congestion and ongoing gunfire a block away complicated initial rescue efforts as emergency crews worked to reach the wounded. Responders transported victims to Crisp County Hospital, Bleckley Memorial Hospital, a hospital in Perry, and Atrium Health Navicent in Macon.
Sheriff Craig Peavy had 22 officers working Friday night during peaceful homecoming festivities, but Sunday morning required support from state and neighboring agencies. Georgia State Patrol, Houston County, Perry Police Department, and Crisp County Sheriff's Office sent personnel to assist Dooly County deputies.
"Please turn yourself in, because we're doing everything we can to find out who you are," Peavy said during a news conference. Peavy explained that people were going in every direction and additional shots were fired about a block away while deputies were already on scene.
"We don't know if it's coming at us or someone else," Peavy said. "You just have to keep doing what you're doing and hope you don't get hit by gunfire."
GBI Director Chris Hosey stated that six investigative work units were activated across the region to identify suspects. Vienna Mayor Eddie Daniels noted the shooting occurred about a block from his home, adding that the city had not issued a permit for the block party.
The block party was being held at the Dooley County Recreation Department's gym located in the 900 block of Pine Street in Vienna.
The incident took place over homecoming weekend for Dooly County High School.
The shooting was not at a school-sponsored event, said Sherrod Willaford, superintendent of the Dooly County School System.
"We recognize that its impact may reach many of our students, families, and staff," he said in a statement. Schools will open Monday, he said, but additional safety measures have been put in place. He did not specify what they are.
Vienna is about 130 miles south of Atlanta and about a 50-mile drive south on the Interstate 75 corridor from the central Georgia city of Macon, where authorities say 12 teens were wounded by gunfire during a confrontation between people at a birthday party last week at a city park.
Deputies found two people dead at the scene and multiple others who had been shot, officials said. Police did not specify how many of the 35 injured had been shot or provide any details about the injuries or their severity. The victims were taken to several hospitals for treatment, the GBI said.
Investigators have not identified any suspects, named a potential motive, or determined how many shooters opened fire. Authorities have not confirmed what specific argument or event triggered the initial gunfire before crowds scattered across the four-block area.
Law enforcement officials urge anyone with information or video of the block party to contact the GBI Perry office at (478) 987-4545 or the tip line at 1-800-597-TIPS (8477). Anonymous tips can also be submitted online at gbi.georgia.gov/submit-tips-online or through the free See Something, Send Something mobile app.
The GBI Medical Examiner's Office will perform autopsies on Jue'Von Jackson and McCaleb Jackson. Once state agents complete their investigation, the full case file will go to the Cordele Judicial Circuit District Attorney's Office for review and prosecution.
Dooly County High School Superintendent Sherrod Willaford confirmed the shooting did not occur at a school-sponsored event. Willaford said schools will open Monday with additional safety measures in place to support students and staff.
The Source: The information in this story was gathered from the Georgia Bureau of Investigation, who provided official details in a news release, as well as the Dooly County Sheriff’s Office. The Associated Press and FOX News contributed to this report. This article has been updated since it was originally published. This story is being reported out of Atlanta.

articles.title_orig: Could Investing $5,000 in SpaceX Help Make You a Millionaire?
articles.title_zh: Could Investing $5,000 in SpaceX Help Make You a Millionaire?
articles.content_orig:
Every investor has had a thought from time to time that goes something like this: "If I had just bought that one stock early enough, I'd be rich now."
It's a tempting thought experiment to go back and calculate how buying Apple , Amazon , Microsoft , or other companies shortly after their initial public offerings (IPOs) could have changed your portfolio.
And some investors are likely thinking this way about Space Exploration Technologies ( SPCX +7.36% ) right now. After all, SpaceX has a leading artificial intelligence business, a successful rocket launch business, and a rapidly growing Starlink satellite internet company.
So, is SpaceX the stock that investors will look back on years from now and wonder if they had just put $5,000 toward it, they'd be a millionaire?
I think not, and here's why.
Image source: The Motley Fool.
SpaceX's share price is about $160 as of this writing. To turn a $5,000 investment into $1 million would require SpaceX's stock to increase by almost 20,000%. That's a nearly impossible feat and highly unlikely considering SpaceX's market cap is $2 trillion already.
Some investors are still optimistic that the company could experience significant share price gains, though. And there are a few legitimate reasons to be optimistic about SpaceX.
For one, the company has a thriving satellite internet business . SpaceX says Starlink has 12 million paid subscribers, with about 3 million of those residing in the U.S. The number of U.S.-based Starlink customers could reach an estimated 15 million in just four years, according to analysts at Oppenheimer .
Starlink accounts for around 60% of SpaceX's top line and is the company's only profitable business, with about $2.6 billion in EBITDA in the second quarter.
An expanding Starlink business could fuel momentum for SpaceX stock over the next several years if the company can continue to expand its user base. Just don't expect out-of-this-world returns for SpaceX stock because of Starlink.
I think one of the biggest inhibitors to SpaceX's stock gains is the company's accelerating capex.
SpaceX spent $28.5 billion in the first six months of 2026, an increase of 309% from the first half of 2025. The vast majority of that was funneled into the company's artificial intelligence initiatives, including building large data centers.
The AI boom is well underway, and many investors have been pretty patient with all of the spending. But their patience is starting to run out for companies that aren't profitable, which SpaceX isn't.
If the company continues on its current capex path, I doubt SpaceX stock will make significant gains from its current level. There are simply too many other AI stocks to choose from that spend less and still deliver impressive profits for their shareholders.
All of which means that if you're on the fence for where to put $5,000 right now, SpaceX probably isn't your best bet -- and it certainly won't help make you a millionaire.

articles.title_orig: Chinese man, 71, discovers hidden US$63,000 fortune after scavenging for 21 years
articles.title_zh: Chinese man, 71, discovers hidden US$63,000 fortune after scavenging for 21 years
articles.content_orig:
Handing Ru the bank card, a social worker advised him to keep it safe, spend wisely, and beware of telecom scams
An elderly man in central China, who has spent the past 21 years making ends meet as a scavenger, experienced a remarkable stroke of luck when he discovered that his pension fund contained over 420,000 yuan (US$63,000).
In late September, the 71-year-old man, surnamed Ru, received a bank card linked to his pension account, which revealed a balance of 424,204 yuan, as reported by Changde Daily.
Completely unaware of his entitlement to pensions over the decades, Ru sobbed as he spoke to the media: “It goes without saying that I am happy. I never expected this to happen. I am grateful for the support from the social assistance authority and other related government departments.”
For the past 21 years, Ru has been scavenging to earn a living in Changde, Hunan province.

Teresa Giudice claimed her daughter Milania had fentanyl in her system as bodycam video showed the 20-year-olds tense encounter with police at Tampa International Airport. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)
" The Real Housewives of New Jersey " star Teresa Giudice's daughter Milania Giudice reflected on her bond with her sister Gabriella in a heartfelt birthday tribute months after her older sibling reportedly called 911 on her during a family dispute.
In May, Milania, 20, was arrested and charged with simple assault following a reported domestic dispute at Teresa's home in Montville Township, New Jersey.
According to TMZ, Gabriella, who turned 22 on Sunday, was reportedly the family member who called 911 during the incident. Per the outlet, Gabriella reported that Milania was allegedly "acting erratically" and "throwing food and candles" at the time.
Teresa Giudice's daughter Milania shared a heartfelt birthday tribute to her sister Gabriella. (Teresa Giudice Instagram)
'REAL HOUSEWIVES' STARS' KIDS FACE LEGAL TROUBLE AFTER CAMERAS STOP ROLLING
On Sunday, Milania appeared to have put the family turmoil behind her as she celebrated Gabriella's birthday with an emotional post on social media .
"Happy birthday @gabriella.guiudice 🤍 you really are the best sister I could ever ask for," Milania wrote in the caption of her post.
"You're genuinely one of the smartest people I know, and I'm so proud of the person you are," she continued.
"I've put you through a lot over the years, and I know I haven't always made being my sister easy, but you've always been there for me, accepted me, and loved me through everything," Milania added.
"I've always told you that you're literally Cinderella in real life, and even with the black hair now, I still stand by it 😂. I can't believe you're 22 already. Time really flies. I love you so much and I'm so lucky to have you as my sister. 🤍"
Milania's post included a series of throwback photos that included snaps of Gabriella with their sisters Gia, 25, and Audriana, 17, as well as Teresa and their father Joe, both 54.
"I love you so much ❤️❤️," Gabriella wrote in the comments section.
Teresa also commented on Milania's post, writing, "Happy Birthday @gabriella.giudice Love you ♥️🎂🎉🎈🥳."
FENTANYL DEATHS COULD NOW COST DRUG DEALERS THEIR LIVES UNDER NEW GOP PROPOSAL
Fox News Digital previously confirmed that the Montville Township Police Department responded to a report of a dispute at a residence in town on May 14.
Officers detained Milania at 6:12 p.m., according to court records reviewed by Fox News Digital.
'ILLICIT' VERSION OF FENTANYL LINKED TO DEADLY NEW MEXICO INCIDENT THAT SICKENED FIRST RESPONDERS
"The investigation resulted in Milania Giudice being charged on a summons complaint with one count of Simple Assault, in violation of N.J.S.A. 2C: 12-1a(1) a Disorderly Persons Offense," Chief Andrew Caggiano said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital at the time.
BRANDI GLANVILLE BELIEVES SHE CONTRACTED 'SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED RINGWORM' IN HER THROAT
"A criminal complaint is merely an accusation," Caggiano added. "Despite this accusation, the defendant is presumed innocent unless and until she has been proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law."
Gabriella was reportedly the family member who called 911 during an alleged domestic dispute before Milania was arrested for simple assault. (Teresa Giudice Instagram)
Milania pleaded not guilty and was released pending an upcoming court appearance . According to Page Six , her next court hearing has been postponed until Dec. 1.
Meanwhile, Teresa recently alleged that Milania had "fentanyl in her system" during an incident at the Tampa International Airport .
REALITY STAR CLAIMS DAUGHTER, 20, 'HAD FENTANYL IN HER SYSTEM' IN AIRPORT BODYCAM
Teresa made the claim while attempting to explain her daughter's behavior during an encounter with officers at the Florida airport last month, according to bodycam footage obtained by Page Six .
Milania fired back in the footage and said, "Cause I was laced ... I go to college," before Gia told her, "You're reckless."
REALITY STAR'S SON, 15, INDICTED ON 7 COUNTS STEMMING FROM ALLEGED ASSAULT
It’s unclear when exactly the fentanyl incident occurred and what substance Milania was allegedly given or who she believed was responsible.
Milania's next court hearing will take place on Dec. 1. (Kevin Mazur)
At the beginning of the bodycam footage obtained by Page Six , Milania requested to speak to her mother. One officer asked Milania to sit down and reminded her that she was "not controlling the situation."
The "RHONJ" star shared a lengthy statement on social media after the bodycam footage was released last week.
"As a mother, there is nothing more important to me than the health, safety, and well-being of my children," she wrote. "The past few months have been incredibly difficult for our family, and I feel it is important to say something while also protecting my daughter during an extremely vulnerable time in her life."

"Milania has experienced tremendous heartbreak and significant psychological trauma after losing two of her best friends," Teresa continued. "Grief affects everyone differently, and watching your child try to process that kind of loss is something no parent can ever truly prepare for. Right now, my only focus is my daughter – making sure she is surrounded by love, family, support, and the care she needs."
Teresa said her daughter was grieving and asked for compassion during the difficult time. (Teresa Giudice/Instagram)

"I understand that because our family has lived much of our lives in the public eye, there will naturally be questions and speculation," she added. "But Milania is my daughter before she is anything else. She is a young woman going through an incredibly difficult and deeply personal time, and she deserves the opportunity to heal without every moment of her pain being analyzed publicly."
"I am asking, from one mother to another, and from one family to all of you, to please show Milania compassion and kindness and allow her the privacy she needs right now. We are incredibly grateful to everyone who has reached out with love, prayers, and support. It means more to our family than you know."
Milania appeared on a number of episodes of "The Real Housewives of New Jersey" with Teresa. (Manny Carabel)

"At this time, we respectfully ask the media and the public to give Milania and our entire family the privacy and space we need as we navigate this together. articles.title_orig: Yemen's government declares a major operation against the Houthis, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Yemen's government declares a major operation against the Houthis, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
The Saudi-led “Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen” pledged full support on Sunday as Yemen’s internationally recognized government announced the start of a major military offensive aimed at rolling back recent gains by the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
Last month, the Iran-backed Houthis carried out a lightning offensive down the Red Sea coast, successfully seizing control of a key port and further putting pressure on the safety of international shipping.
Rashad al-Alimi, head of Yemen’s presidential council, said in a televised speech on Sunday that the ‌military ⁠operations aimed to reclaim the ​remaining ​territory held ‌by Houthis ⁠and restore ​state ​authority across the ⁠country.
An offensive had been widely expected amid dozens of Saudi airstrikes against Houthi positions and further Houthi gains in southern Yemen.
The renewed fighting has already forced tens of thousands of people from their homes, and what happens next could shift the balance of power in Yemen and further exacerbate an already bleak humanitarian crisis. Three out of every four families in parts of Yemen are going hungry because of the surge in fighting, the World Food Program said last week.
Al-Alimi said the decision to launch operations followed “the Houthi militias’ continued mobilization, escalation and attacks, as well as their threats against civilians, facilities, neighboring countries, and international shipping lanes.”
In a separate statement, military spokesperson Majid Al-Nuzaili said government forces had begun a “battle for liberation” aimed at ending Houthi control over remaining territory and restoring state institutions.
Al-Nuzaili also called on fighters aligned with the Houthis to lay down their arms and return to their homes, saying the government remained committed to protecting civilians during the offensive.
The Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said they will continue providing “full operational support” to Yemeni government forces in what he described as efforts to restore state institutions and end “the Houthi coup.”
Al-Maliki also accused the Houthis of continuing attacks against Saudi Arabia and international shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
“Such threats undermine regional and international security, jeopardize freedom of navigation and international trade, the lifeblood of the global economy,” he added.
Yemen’s Houthi-controlled armed forces said on Sunday that Saudi Arabia had carried out 106 air and missile strikes over the previous 24 hours targeting the capital Sanaa and other areas of the country.
The Houthi statement did not provide details on casualties or damage resulting from the reported attacks.
In retaliation for airstrikes against Sanaa and other locations, the Houthis claimed Sunday that they had struck vital Saudi energy facilities.
“The first targeted Aramco company in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco company in the Khurais area,” causing large fires at the targeted sites, a Houthi military statement said.
There has been no word from the Saudis on the claimed strikes.
Early in September, the Houthis took a swath of Yemen’s Red Sea coast as far south as the critical Bab al Mandeb waterway, a chokepoint for commercial shipping crossing into the Indian Ocean.
They announced that Saudi shipping trying to use the strait would be targeted, threatening additional pressure on global trade and energy routes.
The Houthis have fired ballistic missiles and drones at multiple targets in Saudi Arabia since late July, including industrial and energy infrastructure.
Much of the recent fighting has been in the southern region of Taiz, as the Houthis have sought to cut off government forces in the regional capital. The Houthis claimed on Sunday to have taken a critical highway linking Taiz with the seat of the Yemeni government in Aden.
Taiz is the third largest city in Yemen, with a population of several hundred thousands. It is also home to thousands of government troops.
Further east, in the al-Jawf region, the Houthis on Sunday claimed to have inflicted heavy casualties on government forces with a barrage of missiles and drones as they redeployed for the new offensive.
Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi airstrikes and a blockade of Houthi areas, started fighting the Houthis more than a decade ago.
On Monday, officials from Saudi Arabia will convene with Turkish and Pakistani officials in Riyadh to discuss regional developments.
The meeting is part of the Strategic and Political Defense Committee, a NATO-style defense pact established in August , which is committed to organizing security and military cooperation in the region. The Saudi foreign ministry has said that it “does not represent an effort to establish a military axis or a sectarian bloc.”
The war in Yemen, which began in March 2015, had killed 377,000 people by the end of 2021, including those killed by direct and indirect causes, according to the United Nations. Over 150,000 of these deaths were the direct result of the armed conflict, it said, while more have died as a result of hunger and disease due to the humanitarian crisis caused by the war.
A 2022 UN-brokered truce brought a period of relatively low levels of hostilities between the two sides until violence surged again in August.

articles.content_orig:
Tim Mulkerin is a freelance writer, editor, and social media manager who has been working in digital media and the tech world since 2016.
He has a bachelor's degree in art history and is currently pursuing a master's degree in communicative sciences and disorders from New York University. He lives in Brooklyn, New York.
If you’re looking for hints and answers for Strands for Sunday, October 4, 2026, read on—I’ll share some clues and tips, and finally the solution to the puzzle with the theme “Grab your tokens.”
For an easy way to come back to our Strands hints every day, bookmark this page . You can also find our past hints there as well, in case you want to know what you missed in a previous puzzle. (If you play Wordle or Connections , check out our hints for those games, too.)
Below, I’ll give you some oblique hints at today’s Strands answers. And farther down the page, I’ll reveal the spangram and the answers. Scroll slowly and take just the hints you need!
You need tokens to play this kind of thing, perhaps at a mall or a Dave & Buster’s.
We’re about to give away the answers to today’s Strands puzzle.
Today’s spangram is ARCADEGAMES.
The theme words today are ASTEROIDS, FROGGER, CENTIPEDE, SCRAMBLE, PONG.
Here’s what the board looks like when the puzzle is solved:
Is this related to an arcade, maybe? I can make ARCADE in the bottom left, but it’s not a hit. Maybe it’s part of the spangram.
I can make ASTEROIDS, a classic arcade game title, in the upper left. 🔵
Yeah, the spangram is ARCADEGAMES. 🟡
FROGGER is to the right of ASTEROIDS. 🔵
PONG is in the bottom right. 🔵
CENTIPEDE is along the bottom of the spangram. 🔵
You can find the Strands game on the New York Times website and in the NYT Games app.
When you start playing, you’ll see a game board with an assortment of letters, flanked by a clue that gives a hint at the board’s theme—this will be a phrase, like “Better with age.” Your job is to find the hidden words within the board that reflect the puzzle’s theme.
The most important word to find is the “spangram,” a word that more explicitly states the puzzle’s theme. (For example, the spangram for the puzzle with the theme "Better with age" is FERMENTED, which describes products that are, you guessed it, better with age.) The spangram will span the entire game board, either from left to right or top to bottom (hence the name). When you find the spangram, it will be highlighted in yellow. Solving the spangram usually makes the rest of the puzzle much easier to complete.
In Strands, words can travel any direction (up, down, left, right, and diagonal), and you will only use each letter once. There is only one correct solution. When you correctly identify one of the puzzle’s words (for example, KOMBUCHA, MISO, or KIMCHI), it will be highlighted in blue.
If you are struggling to solve the puzzle, you can submit any non-theme words you see (as long as they are four letters or more) to receive credit toward a single hint. If you submit three non-theme words, the “Hint” button will be clickable; if you click it, all of the letters in one of the theme words will be highlighted for you. You will still have to link these highlighted letters in the right order to form one of the theme words. If there is already a hint on the board and you use another hint before solving for that word, that word’s letter order will be revealed.
Unlike Connections and Wordle, you cannot fail Strands. When you submit guesses, you will either correctly identify an answer, receive credit toward a hint, or the text will shake back and forth, indicating that the word you submitted is too short or not valid. You can't run out of guesses, and there is no time limit.
You win when you’ve correctly used all the letters on the board, meaning that you have identified the spangram and all of the theme words. Like other NYT games, upon solving the puzzle, you will see a shareable card that indicates how you performed that day: blue dots 🔵 indicate theme words you found, the yellow dot 🟡 indicates when you found the spangram, and a lightbulb 💡 indicates words that you received a hint for.
Not the day you're after? Here's the solution to today's Strands.

articles.title_orig: Polish activists launch abortion pill locker to bypass near-total ban
articles.title_zh: Polish activists launch abortion pill locker to bypass near-total ban
articles.content_orig:
‘AbortOmat’ in Warsaw offers novel way to challenge country’s restrictions and allow women swift, anonymous access
They call it the “world’s first parcel locker for abortion pills”. Polish campaigners have launched a new means of distribution as part of their ongoing effort to skirt the country’s near-total ban on abortion.
Painted pink and framed by zebra-striped curtains, the 22-compartment “AbortOmat” in Warsaw allows women to access the pills swiftly and anonymously using a six-digit code. The service was envisaged for those who cannot or do not want to wait days for mail delivery due to a missed miscarriage or health complications, or who worry about receiving the pills at home.
“And why not?” said Kinga Jelinska, the director of the Women Help Women foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team, the two groups behind last week’s launch.
“You can order underwear, cosmetics, mascara, whatever and receive it practically the same or next day,” she said. “Why not abortion pills, where in some cases there might be more urgency?”
The innovation comes six years after people across Poland took to the streets to protest against the tightening of abortion laws that already ranked among the strictest in Europe, setting off the country’s largest demonstrations since the fall of communism. In 2023, the protests were credited with helping to propel Donald Tusk, and his promises to overhaul the laws within 100 days, into power.
Since then, political stagnation has set in, said Jelinska, citing comments made last year by Tusk in which the prime minister said there was “simply no majority” to change the laws to allow abortions until the 12th week of pregnancy. Tusk instead hinted that his government was intent on doing things differently, telling reporters that it would not prosecute those who helped to facilitate abortions.
While the possession or ingestion of abortion pills is not outlawed in Poland, provision of the medication or helping someone to obtain it is considered a crime punishable by up to three years in prison.
The locker offers a novel way to challenge these restrictions, said Jelinska. “It’s a little bit of a hack on the law,” she said. “The law is about directly giving to someone. So here we have a machine in between, which makes the legality of everything much more vague.”
The locker sits inside the abortion centre that was opened in March 2025 by the Abortion Dream Team. Described as the first of its kind in democratic Poland, it offers a safe space for people to consult on abortion options or receive support while they take the pill.
after newsletter promotion
Symbolically located across the street from the Polish parliament, the centre has allowed campaigners to shine a spotlight on the continued need for abortion access in Poland while also providing services to a wide array of people, said Jelinska. “It has exceeded our expectations.”
But it had also laid bare how few in power were willing to stand up for them, she said. “The one thing that has surprised us, and it speaks to the political situation, is that there are protests in front of the centre; three, sometimes four times a week.”
While usually less than a dozen people turn up, the protesters regularly use sirens and vuvuzelas to make their point, leaving campaigners worried that the noise levels would eventually result in neighbours asking the centre to relocate. “Neither the city or the police have reacted. So that has been a big disappointment to us,” said Jelinska.
It was a glimpse of how these organisations had increasingly felt abandoned by politicians, even as about 50,000 people in Poland contacted the wider network of pro-choice organisations last year seeking help, said Jelinska. “I think in Poland, abortion access won’t be solved by politics but by women and communities,” she said. “We cannot trust politicians with our own bodies.”

articles.title_orig: They survived World War II and lost decades, but not 2026. Japan's century-old businesses are disappearing at a record pace
articles.title_zh: They survived World War II and lost decades, but not 2026. Japan's century-old businesses are disappearing at a record pace
articles.content_orig:
Founded in 1858, Japanese sesame oil maker Kadoya Sesame Mills has witnessed the country transform over generations — surviving world wars and Japan's asset bubble.
Now, more than two decades after listing on the Jasdaq Securities Exchange in 2004, Kadoya is set to go private through a tender offer backed by Japanese private equity firm Integral. The move comes as the company navigates rising raw-material costs and heightened geopolitical risks.
Japan's long-established businesses are being tested by factors ranging from a shrinking domestic market and labor shortages to succession challenges, experts told CNBC. Bankruptcies among Japanese businesses with more than 100 years of history are occurring at a record pace, reaching 112 in the first eight months of 2026, according to Teikoku Databank.
Japan's century-old companies have achieved enduring prosperity through a long-term perspective fostered by family ownership, strong roots in local communities and a business approach that stays within their means, said Shigeto Nagai, head of Japan economics at Oxford Economics.
Their long histories and years of capital accumulation have also left them with sound balance sheets and stable profit margins.
"However, they are increasingly concerned that they cannot foresee a future of sustained high profits over the long term and fear they will gradually fall into decline," Nagai said.
Rising costs and labor shortages have become major challenges for Japanese companies in the post-pandemic business environment, said Harumi Taguchi, principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
"Although inflation has made it easier for companies to pass on costs than during the deflationary period, many still cannot fully reflect higher expenses in sales prices," Taguchi pointed out.
Higher costs are particularly difficult for smaller and domestically focused Japanese businesses to absorb given their weaker sales bases, she said. Pricing power is therefore a key factor in determining which companies can adapt.
Bankruptcies linked to higher prices jumped 23.8% to 556 in the first half of 2026, while labor-shortage bankruptcies climbed 12.4% to 227, according to Teikoku Databank.
Sube Shoten, a tofu maker founded in 1877 during Japan's Meiji era, reportedly ceased operations in May and began preparing to file for bankruptcy as low profit margins and a recent surge in raw-material costs clouded its business outlook.
Another major challenge is intensifying domestic competition and labor shortages as Japan's birth rate declines and its population ages, Nagai said.
Expanding overseas is another challenge as the domestic market, historically a stable source of revenue, continues to shrink. But there is no "one-size-fits-all" prescription, Nagai added.
Succession is another growing challenge. Bankruptcies linked to a lack of successors rose 16.9% to 312 from a year earlier in the first half of 2026, according to Teikoku Databank.
A weaker yen, corporate governance reforms, activist pressure and succession challenges among founder-owned businesses are pushing owners and boards to reassess their options, alongside broader pressures including inflation, tariffs, labor costs and interest rates, said Paul Aversano, managing director and global practice leader of Alvarez & Marsal's Global Transaction Advisory Group.
"It is that combination, rather than any single issue, that is shaping decisions," he said.
