articles.title_orig: Multiple Security Failures Allowed FlyDubai Pilot Into Cockpit
articles.title_zh: Multiple Security Failures Allowed FlyDubai Pilot Into Cockpit
articles.content_orig:
By Alexander Cornwell and Maayan Lubell
JERUSALEM, Oct 5 (Reuters) - The flydubai co-pilot who stabbed his captain in an alleged attempt to crash the plane has told UAE interrogators he planned the attack before he was hired by ‌the Dubai state-owned airline, according to two Israeli officials with knowledge of the probe.
A third source briefed on the ‌UAE probe said the co-pilot, an Omani national, had planned to crash Wednesday's flight into Ben-Gurion airport near Tel Aviv. He had also operated a flight ​to Tel Aviv earlier this year and intended to hijack and crash the plane then, but opted not to, the source added.
It was not immediately clear why the co-pilot changed his mind on that previous flight, although the co-pilot is thought to have known someone onboard, the source said.
All of the sources spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the investigation. UAE and Israeli authorities did not immediately respond ‌to a request for comment, nor did flydubai.
The ⁠co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073, which was bound for Israel from Dubai last Wednesday, attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said, calling the incident a "terrorist ⁠attack".
Two sources have said the co-pilot is an Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami. Israeli officials have not named the co-pilot but have said he is from Oman. UAE authorities and flydubai have not publicly disclosed the co-pilot's identity.
Reuters has not been able to independently reach al-Hammami, who ​is ​in UAE custody, for comment. The UAE has not announced any formal ​charges against him and it is not known if ‌he has appointed legal counsel. Oman has not commented on the incident.
The two Israeli officials said the co-pilot told interrogators that he had applied for a job at Dubai state-owned flydubai after searching for airlines that fly to Tel Aviv.
The third source said that Israel was being continuously updated about the investigation from the UAE.
Disaster on board flight FZ1073 was averted after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot. The pilot, Indian national Smit Machchhar, survived the attack and has been hailed as a hero for managing to open ‌the cockpit door. The plane was carrying more than 170 passengers and ​crew, most of them Israeli.
A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took ​control of the aircraft and landed it at a ​regional airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities and later transferred ‌to the UAE on Thursday.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ​has said pilots who are citizens ​of countries that Israel does not have diplomatic relations with, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to Israel. It is not clear how the co-pilot came to be assigned to the flight to Tel Aviv, and Netanyahu has ​since ordered a review of foreign airlines ‌flying to Israel.
A multi-agency Australian counterterrorism unit is investigating links to Australia of the co-pilot, who was once enrolled ​at RMIT University in Melbourne, Victoria. A fourth source said that the co-pilot studied there around a decade ​ago.
(Reporting by Alexander Cornwell and Maayan Lubell; Editing by Edwina Gibbs)

articles.title_orig: Florida GOP governor candidate Byron Donalds courts skeptical Black voters
articles.title_zh: Florida GOP governor candidate Byron Donalds courts skeptical Black voters
articles.content_orig:
MIAMI — For most of his nine years in Congress and Florida's state House, Republican Rep. Byron Donalds, of Florida, rarely made his race part of his political pitch. This past weekend, in a string of Black voter outreach events across the Miami area, he did — carefully, and on his own terms.
In an interview with CBS News, the Republican nominee for Florida governor said he's now targeting "north of 20%" of the Black vote.
"I think there's a lot of Black voters who are looking at my campaign because they're just trying to figure out who's going to be the best person to lead Florida into the future," Donalds said. "I think the other thing with Black voters: they're starting to not be as monolithically tied to the Democrat Party."
For comparison, around 13% of Black voters backed Gov. Ron DeSantis's reelection bid in 2022, according to CBS News exit polls. President Trump won around 15% of Black votes in Florida during his 2024 presidential bid.
In 2024, Donalds was one of Mr. Trump's most visible surrogates to Black voters nationally, co-headlining a multi-city tour with Rep. Wesley Hunt of Texas billed as "Congress, Cigars & Cognac" — informal, sit-down conversations meant to make the case for Mr. Trump in rooms that weren't always receptive. Now he's running that same playbook for himself, as the principal rather than the surrogate.
A potential win for Donalds would put him in an exclusive club of Black state executives. Only three elected governors have been Black in U.S. history. Donalds is among three nominees this year who would be the first Black Republican governors ever elected.
Asked what it would mean to him to make history, Donalds paused, smiled to himself, and let his guard down for a moment. "It's wild, honestly," he told CBS News — a rare admission from a candidate who has spent his campaign avoiding identity-based appeals.
"I don't talk about my race in this campaign," Donalds told a crowd at the Black Professionals Summit's Legacy Con on Saturday, one of several stops targeting the key voting bloc. "Florida is a meritocracy. Here in Florida, we have people who have come from so many different parts of the country. What they really care about now is: Can you get the job done?"
Legacy Con's organizers told CBS News they also invited Democratic nominee David Jolly to address the summit, but he didn't attend, citing a scheduling conflict.
With less than a month of campaigning left, Donalds also pushed back on criticism that his minority outreach was new or narrow. "We're actually targeting every voter," he said, pointing to his team's door-knocking aimed at Black voters in North Miami and Broward County, Hispanic voters in Doral and Hialeah, and more.
But some voters he met during his South Florida swing say his loyalty to the president is clouding their opinion of him. At a retail stop at the Black-owned Lorna's Caribbean Restaurant in Miami Gardens, Jermaine Woodside, 54, said he came in skeptical but left more open to the congressman after an hour-long dinner conversation, even as he said bluntly that Donalds should not associate himself with Mr. Trump. "That's going to hurt him, and that's the reason why I was reluctant to be a part of his campaign," Woodside told CBS News.
Donalds told CBS News voters shouldn't judge him solely on his history with Mr. Trump.
"Look at the issues I'm pushing forward. Look at the ideas that I talk about. Yes, the president's endorsed me. Yes, a couple years ago I endorsed him to be president. But I'm running to be governor of Florida," he said.
Not everyone was swayed. Miami resident Kalyn James came alone to a meet-and-greet Donalds hosted at an outdoor event space in the predominantly Black Overtown neighborhood. James quietly protested the event by holding a sign that read "Vote Blue" with Donalds' name crossed out while he worked the room, talking to other attendees.
"I just don't think that he has a buy-in that he thinks he has," James told CBS News. "And honestly, [his win] would make history, but I think he'd be on the wrong side of history."
Jasmine Burney-Clark, founder of the nonpartisan voting rights group Equal Ground, had sharper criticism. She noted Donalds declined to sign her organization's candidate pledge, affirming an intent to sign into law a Democratic-backed state voting rights bill — which Jolly did sign — and argued his weekend events were not genuine.
"Byron Donalds has been Black at the start of this election, and he will be Black at the end of this election," Burney-Clark told CBS News. "Black voters are not going to be fooled by his targeting and his manipulation tactics to pander to get their vote."
The outreach comes as recent polling shows a surprisingly tight race for an office a Democrat hasn't won since the 1990s. For Donalds, the math is clear even if the politics are complicated: close the gap with Black voters, and Democrats' path back to the governor's mansion gets much harder.

articles.title_orig: The magical world of ‘The Tempest’ on stage at American Shakespeare Center
articles.title_zh: The magical world of ‘The Tempest’ on stage at American Shakespeare Center
articles.content_orig:
Well, that was fast — fall has arrived, the temperature dropping from 90 to 60 like it had just spotted a state trooper, as some internet jokester has observed.
The time is more than ripe for all of us to get out of town, explore the colors of the season, grab a half bushel of apples, and, of course, check out the new Fall Repertory at the American Shakespeare Center in Staunton, Virginia.
Leading off this season’s rep is The Tempest , Shakespeare’s swan song, in which Prospero, an exiled nobleman, washed up for years on a strange foreign isle, earns his way back home with his political powers restored. And he seems to manage this by way of his fantastical book learning (I mean, fall being back-to-school time, it seems fitting to remind our kids that books can sometimes have truly miraculous powers).
Co-directors Doreen Bechtol and Matt Radford Davies have created a magical world in the Blackfriars Playhouse. With their cast, led by the magisterial Angela Iannone as Prospero, we are given a tour of an exotic locale, and get to study the all-too-human goings-on of its inhabitants.
As the pre-show music fades away, we see Miranda, played with ebullient charm by Isabel Sanchez , waving hello to a ship she sees off in the distance, only to watch as it is suddenly engulfed in a storm staged in true Blackfriars passion, with ropes a-tangle and actors tossed every which way. That none of them will perish, and that they will survive to endure far greater personal challenges than a storm at sea, is of course the ultimate goal.
Miranda’s shock and dismay are eased by her father’s assurances — to explain to her why the storm had to happen; however, Prospero also decides it is time for Miranda to learn of her true origins and her father’s long ordeal. Iannone’s Prospero — decked out powerfully by Elizabeth Wislar ’s costumes — is a study in calm authority; the measured tone she adopts throughout this opening scene can be deceiving, because it is part and parcel with Prospero’s sober, carefully choreographed revenge on her persecutors.
The story unfolds, of course, at numerous places on Prospero’s island — father is separated from son, son is separated from the rest, servants are separated from their masters. This creates the perfect setting for Shakespeare’s multiple plots to unfold, in parallel. Each shipwrecked party is brought out one by one, each with their own storyline. And the confusion that seems to reign in so many of the later plays ( Cymbeline , anyone?) is here resolved with a masterly touch.
Prospero guarantees that the nobility are isolated from the rest of their party — and we see that even on a desert island they’re still up to their old tricks. The conniving Duke Antonio of Milan (pronounced like “villain,” naturally), who had usurped Prospero years before, is played here with relish by Christopher Seiler ; and he is no sooner safe on dry land than he plots another coup, on behalf of his companion Sebastian ( Ronan Melomo , an able partner-in-crime), brother to King Alonso of Naples. That this plot is foiled by Prospero’s powerful spirit, Ariel — the sharp Isa Guitian , who soon busies herself putting out fires all over the island — is to be expected.
This story of brothers plotting against brothers is contrasted nicely with a classic love-at-first-sight encounter between Miranda and Ferdinand, Prince of Naples. As Ferdinand, Nick Ericksen is every inch the romantic lead, but not without a moment of clumsy silliness so that we don’t get too dreamy-eyed about him.
For comic relief, it’s hard to beat the way Shakespeare sets up Morgan Rose Ford ’s Trinculo and K.P. Powell ’s Stephano. You’ve got a court jester and butler, washed up with a barrel of the good stuff to drink — having stumbled on with a barrel, they will of course stumble a long while to come. And Caliban’s discovery of this pair of drunkards and their divine liquor leads to some comical moments indeed. Which leads me to…
The most striking element here is the treatment of Caliban, played here with wary resentment by Ronald Román-Meléndez . His Caliban draws strategically from Manuel Palazon Blasco ’s Spanish translation La Tempestad , a nod to The Tempest ‘s origins in fantastical tales of the New World, which had already filtered back to Shakespeare’s London. The mixture of English — directed toward Prospero & Co. — and Spanish, spoken under his breath, creates a fascinating new dimension to the play. Half the point is that Caliban already had his own language; it was his own island after all; but he then had to learn the language of his colonial master in order to survive. That Román-Meléndez’s Caliban is entitled to his own language and — even more radically — his own thoughts is an apt reflection on the complicated legacy of the play, and of Europe’s presence in the New World.
It seems fitting that Román-Meléndez opens the musical pre-show by serenading us with Juanes ’ ballad “La Camisa Negra” (The Black Shirt), a song of betrayal that — although about a lover — seems to channel some of Caliban’s own resentment. Other memorable selections include K.P. Powell leading the audience in a rousing chorus of George Michael ’s anthem, “Freedom,” followed by Isabel Sanchez singing Patty Griffin ’s pensive “Row, Row, Row.” At intermission, the cast also pays homage to the late Dolly Parton with a beautiful version of “Islands in the Stream”; then, with ukelele in hand, Ericksen and Seiler team up to pay homage to Israel Kamakawiwo’ole ’s “Over the Rainbow/What a Wonderful World.”
The Blackfriars Playhouse has just celebrated its first 25 years in Staunton, and the ASC’s new production of The Tempest is a great way to show the company’s strengths. They have demonstrated how much is to be gained from a commitment to fun, lights-on theater. OK, so some will call it “original practices,” but let’s be clear: the original theaters of Shakespeare’s day were a helluva lot more fun than the black-box, lights-out, pseudo-Calvinist aesthetic of so many other playhouses these days.
Running Time: Two hours and 30 minutes, including one 15-minute intermission.
The Tempest plays through November 13, 2026, in repertory with David Catlin’s adaptation of Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein (through November 14) and Jen Silverman’s Witch (through November 14), presented by American Shakespeare Center at the Blackfriars Playhouse, 10 South Market Street, Staunton, VA. For tickets (starting at $39), call the box office at (540) 851-3400 or purchase them online. ASC also offers a Local Rush deal of 50% off tickets on Wednesdays and Thursdays. Learn more here.

articles.title_orig: Brit-born rock singer & Canadian Idol star Sass Jordan dies aged 63 as heartbreaking tributes flood in
articles.title_zh: Brit-born rock singer & Canadian Idol star Sass Jordan dies aged 63 as heartbreaking tributes flood in
articles.content_orig:
Sass Jordan, the Montreal-raised rock singer whose career spanned nearly four decades, has died at 65.
Jordan died Friday surrounded by those who loved her most, said a statement from family spokesperson Eric Alper.
The statement described Jordan as an inimitable force of nature and an irreplaceable being of light and joy.
A cause of death has not been released.
Jordan's debut album, Tell Somebody , was released in 1988, and she won the Juno Award for most promising female vocalist of the year in 1989. Her second album, Racine , released in 1992, included hits like Make You a Believer .
She was nominated several times for a Juno Award for best female vocalist. She was also a judge on all six seasons of the reality television competition show Canadian Idol .
Then and now: Sass Jordan on the 30th anniversary of Tell Somebody
She was born on Dec. 23, 1960 in Birmingham, England, and raised in Montreal, according to the statement.
Geoff Kulawick, former president of Stony Plain Records, which released Jordan's last two albums, described her as "bold, beautiful and brave."
Jordan recorded her 2020 album, Rebel Moon Blues , and her 2022 album, Bitches Blues , with her husband Derek Sharp while signed with Stony Plains.
Kulawick said he was a fan even before Jordan signed to his label, and that he convinced her she could "really belt out the blues" on her final two records.
"Her voice really stood out and the way she was able to connect emotionally … brought her tons of fans," he said.
Canadian producer and songwriter Derek Downham said they "really hit it off" when they first met at Toronto's Massey Hall a few years ago.
"She was a ray of light and a really hilarious person," said Downham, who also played drums alongside Jordan last December at singer-songwriter Andy Kim's annual holiday charity concert in Montreal.
"The biggest heartbreak for me is that I won't get to see that laugh again."
As one of the few women in rock when she started out, Jordan helped make space for other woman in a male-dominated genre, he said.
"She was coming up in a time where it wasn't easy," he said. "It's nice to see a strong female poke through and really show people how it's done."
Sass Jordan says she thinks of 'music as medicine' and she still loves to connect with fans
Downham said Jordan was an inspiration to all young performers.
"I hope that people remember her for leading the way and that she led with love every time."

Russia has struck a key bridge in Kyiv just as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital to meet President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The unannounced visit, marked by the sound of air sirens and explosions, came on Sunday to underscore Germany’s support for the nation at a time when Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities are increasing.
In a written statement, Merz said he “travelled to Kyiv today because Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks”.
“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said.
Merz and Zelenskyy met at the National Academy of Sciences, which was struck by a Russian drone on September 28.
Zelenskyy told Merz that Kyiv’s citizens are going through “terrible nights and days” due to the ongoing Russian attacks.
Merz was accompanied by his economy minister, as well as executives from several large German companies, such as Siemens Energy and Diehl Defence.
Ukraine and Germany are also expected to finalise a deal to produce drones and other weapons together that can travel more than 600 miles (965.6km) in an effort to strike deeper into Russia.
Germany has been one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters. In April, the two countries signed a military pact worth more than $4bn. On Sunday, a $1.1bn military aid package is set to be announced, alongside $394m to repair damage to Ukraine’s energy sector.
Merz’s visit comes a day after Russia warned foreign diplomats and nationals to leave the capital to avoid getting hurt.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence promised to intensify strikes on Ukraine after Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Reuters news agency that it is doubling down on targeting Russian oil refineries after several civilians were killed and wounded over the weekend.
The strike that hit the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River on Sunday also damaged a road and the supply of hot water in the area, according to a social media statement from Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko. It is the second bridge in the capital to be hit this weekend.
Russia’s all-out war on Ukraine is in its fifth year. Both sides have increased the number of drone and missile attacks on infrastructure, logistics and military sites in recent months.

articles.title_orig: How was Flydubai co-pilot cleared despite being deemed a security risk?
articles.title_zh: How was Flydubai co-pilot cleared despite being deemed a security risk?
articles.content_orig:
A Flydubai co-pilot accused of attacking his captain with an emergency axe and attempting to seize control of the flight bound for Israel had previously been barred from flying over concerns about alleged “extremist” views, raising questions about how he was allowed to fly to Tel Aviv.
The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national, according to multiple media reports.
The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has described the September 30 incident aboard Flight FZ1073 as an attempted “terrorist” operation .
But investigators are still working to establish the motive and whether anyone else was connected to the attack, which has raised concerns about pilot vetting and aviation security.
So, what security checks do pilots have to go through and how al-Hammami may have evaded background checks?
That is now one of the central questions facing investigators.
Al-Hammami had previously been barred from flying in Oman because of concerns that he had adopted “extremist” views and was instead moved to an administrative role at Oman Air, according to sources who spoke to the AP news agency.
He was subsequently hired by Flydubai.
A Gulf diplomat told AP that al-Hammami had undergone standard security checks before being hired. It wasn’t immediately clear to what extent the co-pilot was vetted.
The US-based network CNN reported that a LinkedIn profile bearing al-Hammami’s name said he had spent seven years at Oman Air before leaving in February 2025. The profile said he joined Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 and left in January this year.
It is unclear what those alleged views were or whether Oman informed other countries or airlines about its concerns.
Background checks for commercial pilots vary by airline and country, with no single global standard governing the process, an airline pilot and instructor told Al Jazeera.
The captain with an international airline who chose to remain anonymous said pilots are generally required to obtain aviation medical certification from the regulator in the country where they are licensed to fly.
In the UAE, that is overseen by the General Civil Aviation Authority (GCAA), he said.
Some airlines also require prospective pilots to provide police clearance certificates from their country of residence as part of pre-employment screening, the pilot added.
One type of check is a Class 1 medical assessment, which typically examines areas including vision, hearing, cardiovascular and neurological health, as well as conditions that could cause sudden incapacitation.
When it comes to security checks, aviation rules require background checks for personnel who have unescorted access to security-restricted areas.
Psychological assessments, drug and alcohol testing and other evaluations may be required depending on the jurisdiction.
Israel has some of the world’s toughest aviation security measures.
As a result, questions have been raised over how the alleged attacker was allowed to operate a flight to Israel, despite reportedly being an Omani national and Oman having no diplomatic relations with Israel.
According to the Haaretz newspaper, Israeli authorities received the Flydubai flight’s crew and passenger lists before it departed. Under a law passed in 2023, airlines are required to provide information about passengers and crew members, including their names and nationalities, to Israel up to 48 hours before a flight.
The Israel Tax Authority confirmed to Haaretz that it had received the lists for the Flydubai flight. The media outlet reported that the information is also supposed to be available to Israeli security bodies, including the Mossad, police and Shin Bet, to identify people who may pose a security risk.
According to security sources who spoke to Haaretz, the Transportation Ministry’s Security Department and the Mossad are responsible for checking foreign flight crews and issuing alerts if concerns arise.
However, two security sources told Haaretz that while the Transportation Ministry holds responsibility “on paper”, it does not have its own intelligence capacity.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that Israel has longstanding arrangements with foreign airlines aimed at preventing pilots who are nationals of countries without diplomatic relations with Israel from flying there.
Netanyahu has described what happened as a “loophole” and Israel says it will now strengthen its checks.
The UAE has not yet publicly established a motive or announced whether investigators believe al-Hammami acted alone.
UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said on Saturday that the latest ‘terrorist’ attack is a new warning that the region’s fight against “extremism” is not over.
“This underscores the importance of the UAE’s early and firm stance: no tolerance for extremism and no leniency towards its rhetoric. Security begins with confronting hatred and drying up the sources of extremism,” he posted on X.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Rushes to Withdraw Bombers From U.K. Air Base After New Threats
articles.title_zh: U.S. Rushes to Withdraw Bombers From U.K. Air Base After New Threats
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Air Force withdrew all of its B-1 bombers stationed at an air base in southern England that is used by American military forces to strike Iran after an investigation discovered a planned terror attack, The Associated Press reported Sunday.
The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the United States, AP reported, citing a Pentagon official who was not authorized to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on condition of anonymity.
Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance and others have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war, AP said. These observers saw many B-1 bombers take off from the base on Sunday.
A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, authorities took six individuals into custody and later released them on bail during the investigation.
British authorities have linked the terror plot to Tehran, although Iran has denied involvement.
RAF Fairford is located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London and has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
At least two vessels were struck over the weekend in waters near Oman and Iran , the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported, as Tehran reiterated its position on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen unless its conditions for ending the war with the U.S. are met.
On Saturday, the UKMTO, a British maritime security alert service, said it received a report of a crude oil tanker being hit by an unknown projectile four nautical miles east of Oman. It said another tanker was reported as being similarly struck Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz, causing damage to its engine room.
Attacks on shipping in the strait, through which about a fifth of the world's oil supplies moved before the start of the U.S. and Israel-led war on Feb. 28, have been happening on a regular basis for weeks.
"The Strait of Hormuz will not open until Iran's seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum are met, and Iran will not regulate its national security with tweets from American officials," Iranian state media agency Nour News quoted Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf as saying Sunday.
President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed an interim deal in June, known as the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, that resulted in a brief hiatus in fighting.
Tehran's conditions for allowing ships to proceed freely through the Strait of Hormuz include a halt to U.S. "acts of aggression," an end to the U.S. naval blockade of its ports and economic warfare, and the release of Iranian assets.
A key demand of the U.S. has been that Iran dismantle its nuclear weapons program.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure reportedly came under renewed attacks.
Reuters reported Saturday that Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they had targeted a facility owned by Saudi Arabian oil giant Aramco in the capital Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones. The group said the attack was in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen's Sanaa and other provinces.
A large plume of smoke and fire rose above the facility, Reuters quoted a witness as saying.
Saudi authorities have not commented on the reported attack. Aramco did not immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request for comment.
If confirmed, it would be the latest escalation in what has effectively become a second front in the Iran war.
Some investors say they expect full-scale fighting to resume in the Middle East.
"The situation is fluid and volatile. To me, as we are developing and looking at the situation, it's not a question of if, but when the conflict resumes full force," Bader Al-Saif, founding president of Al-Saif Consulting, told CNBC's Access Middle East show on Friday.
The ongoing attacks and prospect of a further escalation have driven energy prices higher in recent weeks, raising inflation expectations globally and putting upward pressure on government borrowing costs .
Reports that the U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, along with an amphibious force carrying 2,000 Marines, pushed crude oil prices higher on Thursday. But prices edged lower Friday, after the Group of Seven nations announced the release of diesel and crude stocks to ease the burden on consumers.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, lost 6 cents to close at $102.25 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude shed $1.76 to settle at $91.11 per barrel.
— The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Digital media can be dangerous. Kids use it anyway. Here’s what parents can do
articles.title_zh: Digital media can be dangerous. Kids use it anyway. Here’s what parents can do
articles.content_orig:
In case you hadn’t heard from everyone that digital media can be bad for kids, new research warns just how harmful it can be to their health.
About 20% of instances of depression and 15% of obesity cases in young people are associated with excessive screen time, according to a meta-analysis of 121 global studies of children and digital media published Sunday as part of a series of papers in the medical journal The Lancet.
The research adds to the understanding of the extent to which kids’ digital media use has become a public health problem that health authorities should govern and regulate, said Louise Holly, lead author of the research on kids and digital media. It shouldn’t just fall on parents to solve these problems, said Holly, policy and research coordinator at the Digital Transformations for Health Lab, a Geneva, Switzerland-based global consortium.
12-year-olds with smartphones are more likely to develop eating disorders by 14
Not all kids face the same risks: Young people who have mental health vulnerabilities, less offline support and lower digital literacy are more likely to be harmed, according to the research.
The research utilized studies that often self-reported kids’ screen use, and many found that digital media use was associated with harms but couldn’t definitively say it caused them, Holly said.
Using digital media also causes far more cases of adverse health outcomes than beneficial ones in youth, according to the research.
Still, there are ways it can benefit kids’ health. It can give them outlets to achieve autonomy, explore their identities, find information, entertain themselves and make social connections, the research found.
It can have positive impacts on children when it “fulfills what they want it to do,” Holly said, and is used purposefully with support and supervision from caregivers, parents or guardians.
Since no amount of warnings seems to get kids off digital media, I recommend focusing on how it can be healthy for kids — and helping them avoid the risks.
Start by explaining to young people what’s happening in their heads, said Dr. Nicole Amoyal Pensak, a clinical psychologist and founder of Atlantic Coast Mind and Body in Little Silver, New Jersey. She was not involved in the research.
“They’re in a specific period of both vulnerability and opportunity because their brain is developing rapidly,” she said. “They have more power and control than they think.”
That’s because brains are very plastic in youth. Parts of their brains that kids use get strengthened, while those they don’t use atrophy.
Some of what happens during youth can’t be reversed. It’s another reason to rethink kids’ screen time
Try explaining it like driving, Pensak said. Adults want kids to be in the driver’s seat. Teach them “how to build new roads but get rid of old roads that are not serving them,” she said.
Pensak gives kids in her practice prunes to taste. Most don’t like them, so they try to avoid them in the future. That’s how we prune things from our brains, too, she said.
“When you don’t like something, or when something doesn’t make you feel good, you try to get rid of it,” she said — or at least reduce it. To figure out what to prune, teach kids to pay attention to how they think, act and feel when using digital media, Pensak said.
If a girl is comparing her body with others on social media, it’s time to reset.
“They need to not focus on that, not go over those roads,” Pensak said. If they do, their brain will learn to think that way and it will affect their mood and behaviors.
Be a shepherd helping kids find their way rather than someone who only controls access to their devices, Pensak said. You can do so by asking questions about their social media use and consuming content together.
Parents should also help kids explore roads that can be healthy for them.
Digital media shouldn’t replace in-person interactions, but it can complement them by helping children plan social gatherings or connect with like-minded people (as long as they do so safely).
It can also help young people learn new things, so yes to videos that teach them how to crochet, otherwise be creative or do things with their hands.
“It’s really hard to be depressed and anxious and thinking negative thoughts when you’re actively doing stuff with your hands,” Pensak said.
What makes young people reduce their social media use
Digital media can be especially helpful when kids are interested in activities that aren’t offered at school or they don’t do formally, she said. Maybe friends get together and make up a dance, recording it on video.
Things that pose challenges — think getting to the next level of a video game — are also great for kids’ brains. “As you build self-efficacy and confidence doing that, then you’ll take on another challenge,” Pensak said. “And this builds your brain in a really healthy, great way.”
This latest research confirms what parents know — digital media can be terrible for our kids. Unfortunately, more data is unlikely to get most kids off their devices. So, let’s try redirecting how they use them.
Kara Alaimo is a professor of communication at Fairleigh Dickinson University and advises parents, students and teachers on how to manage screen time. Her book “Over the Influence: Why Social Media Is Toxic for Women and Girls — And How We Can Take It Back” was published in 2024.

articles.title_orig: Cornell University to take ‘serious look’ at fraternities after rape allegations
articles.title_zh: Cornell University to take ‘serious look’ at fraternities after rape allegations
articles.content_orig:
Ivy League school’s president promises action after woman alleged she was drugged ⁠and raped by fraternity members
Cornell University will examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus after an outcry over the school’s handling ⁠of a student’s rape allegations, the Ivy League school’s president has said.
A civil lawsuit filed last month by the woman , who ⁠alleges she was drugged ⁠and raped in ​2024 by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity, has prompted outrage and soul-searching at Cornell over its campus culture at the ⁠school in Ithaca, New York.
In a video message on Saturday, the Cornell University president, Michael Kotlikoff, said the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the ⁠future. That included “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, Kotlikoff said.
“At ​their best, these organisations can provide ‌students with friendship, belonging, mentorship ‌and a powerful sense of community,” he said. “But being part of a group can never diminish ‌individual responsibility.“
The university would seek input, he said, from students, alumni and others on how to “preserve what is valuable about Greek life while strengthening individual accountability, transparency and a culture in which every member understands their responsibility to protect the safety and wellbeing of others”.
The lawsuit against Cornell, seven fraternity members and others, alleges that the school failed to adequately punish ‌some of the accused students.
The accused men have denied all wrongdoing, the New York Times has reported.
Cornell has defended its handling of the matter, saying that in 2024 it launched ​a comprehensive investigation and barred the Chi Phi fraternity from campus. The school said it also imposed a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions.
But “we must do better”, Kotlikoff said, adding: “We don’t have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves.”
He vowed that ⁠university officials would “be more transparent” about their actions related to the 2024 incident, but ​he did not detail ​specific initiatives that the university would take. “In ​the coming weeks, we will create additional opportunities for members of our ​community to ask ‌questions and hear directly ​from university leadership,” ​he said.
The case has reignited scrutiny of how law enforcement and universities handle sexual assault complaints, with students questioning whether processes are enough to protect them. It has also drawn the attention of New York state officials, who have appointed a special prosecutor to investigate.
As the special prosecutor, Letitia James, the New York attorney general, investigates, new attention has been drawn to the findings of a state-mandated sexual violence survey conducted by Cornell in 2025, which found that 35% of female undergraduates who completed the survey reported that they had experienced nonconsensual sexual contact while at the university.
The 2025 version of the survey was the first to specifically include unwanted choking or strangulation in the definition of nonconsensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation that students were asked about, in addition to nonconsensual penetration and/or sexual touching.
Guardian staff contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Why even resilient forests are struggling to regrow after wildfires
articles.title_zh: Why even resilient forests are struggling to regrow after wildfires
articles.content_orig:
Kim Desiato, a firefighter from Tucson, Arizona, stops to look for hot spots in the aftermath of the Lewis Lake Fire in Yellowstone National Park in August 1988. The fire forced the closure of the south entrance to the park.
(CNN) — As Monica Turner trekked across the western hills of Yellowstone National Park, the cold rain was inescapable. Even the constant movement of putting one foot in front of the other as she fought through a slew of dense branches could not warm her body. It was easy to forget it was July.
Four years later in 2017, Turner made the same journey. But instead of fighting the once compact forest, she was met with a desolate clearing as the sun pounded above her. After the Maple Fire the year before, all that was left of the towering trees was a smattering of survivors looking over a sea of skinny, pencil-like sticks sprouting from the charred dirt.
In Turner’s time as a researcher, she has seen massive destruction and its subsequent regrowth as she studied the impacts of Yellowstone’s 1988 fires, which left a crown jewel of the national park system scorched. This made the level of destruction Turner witnessed in 2017 even more shocking — especially as the area had burned before without this level of loss.
Researchers across the US are seeing a similar trend — forests that are historically adapted to fire are now often being obliterated by the fast-moving, high temperature wildfires that are becoming increasingly more common with climate change . These researchers are grappling with what it will mean for our world if the trees that are the centerpiece of these landscapes we love don’t recover like they once did.
The fire itself is not inherently the problem. Every scientist CNN spoke with emphasized the need for fire on the landscapes they researched. But the lack of prescribed burning, a practice long used by indigenous people to clear out dead plants and to keep landscapes healthy, has left these trees vulnerable . It means their futures — when they encounter hotter, more vicious fires — are uncertain.
As these ecologies start to shift, it’s unclear if or when these different areas around the US will hit a tipping point where the trees won’t come back. Instead, researchers say it’s more likely there will be a gradual conversion over time, with once towering forests becoming robust scrublands or large fields of grassland.
Here’s how some places around the country are changing, and how one state is succeeding in preserving its native wildlife.
As Turner stood on the dirt field, the air was hot — much hotter than during her previous 2013 visit. Cool summers and rain had been the norm for Yellowstone during her years of research. The heat was so intense this time that a field assistant was hospitalized for dehydration during the trip, said Turner, who works at the University of Wisconsin-Madison as the Eugene P. Odum Professor of Ecology and a Vilas Research Professor.
The ash coating the former forest floor reminded her of the ash she walked through during the 1988 fires — ash that covered her face and caked her socks. For a long time, Turner thought the wildfires from that summer 38 years ago represented how forests could and would recover. Despite miles of charred trees, the research in her field showed the forest would come back, and with a high density of trees, she said. But Turner said she didn’t appreciate “how much things could change in a relatively short time.”
“We could see what we call ghost logs, which is where there had been large logs on the ground, and they were completely combusted,” she said. “And then you can see their shadows where the white ash is left behind from the hot temperatures.”
Only about 5 percent of the tree seedlings have grown back so far from the 2016 fire, compared to what burned. In place of the trees, grasses blow in the exposed meadow, now dotted with wildflowers that commonly sprout after a wildfire. Turner said she is seeing “a slow but detectable shift” to plants that are “more tolerant of warmer, drier conditions” and can grow back more easily if more wildfires come.
Slowly but surely, these changes could impact visitors to the park, Turner said. People like trees, for both how they look and the practical element of shade during hikes, she said, and the changes the forest is undergoing could impact how and when people visit the park.
The repercussions are seen in more unexpected ways as well — at one point, the park had a temporary ban on fishing, including catch and release, because the fish were already too stressed out from low water levels and the high water temperatures that were partially due to the lack of shade, she said.
“What will be the consequences for lots of other values that people care about in that region?” Turner said. “That could be wildlife habitat. It could be water availability. It could be shade if you’re hiking.”
But ultimately, it’s not yet clear what the future Yellowstone will look like.
About 100 miles northeast of California’s state capital, Derek Young stood in the middle of a clearing in Plumas National Forest. The carcasses of burnt trees that surrounded him felt like a graveyard, the remains left in the wake of the 2021 Dixie Fire.
An occasional bird would chirp in the distance, but the forest emanated an eerie stillness, said Young, a research ecologist at the University of California, Davis. Fifteen years ago, Young started studying these landscapes as a PhD student. Many of them are now unrecognizable compared to the thriving forests they once were.
“It’s really actually crazy to how much change has happened,” he said.
Many of the areas Young studies are changing from dazzling emerald trees to fields of shrubs — even years after the wildfires.
The shrubs, ranging from deer brush to white thorn shrub, are incredibly good at resprouting, Young said. While fire might lop off the shrub tops, their roots remain, helping the plants return quickly, he said. It’s stiff competition for trees to endure, which need specific conditions to grow back compared to the hardy, drought-tolerant shrubs, he said.
In just a few years, the shrubs can grow to be as tall as a person, covering the entirety of an area, Young said. “It can really feel like you’re swimming in a sea of shrubs. You can’t see more than a few feet ahead of you.”
There are a couple of factors required for trees to successfully reemerge. Some species of trees can grow in the shade, but those species are also more likely to be destroyed during a high temperature fire, he said. Others need the heat of a fire to release their seeds, while many others don’t, Young said. Those seeds then need to land in an area where they can grow and survive, which can be impacted by wind and wildlife, he added. A lot needs to happen in a short window of time in order for them to regrow.
As he sees these landscapes shift, it’s hard to weigh if this is inherently a bad change — although he noted the important services forests currently provide humans, namely capturing and holding carbon dioxide through carbon sequestration.
“As forests burn up, they release carbon, contribute to climate change, which makes it more likely for more fires to burn and convert more forests,” he said. “You could say, if you care about humanity’s well-being, that that’s actually a reason to favor maintenance and restoration of forests in place of post-fire shrub fields.”
“I do sometimes try to think from the perspective of like, what if there were no humans, and there is no society to decide what our values are,” he said. “In that scenario, I think the sort of definitive answer is the most valuable ecosystem is the one that is adapted to the site in the absence of all the human intervention.”
But he notes this change to shrubs is not happening in that theoretical vacuum without humans.
“It’s not that the system naturally wanted to be shrubs. We created that condition by suppressing fires for 100 years,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Houthis Claim Attack on Aramco as Yemen Conflict Escalates
articles.title_zh: Houthis Claim Attack on Aramco as Yemen Conflict Escalates
articles.content_orig:
The announcement came hours after Iranian-backed Houthis reportedly cut a vital supply route to besieged city of Taiz
Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis , even as the militant group made fresh gains on the ground, reportedly encircling a government-held city.
Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen’s presidential council, said in a statement on Sunday: “I announce today the start of military operations to retake the remaining territories of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory.”
The announcement sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia . The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.
The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.
Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.
Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.
Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.
Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.
A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.
The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led ‌air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Saudi oil exports were already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title_orig: Germany's chancellor arrives in Kyiv on unannounced visit to pledge more military support to Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Germany's chancellor arrives in Kyiv on unannounced visit to pledge more military support to Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on Sunday and called on Russian President Vladimir Putin to stop his "barbaric attacks" and end what he called a "senseless war."
Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the badly damaged building of Ukraine's Academy of Sciences, where at least two people died in a drone strike last week, Merz said:
"We are ready for ​talks, we are ‌ready to discuss bringing this war to an end, but these barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop. I can only repeat once ​again: Mr Putin, put an end to this senseless war."
Merz arrived in Kyiv by train early on Sunday morning, accompanied by German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and a delegation of leading figures from German business, including executives from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defense and Quantum Systems.
"If Russia is not stopped, it will turn its war machine against us sooner or later," Merz said upon arrival.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Air raid sirens blared across the Ukrainian capital throughout the morning, as Kyiv's mayor announced one of the city's bridges had been hit by a Russian drone.
Zelenskyy condemned the attacks and said the capital was experiencing a "terrible situation" with "horrific days and nights." He labeled the Russian attackers "absolute barbarians" and said: "It is vital that Ukraine is not left alone in the face of this terror."
Merz pledged further military and energy assistance during his visit, with Zelenskyy announcing a German support package worth more than €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion).
The package includes €1 billion in military aid and €350 million for energy sector repairs ahead of winter.
Zelenskyy said the two countries had reached 15 agreements worth more than €8.5 billion ($9.6 billion), covering defense cooperation, production, procurement and joint projects in Ukraine .
According to German government sources cited by Reuters and the DPA news agency, the planned cooperation includes the development and delivery of thousands of interceptor drones capable of countering the fast, jet-powered drones Russia increasingly deploys against Ukrainian infrastructure.
The plans also envisage expanding production of long-range weapons capable of striking targets more than 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) away.
Merz emphasized that the partnership would also benefit Germany, with companies from both countries developing technology to strengthen their security.
"German and Ukrainian companies are jointly developing technologies that benefit both countries. That makes us safer and stronger," he said.
The visit came just hours after the Russian Foreign Ministry warned foreign diplomats and other visitors to avoid the Ukrainian capital, and military and government buildings in particular.
"The responsibility for any negative consequences lies entirely with those who ignore this warning," read a statement, which claimed that Russian strikes were responses to "terrorist acts by the Ukrainian armed forces against our country's civilian infrastructure."
In recent days, Russia has attacked several bridges across the Dnipro river as well as energy infrastructure, and the city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, on Friday said that Kyiv was in a "very dramatic situation."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Further strikes followed on Sunday during Merz's visit, with Klitschko confirming that a bridge had been struck.
"Impact on the road surface of the Northern Bridge. Emergency services are heading to the scene," the mayor wrote on the Telegram messaging service.
But the German delegation was not deterred, with Merz saying upon arrival that "Ukraine will need all our support in the coming weeks" as winter approaches and Russian attacks intensify.
"A fifth winter of war is about to begin," he said. "Russia is bombarding cities, apartments and power stations. I will tell President Zelenskyy today: 'You can count on our help.'"
Merz's arrival in Kyiv marks the fourth such visit to Ukraine by a German chancellor since the full-scale Russian invasion began in February 2022.
His predecessor, Olaf Scholz, visited twice during his three-year tenure, while Merz himself first traveled to Kyiv in May 2025 – just four days after taking office. He was accompanied on that occasion by French President Emmanuel Macron , Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
Sunday's visit comes just days after Merz had assured Ukraine of Germany's support, despite isolated resistance and criticism at home.
"If we in Germany waver, Europe wavers," he said on Thursday after conferring the international Westphalian Peace Prize upon the NATO military alliance and its secretary general, Mark Rutte. "And if Europe wavers, Ukraine wavers."
Germany remains Ukraine's most important backer, both militarily and financially, but state elections in September saw significant gains for parties at both ends of the political spectrum who are critical of expenditure on Ukraine: the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the socialist Left Party in Berlin .
In his speech on Thursday, Merz called out in particular "the AfD and their Russian backers" and promised Ukraine that Germany would not be divided.
Edited by: Zac Crellin, Natalie Muller

articles.title_orig: The new Fitbit Edge leaks
articles.title_zh: The new Fitbit Edge leaks
articles.content_orig:
Google’s midrange Fitbit Edge shows off is many sides and colors in leaked images.
Google’s midrange Fitbit Edge shows off is many sides and colors in leaked images.
We don’t know a ton about the Fitbit Edge, but it appears to be a successor to the midrange Charge line. It had leaked previously , but we can clearly see in these images posted by Android Headlines , you can see that Google’s rumored fitness tracker sort of splits the difference between the Pixel Watch and the Fitbit Air . It has a small screen that is able to display some widgets, but clearly isn’t as expansive as a proper smartwatch.
Supposedly, this fitness-first wearable will have a seven-day battery life, as well as built-in GPS and an altimeter, making it far more capable than the minimalist Air. It will also have limited app support for things like Google Maps and YouTube Music. Beyond that, not a ton is known.
The Fitbit Charge line was last updated in 2023, so a new midrange tracker is long overdue. While we don’t have any word on price or release date yet, somewhere in the $150 to $200 range seems like a safe bet. The Air costs $99.99 and the Watch starts at $399.99, so the Edge would clearly fall somewhere in the middle. The Charge 6 currently goes for $159.95.

articles.title_orig: Elder Thabo Lebethoa: ‘Jesus Christ Is the Light and Life of the World’
articles.title_zh: Elder Thabo Lebethoa: ‘Jesus Christ Is the Light and Life of the World’
articles.content_orig:
Elder Thabo Lebethoa , General Authority Seventy, spoke during the Sunday afternoon session of October 2026 general conference about how to receive more of the Savior’s light. The following is a summary of what he said.
The Savior said: “I am the light and the life of the world.”
“Through His Spirit, He enlightens our minds. His light is also revealed through His perfect life and teachings.”
Whatever concerns, challenges and struggles come in life, the answer is always Jesus Christ.
“Jesus Christ can bring light in our moments of darkness and restore hope where there is hopelessness.”
To receive more of the Savior’s light in one’s life: First, increase faith in Him; second, study the scriptures daily, especially the Book of Mormon; third, practice repentance daily.
“Having faith in Jesus Christ means trusting that He understands our daily difficulties and knows how to help us rise above them, because He has experienced all our pains, afflictions and infirmities.”
The method, timing and length of scripture study matter less than the consistency and sincerity of the effort.
Repentance means a change of mind and a turning of the heart to God.
“I testify that today can be a new day, and tomorrow will be a better day, for all who come unto Jesus Christ and receive His light in their lives. He lovingly beckons: ‘Come unto me, and I will give you rest.’”
“Whatever concerns, challenges and struggles we may have in our lives, the answer is always Jesus Christ.”
“Let us ponder about the changes that we need to make in our lives, and these may include how we use our time, the things we watch or listen to, and the language and tone we use as we communicate with others.”
“I testify that today can be a new day, and tomorrow will be a better day, for all who come unto Jesus Christ and receive His light in their lives.”

articles.title_orig: Microsoft shared Windows 11 26H2 Group Policy templates, settings guidance for admins
articles.title_zh: Microsoft shared Windows 11 26H2 Group Policy templates, settings guidance for admins
articles.content_orig:
Windows powers how people around the world work, learn, create, and connect every day. Today, we’re announcing the availability of the Windows 11 2026 Update, also known as Windows 11, version 26H2. Built on the same servicing foundation as recent Windows 11 releases, version 26H2 delivers the latest Windows innovations with a streamlined update experience designed to minimize disruption and help you stay secure, productive, and up to date.
As organizations and individuals continue to expect faster deployments and less downtime, Windows 11, version 26H2 takes advantage of the same modern servicing technologies that have simplified recent feature updates. For many eligible devices, moving to version 26H2 is as simple as installing a small enablement package, allowing people to start using this new release with minimal download size, quick installation, and a single restart.
Windows 11, version 26H2 is delivered as an enablement package for eligible devices running Windows 11, versions 25H2 and 24H2.
An enablement package is a lightweight update that activates new features already included in the operating system through previous monthly servicing updates. Because versions 26H2, 25H2, and 24H2 share a common servicing branch and underlying codebase, many of the components required for version 26H2 are already present on devices before the feature update becomes available.
This approach enables a significantly faster update experience compared to a traditional operating system upgrade. For eligible devices, installation is similar to a monthly update, requiring only a small download and a quick restart to transition to Windows 11, version 26H2.
As with every Windows release, version 26H2 includes the latest quality, reliability, and security improvements designed to help protect people and organizations while delivering a dependable Windows experience.
Windows 11, version 26H2 is now available for eligible devices running Windows 11, versions 25H2 and 24H2.
To be among the first to receive the update, go to Settings > Windows Update and turn on Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available . Once your device is eligible, you’ll see the option to download and install Windows 11, version 26H2.
As always, we take a measured and data-driven approach to broad availability and will be releasing version 26H2 using a controlled feature rollout. During rollout, we might place safeguard holds on devices where we detect a known compatibility issue that could impact the update experience. We will continue expanding availability over time and provide updates through the Windows release health hub.
Windows 11, version 26H2 is available now through the tools organizations use to manage Windows updates, including Windows Autopatch and the Microsoft 365 admin center [i] .
Existing management tools, update rings, policies, and deployment practices can continue to be used. We recommend that commercial and education customers begin targeted deployments to validate applications, devices, and business-critical workflows before expanding deployment more broadly throughout their organizations.
Windows 11, version 26H2 continues the annual Windows feature update cadence, with a new Windows 11 feature update released during the second half of the calendar year. As with previous annual releases, installing version 26H2 resets the support lifecycle for supported editions of Windows 11. That means 24 months of support for Home and Pro editions and 36 months of support for Enterprise and Education editions.
Select features and enhancements initially released as disabled by default in version 25H2 will be enabled by default in version 26H2. You can find more information on these features, plus guidance to help with planning and deployment, in the Windows IT Pro Blog .
We recommend updating eligible devices to Windows 11, version 26H2 to take advantage of the latest Windows innovations, quality improvements, and security enhancements.
We’ll continue to closely monitor the rollout and share information about known issues, safeguards, and rollout progress through the Windows release health hub and official Windows communications channels.
Thank you for your feedback and partnership as we continue to improve Windows for people and organizations around the world. We love to hear about your experience, so please keep your comments and suggestions coming in via Feedback Hub.
[i] Downloads in the Microsoft 365 admin center and similar channels may be delayed.

articles.title_orig: Rally Italia Sardegna: Day 4 - Evans and Martin win world title with TGR-WRT in thrilling finale
articles.title_zh: Rally Italia Sardegna: Day 4 - Evans and Martin win world title with TGR-WRT in thrilling finale
articles.content_orig:
TOYOTA GAZOO Racing World Rally Team’s Elfyn Evans and Scott Martin have won their first FIA World Rally Championship drivers’ and co-drivers’ titles after a thrilling intra-team battle decided in a dramatic final stage of the season at Rally Italia Sardegna.
Evans went head-to-head with his team-mates Sami Pajari and Oliver Solberg in the deciding rally with all three vying to be crowned world champion for the first time.
Playing host to the season finale for the first time, the sandy and rough gravel roads of the Italian island proved as demanding as usual. Following a hot and dry summer, the loose and sandy surface would produce a significant road cleaning effect for the three contenders to deal with during the first full day on Friday.
While Evans entered the final round with a lead of 17 points over Pajari and 21 over Solberg, he also faced the toughest task opening the road and finished Friday in sixth overall. While Pajari was just one position ahead in fifth, Solberg took advantage of his more advantageous position to end Friday in third and within striking distance of the rally lead, which he then seized on Saturday morning.
With Solberg comfortably leading the rally into the final day and Evans in fifth overall, and the virtual gap between them reduced to six points, the battle would be decided by the 10 bonus points available across the Super Sunday and Power Stage classifications.
Continuing to show impressive pace, Solberg established an early lead in the Sunday standings with a strong stage win in the opening Osilo – Tergu test, but the subsequent Sassari – Argentiera beach – noted for its sandy downhill finish – would provide a different dynamic with conditions deteriorating for later runners.
A major twist followed in the second pass of Osilo – Tergu when Evans stopped to change a punctured tyre, conceding close to two minutes. While he held on to fifth overall, he dropped out of contention for Sunday points and headed into the rally-ending Power Stage with a virtual lead of just one point over Solberg.
The final stage of the season therefore effectively became a straight shootout between the two in the knowledge that whoever set the quicker time would be world champion. Knowing the time of Evans that he had to beat, Solberg was faster on the split times during a committed run but ran off the road in the final stretch. While Solberg managed to get back on the road and still secure the rally victory, he finished the stage 8.9s down on Evans.
Evans and Martin’s first world title represents a hard-earned reward after seven seasons consistently fighting at the front of the field with TGR-WRT, during which they finished as championship runners-up in five of the previous six years. Their 2026 campaign has been built on typically strong consistency, as well as two impressive victories in Sweden and Japan and calculated pace when required to score well on Sundays even when opening the road through a string of consecutive gravel rallies.
Evans is the first Welsh driver to ever win the title, and follows in the footsteps of Scotland’s Colin McRae and England’s Richard Burns as a World Rally Champion from the United Kingdom. Martin is the first English co-driver to win the title, joining fellow Britons David Richards, Derek Ringer, Robert Reid and Phil Mills on that honour list.
It is the seventh time in eight years that a TGR-WRT crew has been crowned world champions, and the fifth time in six years that the team has swept all three championships having already secured the manufacturers’ crown at the previous round in Chile.
Solberg finishes just five points behind in the championship along with co-driver Elliott Edmondson in their first full season competing at the highest level. They began the season with an epic victory at Rallye Monte-Carlo, and their speed was never in doubt, winning more stages than anybody else through the season. After a character-building mid-season period, they have bounced back from being 59 points adrift to end the year with back-to-back victories in Chile and Sardinia.
Their win is a record-equalling 12th from 13 rallies this season – and record-extending 48th in total – for the GR YARIS Rally1 car in its fifth and final season of the current homologation cycle before new technical regulations are introduced for 2027.
Pajari finishes third in the championship, six points behind, together with co-driver Marko Salminen after a breakthrough season of their own – just their second full campaign at the top level. Their Sardinia podium is their ninth of the season – more than anybody else – and Pajari matches Solberg in taking three victories.
Sébastien Ogier finished second in the rally to claim a record 121st WRC podium, moving ahead of fellow nine-time world champion Sébastien Loeb, on the very same event that he made a record 214th start, surpassing his Team Principal Jari-Matti Latvala. Ogier and co-driver Vincent Landais finish the year fourth in the standings with six podiums from 11 rallies entered.
Takamoto Katsuta made it five GR YARIS Rally1 drivers in the top six of the rally and the points standings at the end of a breakout year with co-driver Aaron Johnston that included their first wins in Kenya and Croatia, Katsuta becoming the first Japanese driver to lead the championship in the process.
Roope Korhonen and Anssi Viinikka secured their second WRC2 victory of the year by just 0.7s driving their GR Yaris Rally2 car entered by Rautio Motorsport and run by Printsport, a result that allows them to finish second in the championship standings.
Quotes: Akio Toyoda (TGR-WRT Chairman) “I'd like to send three messages to Elfyn and Scott, who have finally become world champions: congratulations, thank you, and sorry.
Since joining the TOYOTA GAZOO Racing family in 2020, Elfyn has finished just one place short of the championship five times, including three consecutive seasons from 2023 onward. After so many seasons of coming painfully close, he has finally achieved the title he has worked so hard for. Congratulations, Elfyn. You really deserve it!
Of course, I can’t really say that out loud. Publicly, I have to say that I want all our drivers to win. But if I’m being honest, this year I was cheering for Elfyn. Sorry, Sami and Oliver, but I simply couldn’t let Elfyn and Scott end up second again. Elfyn, congratulations. Truly, truly congratulations!
The “thank you” is for everything Elfyn and Scott have done for the team over the years. Those five second-place championship finishes are proof of how consistently they have delivered points. Thanks to the points they contributed season after season, TOYOTA GAZOO Racing has been able to keep winning manufacturers’ titles.
Their contribution goes far beyond points. At the final round of the 2021 season, with the drivers’ championship on the line, Elfyn and Scott went off the road. Afterwards, they shared information with the team about sections where grip was particularly low. Thanks to that information, Seb was able to secure the championship. They are the kind of drivers who always think not only about themselves, but about the team as well. Thank you both, truly! (And I think everyone can now understand why I was cheering for Elfyn.)
The “sorry” is because I couldn’t be there with them during the fight for the championship. Whenever I was there, Elfyn has almost always delivered a strong result: four victories and three second-place finishes. That's why I wanted to be there for the rally where he could become champion. Sorry to the other drivers, but I was planning to go to Saudi Arabia. Unfortunately, my schedule didn't allow me to attend Sardinia, so I'm relieved that he was able to clinch the title there.
Oliver and Elliott also fought incredibly hard right to the very end. Let's keep pushing together next year!
This rally marks the end of the GR YARIS Rally1's journey. It is a car that has continued to win championships throughout the five seasons since 2022. Thi

articles.title_orig: Scoop: White House monitors suspected plague outbreak in Russia
articles.title_zh: Scoop: White House monitors suspected plague outbreak in Russia
articles.content_orig:
Health authorities in Siberia’s Irkutsk region have placed nearly 200 people under medical observation after a laboratory worker died from plague, according to media reports and a statement by a regional leader Friday.
Alexei Tsydenov, head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia, confirmed that the woman had died from an unspecified form of plague. Irkutsk officials had previously described the illness only as a “particularly dangerous infection.”
Citing information from Russia’s consumer safety watchdog Rospotrebnadzor and Buryatia’s government, Tsydenov said the woman had not visited his republic and that her infection was unrelated to the region.
“There are no plague outbreaks in the republic, including in areas bordering Mongolia,” he wrote on social media.
The woman was identified as Daria Sh., a 27- or 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk anti-plague institute, by the exiled news outlet Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal) and pro-Kremlin broadcaster REN TV .
She reportedly told medical staff that she had accidentally broken a test tube containing live bacteria while collecting samples for testing.
She was hospitalized Tuesday with symptoms of severe pneumonia in Shelekhov, a town near the regional capital of Irkutsk. She was placed on a ventilator and died Thursday, according to the reports.
The Shelekhov district hospital was placed under quarantine pending an assessment by a special commission.
At least 197 people who may have had contact with her were reportedly placed under medical isolation , including more than 100 in hospital wards.
Authorities canceled planned public events in Irkutsk, while law enforcement reportedly opened a criminal investigation into potential health safety violations resulting in death.
Irkutsk region Governor Igor Kobzev urged the public to remain calm after meeting with Rospotrebnadzor chief Anna Popova to coordinate emergency containment measures.
“All identified contact persons have been placed under medical observation. As of today, the contacts show no signs of illness, and their laboratory test results are negative,” Kobzev wrote on Telegram on Friday. He did not mention the reports of the laboratory worker’s death.
Media reports have described the suspected infection as pneumonic plague, which affects the lungs and can spread between humans through respiratory droplets. Tsydenov’s statement did not specify the form of plague.
