articles.title_orig: Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for? | Emma Beddington
articles.title_zh: Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for? | Emma Beddington
articles.content_orig:
Their careers are peaking, they’re rich in money and time – and young people think they’re cool. But maybe it’s not as simple as that
‘S top sleeping on gen X.” I heard this on TikTok recently. I misinterpreted it, with a guilty start, as: “Stop sleeping, gen X,” because I am 51 (peak X), so always tired; while not sleeping at the time, I may have been resting my eyes. In fact, Joel Marlinarson, a marketing guru , was suggesting my generation have become a powerful, if underrated, force online.
Aged between 46 and 61, gen Xers with proper jobs are peaking, career-wise (although it’s a different story for those out of work, as a report last month on the struggles of over-50s jobseekers made plain). We’re more likely to own homes than the following generations ; we’re emerging from the trenches of childrearing and, the argument goes, ready to indulge in some me-time. “If gen X were a country, it would be the world’s second-largest consumer market,” the World Economic Forum reported last year , with gen X women in particular influencing 70% to 80% of all consumer spending.
That makes us great customers – witness the tidal wave of menopause-washed wellness guff (Which? reported last month that many pricey supplements were no better than a cheap multivitamin ) and beauty brands for people suddenly horrified by their necks . But does it give us content-creating clout? We’re supposed to be (or at least meme lore presents us as ) the forgotten generation, low-key, countercultural slackers on the sidelines in the grudge match between millennials and boomers; aspiration and self-promotion aren’t really part of our brand.
Sure, kids are scrambling for Oasis tickets and rediscovering zines ; US Vogue called us “the cool ones” and the New York Times went further with “the greatest generation”. I get the argument that it’s our time to shine. But real gen Xers have a lot on their plate and it doesn’t necessarily lend itself to fun, aspirational content.
Being peak career means peak responsibility: our parents are faltering (I’m writing this as my mother-in-law is moving into sheltered accommodation) and our kids are facing awful geopolitical and economic prospects that undermine their mental health and chances of independence. We’re falling apart physically: for women, the sorting hat of perimenopause doles out a set of grim symptoms, while men are wondering what will fell them next – heart, stomach, back or knees? Who wants to hear about that? And who can be arsed to make perky TikToks?
I’ll tell you who: Kathryn Turner . I was introduced to Turner, M&S Food’s director of product development, by Marlinarson, for whom she is evidence that over-50s employees are “ the next biggest influencers ”. Turner, a cheery woman in smart trousers who exudes quiet competence, has worked for M&S since 1995. She launched her account in May, but her TikToks already garner up to 2m views and her nearly 250,000 fans are devoted: “Would follow that woman into war,” commented one . “Why did we give Andy Burnham the job over her,” asked another . “ I love you Kathryn turner [sic],” wrote an account claiming to be the Heartstopper actor Joe Locke . I love her, too: Turner’s calm sunniness, as she talks viewers through innovations in the picky bits space, is a balm in a fractious world.
Turner isn’t Kate Moss, Miranda July or any of the other impossibly glamorous gen X figureheads – she seems like a normal, middle-aged woman who knows her stuff and does it well. I love that she’s popping up on TikTok and I get it – I’m projecting, but I bet Turner’s great in a crisis, her desk drawer and handbag well stocked with protein-rich treats, blister plasters and ibuprofen.
Maybe this is our online USP. Could watching grownups quietly bossing their busy, complex lives be the next ASMR? Because, mostly, gen X aren’t the “cool ones”: they’re the knackered ones, dealing with life, death, work and frozen shoulders. I don’t know any Mosses or Chloë Sevignys, but I know lots of Turners and I, too, would follow them into war, or at least get a dopamine hit from watching them be extremely competent in short-form videos. No one would want to watch me staring at a screen then breaking to fold some pants, obviously, but I’d love to see more of my capable peers ditch the self-deprecation (very gen X) and shine online.
Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

articles.title_orig: Beyond mining tunnels: China's coal-rich province accelerates smarter, greener energy transition
articles.title_zh: Beyond mining tunnels: China's coal-rich province accelerates smarter, greener energy transition
articles.content_orig:
This photo taken on Sept. 4, 2026 shows a view outside the main venue of the 2026 Taiyuan Energy Low-Carbon Development Forum in Taiyuan, north China's Shanxi Province. (Xinhua/Yang Chenguang)
TAIYUAN, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- From intelligent coal mines to digital power-grid management, north China's Shanxi Province is accelerating its energy transition and maintaining stable coal supplies.
As one of China's major coal-producing provinces and a key national energy base, Shanxi is seeking to make its energy system smarter, more diversified and more efficient.
The province is upgrading its traditional coal industry through smarter technologies and cleaner production, while expanding wind and solar power to diversify its energy mix. Backed by increasingly flexible power management, these efforts are reshaping how Shanxi produces, supplies and uses energy as China pursues greener development.
For 50-year-old Zhao Huacheng, deputy head of a fully mechanized mining team at Huayang New Material Technology Group Co., Ltd., a major coal mining enterprise in Shanxi, the transformation of coal mining is evident in his daily work.
Zhao has worked in the industry for nearly 30 years, taking on almost every frontline role in his team, from coal miner and powered-support operator to safety officer.
Huayang's No. 1 Mine, with an annual production capacity of 8.5 million tonnes, is among China's first batch of intelligent demonstration coal mines. Its intelligent mining faces use 5G technology and automated equipment to enable remote control and reduce the need for underground workers.
The number of workers required underground for a shift at Zhao's team has already fallen from 24 to 16.
Operating a coal-cutting machine was once one of the toughest jobs. Three operators had to work together, with one controlling the machine from a platform and the other two observing the terrain from the front and rear.
When the machine started up, clouds of coal dust often made it nearly impossible to see, and flying chunks of coal posed a real risk of injury. Zhao still has a scar near his right eye as a reminder.
"With advances in technology, the operator in the middle is no longer needed. The operators in front and behind can control the machine remotely from six meters away, reducing the risks," Zhao said. "We used to get bumped and bruised almost constantly. Now, such incidents are rare."
Today, intelligent equipment has taken over most labor-intensive tasks. Clean mine tunnels, dust-suppression systems and enclosed control rooms have replaced the once dusty and hazardous working conditions.
Productivity has also seen a sharp increase. A production shift that once yielded about 3,000 to 4,000 tonnes of coal can now produce 5,000 to 6,000 tonnes, according to Zhao.
The transformation at Zhao's workplace is part of a broader push to make coal mining smarter and cleaner in Shanxi. By the end of November 2025, the province had built 369 intelligent coal mines, accounting for more than one-third of the national total, as well as 75 demonstration mines for green mining.
On the national level, China aims to make virtually all types of coal mines intelligent by 2035 by leveraging advanced technologies, according to the National Development and Reform Commission.
While making coal production smarter and cleaner, Shanxi is also reshaping its energy mix, with renewable energy becoming an increasingly important source of new capacity and power generation.
At Shanxi Jinnan Steel Group Co., Ltd. in Quwo County, Linfen City, photovoltaic panels cover unused spaces ranging from rooftops and south-facing walls to hillside slopes and areas near an artificial lake.
The company produces nearly 6 million tonnes of steel annually. Over the past five years, it has invested heavily in clean energy projects to reduce the carbon intensity of its energy consumption.
Three months ago, the company partnered with PowerChina New Energy Group Co., Ltd. to develop green electricity by tapping the region's mountainous and valley resources. The two sides plan to use a "green electricity direct supply" model to better match the company's energy needs.
"We have developed photovoltaic projects with a combined capacity of 550 megawatts, generating more than 1 billion kWh of electricity annually," said Zhang Tianfu, president of Shanxi Jinnan Steel Group Co., Ltd.
Green electricity currently accounts for 15 percent of the company's power consumption. Zhang said the company will continue expanding its renewable energy portfolio and plans to raise the share to 50 percent by 2029.
The company's growing investment in green electricity comes as renewable energy has become the main source of newly added power generation capacity and electricity generation in Shanxi.
By the end of June this year, the province's installed capacity of wind and solar power had exceeded 80 million kW. In 2020, roughly one in every seven kWh generated in Shanxi came from renewable sources. Today, despite a substantial increase in total power generation, the share has risen to one in every four kWh.
A historic shift has taken place in Shanxi's energy mix. By the end of September last year, installed capacity of new and clean energy sources accounted for 54.55 percent of the province's total, marking a historic shift from a fossil-fuel-dominated energy mix toward one led by clean energy.
As wind and solar power generation expands, Shanxi faces a new challenge: how to accommodate increasingly variable renewable generation while keeping the power grid stable.
Virtual power plants are emerging as one solution.
Shanxi Fengxingcekong Co., Ltd. operates China's first virtual power plant participating in the electricity spot market. Nan Dou, deputy general manager of the company, said the spot market generates a new electricity price every five minutes.
The virtual power plant aggregates scattered electricity-consuming resources and dispatches them through a digital platform, using algorithms to adjust the power loads of participating enterprises in response to changes in electricity prices and grid demand.
"When electricity prices are low and renewable power generation is high, we encourage enterprises to consume more electricity, maximizing the use of renewable power. When prices are high and the grid is under pressure, we organize enterprises to reduce their loads during peak periods, helping ensure safe and stable grid operation," Nan said.
"This benefits all three sides by ensuring power supplies, facilitating renewable power consumption and reducing energy costs for enterprises," he added.
From August 2023 to June 2026, the virtual power plant helped facilitate the consumption of 350 million kWh of renewable electricity, equivalent to reducing carbon dioxide emissions by about 350,000 tonnes, the operators said. It also saved about 210 million kWh of electricity.
Over the three years since entering the electricity market, the company's ability to aggregate and dispatch resources has continued to improve. The number of users on its platform has risen from five to more than 60, while its aggregated capacity has jumped from 80,000 kW to 2.282 million kW.
"The most important improvement is that our control success rate has risen from 33 percent to 80 percent. Only by improving the quality of regulation can we achieve the desired results," Nan said.
As of September 2026, 14 virtual power plants in Shanxi had participated in market trading, aggregating 1,459 users. Their combined capacity in the Shanxi electricity market had reached 6.4548 million kW, with a maximum adjustable load of 1.545 million kW.
Traditional coal-fired power plants are also undergoing flexibility upgrades in response to market signals. The upgrades allow them to reduce output when wind and solar generation is abundant, creating more room for renewable power, and quickly ramp up output when renewable generation falls short, helping ensure electricity supplies.

articles.title_orig: Minecraft Dungeons II Reviews Praise Local Co-Op but Fault the Open World
articles.title_zh: Minecraft Dungeons II Reviews Praise Local Co-Op but Fault the Open World
articles.content_orig:
Nintendo Life called Minecraft Dungeons II a fun but flawed sequel in its Switch 2 review, with co-operative play as the high point. A second review, from Shacknews , reached a similar verdict and said the game works best with friends sitting in the same room.
The game follows Minecraft Dungeons, which came out in 2020 as a loot-driven dungeon crawler. Families who play together on one console are the audience both reviewers had in mind.
Nintendo Life said the sequel swaps the first game's episodic progression for an open world. Its reviewer said developer Mojang stretched the appeal too thin in doing so.
Dungeons are scattered across the Overworld, and portals lead to a new biome called The Sift, which the review found lovely to look at.
The story picks up after the first game. An Illager High Council, a trio of magic users wielding soul power, invades the land, and the player's custom hero starts in the hub town of Brave Haven.
Nintendo Life put the main campaign at about 12 to 15 hours and said it is easy.
Nintendo Life said customisation remains the strongest part of the game. Loot drops steadily from enemies and chests, and all weapons and gear can be enchanted.
Artefacts grant up to three crowd-control abilities in exchange for soul power, while Talismans are new and add stat boosts and resistances. Jumping now adds variety to melee and ranged attacks.
The reviewer wrote that players mostly use those builds against the same enemies in similar-looking locations. Endermen, which appear as random encounters, were singled out as a tense source of good gear.
Shacknews writer Ozzie Mejia said he mostly played online and found it frustrating for several reasons. He enjoyed offline play with friends and family far more.
Players must choose online or offline when they create a character, and the choice cannot be reversed. A hero built for online sessions cannot be moved to a living-room game, so a new character is required.
Both modes allow players to join and leave mid-game, and online players can connect through party codes or matchmaking.
Mejia described the storytelling as minimalistic. The game has few cutscenes and almost no voiceover beyond some narration, and it leans on text.
He said the cutscenes look gorgeous in Unreal Engine 5, and that the narrated quest text reminded him of a Dungeons & Dragons campaign. He said the format grew on him by the end.
Shacknews said the sequel keeps the first game's simple loop while adding depth drawn from the Minecraft source material. Mojang developed the game with Double Eleven.
I cover what the internet is actually talking about: the new release, the viral moment, the creator beef, the product launch. My job is to explain it fast and clearly, without the breathless hype. I read the timeline…

articles.title_orig: Yemeni government launches offensive to seize all areas from Iran-backed Houthis
articles.title_zh: Yemeni government launches offensive to seize all areas from Iran-backed Houthis
articles.content_orig:
The announcement came hours after Iranian-backed Houthis reportedly cut a vital supply route to besieged city of Taiz
Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis , even as the militant group made fresh gains on the ground, reportedly encircling a government-held city.
Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen’s presidential council, said in a statement on Sunday: “I announce today the start of military operations to retake the remaining territories of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory.”
The announcement sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia . The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.
The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.
Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.
Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.
Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.
Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.
A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.
The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led ‌air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Saudi oil exports were already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title_orig: FlyDubai captain reveals new details of attack in Netanyahu phone call
articles.title_zh: FlyDubai captain reveals new details of attack in Netanyahu phone call
articles.content_orig:
The FlyDubai hero captain revealed new details of his fight to save the passengers aboard flight FZ1073 in an emotional telephone conversation with Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, released by his office on Saturday evening.
The UAE, which is leading the investigation, said the co-pilot attacked the flight’s captain with the cockpit’s crash ax and tried to take control of the plummeting plane in a “terrorist attack” on Wednesday.
Captain Smit Machchhar told Netanyahu he felt he had “one more fight left” in him when in a critical state he reached for the cockpit door once again to save the 174 passengers and 6 crew members, while the co-pilot kept attacking him and putting the aircraft in a steep defence.
He described how the attack started saying that the co-pilot asked to pray in the cockpit which he did not consider an unusual request and “and out of respect for him, I didn’t look back.”
“After 4-5 minutes, I felt a heavy blow to the back of my head. My first thought was that catastrophic damage had been caused to the plane and something was wrong, but the blows kept coming one after another, and then I realized it wasn't the plane... it was the other guy who was with me in the cockpit," the captain described the attack.
Machchhar said his vision became badly blurred from the blows and he felt how the aircraft went into a steep descent. He tried to open the cockpit door once again, but the co-pilot kept closing it while passengers were trying to get in using the access code.
Netanyahu asked him if the door was closed with a pin mechanism and the captain answered that on the inside of the cockpit the door had a twist handle and that from the outside it could be opened with a code.
Machchhar remembered hearing the whooshing sound of the aircraft plunging downwards and the passengers screaming.
Realising what was happening, he told Netanyahu how he reached for the internal twist handle and with “a sharp, quick turn” managed to finally open the door, letting the passengers in who subdued the co-pilot and stabilised the plane.
The captain said that the co-pilot "locked the cockpit door and I was lying on the floor. I heard people screaming. I realized I had one last fight left: if I don't do this, I will die with the last of my strength, I opened the door, and people were already waiting right outside and jumped in".
“I knew I couldn't let the passengers die,” Machchhar said.
The Israeli prime minister told him that he is a hero with “an unbelievable courage, inviting him and Indian prime minister Narendra Modi to light a celebratory flame on Israel’s next Independence Day, the highest honour usually reserved for Israeli citizens.
“You are a true hero of the brave peoples of India and Israel, and you are a hero of the entire world. I wish you a very speedy and complete recovery," Netanyahu told captain Machchhar.
Israeli Ambassador to the UAE Yossi Shelley was at his bedside during the call and together with Netanyahu invited Machchhar and his family to visit Israel as soon as he is able, to receive the embrace and love that the entire country wants to give him.
Dubai's Crown Prince and UAE Minister of Defence Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid also visited Machchhar in hospital hailing the captain’s bravery, stating that he “embodied the highest degrees of courage, responsibility, and care for human life.”
“From us, and from the leadership of the nation, he has our full appreciation and praise. We are proud that he is part of our team, part of the story of our nation and part of what the UAE stands for a nation of compassion, a nation of peace and a nation of life,” Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed said.
In a new development on Sunday, British newspaper The Telegraph reported that the FlyDubai flight copilot, named by multiple media outlets as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, studied aviation at the UK-based Buckinghamshire New University.
The Telegraph said that during his time at the university, al-Hammami commented in social media posts that women should be “stomped on” and praised giving a woman a “pre-emptive slap.” He also appeared to praise Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, The Telegraph said.
The co-pilot used a crash axe against the captain and “attempted to carry out a terrorist attack”, the United Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said on Saturday, while the UAE president's diplomatic adviser Dr Anwar Gargash called the incident "a dangerous terrorist act".
Meanwhile on Sunday, regional officials said that the UAE authorities shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of the FlyDubai flight, including their nationalities, raising new questions over how the attacker evaded detection, the Associated Press reported.
According to AP, who quoted regional officials, Israel hadn’t raised red flags on any passenger or member of the crew.
Prime Minister Netanyahu later told the head of the National Security Council to appoint an examiner to review “all security aspects regarding foreign civil aviation to Israel.”
The Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, said the Transportation Ministry is responsible for vetting passenger lists from foreign flights. Transportation Minister Miri Regev told Israel’s public broadcaster Kan that the security agencies are responsible for flight security and that her ministry wasn’t given a list of passengers or any warnings.
Sharing the list is standard aviation procedure. But the head of aviation security at the Transportation Ministry, Dvir Rubenstien, told Army Radio that the ministry relies on local security checks and does not have the tools or the ability to run checks on each passenger on every flight.
Prime Minister Netanyahu said Thursday that Israel has long-standing agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don’t maintain diplomatic relations with Israel.
It also remains unclear how FlyDubai, a low-cost Emirati airline that operates flights between Israel and the UAE, had failed to identify the Omani pilot as a security risk and allowed him to fly the sensitive route to Israel.
Ahead of the elections at the end of the month, some opposition candidates have seized on the security failures to highlight what they perceive as negligence on the part of Netanyahu and his supporters. Transportation Minister Miri Regev is a member of Netanyahu’s Likud party and a staunch supporter.
“This is exactly what system collapse looks like,” Yair Golan, head of the opposition Democrats party, wrote on X. “A transportation minister who completely abandons our skies, and a prime minister who abandons national security.”
The UAE is leading the investigation and security agencies from four regional countries including Israel were working to establish the co-pilot’s motives, aided by the United States and other Western governments, according to the AP.

articles.title_orig: Evans ends Britain’s wait for world rally title after Solberg crashes two corners from glory
articles.title_zh: Evans ends Britain’s wait for world rally title after Solberg crashes two corners from glory
articles.content_orig:
Elfyn Evans becomes first British winner since 2001
Oliver Solberg’s hopes shattered by tumble down bank
⁠Elfyn Evans ended years of heartache, and a quarter-of-a-century wait for Britain, by winning the World Rally Championship title with Toyota after a dramatic season ⁠finale in Sardinia on Sunday.
The ⁠Welshman had been ​championship runner-up five times in the last six years but emerged triumphant after a final Powerstage duel with teammate Oliver Solberg ended with the charging Swede crashing ⁠out two corners from the finish while on course to take the crown.
Solberg, 25, ran wide and careered down a bank before getting the car back on the road. ⁠He still won the rally but lost the crucial bonus points on offer for the top five in the ​final stage.
Evans, with co-driver Scott Martin at his side, ‌became the first British world ‌rally champion since Englishman Richard Burns in 2001 and only the third since Scottish driver Colin McRae became ‌the first in 1995.
Sweden’s Solberg, son of Norway’s 2003 champion Petter, ended the season as runner-up. The final standings left Evans on 243 points, Solberg on 238 and Sami Pajari on 237 in what was also the end of an era for the sport with new regulations in force next year.
Evans said: “It hasn’t sunk in. I was sure it was over. I didn’t drive the best ‌stage but threw everything at it but it wasn’t clean. I feel for Oliver. He had an incredible weekend.” The Welshman completed his final run first and had to ​watch and wait to see whether he had done enough to take the title.
“I don’t really know what my reaction is, it’s surreal with how it happened. It’s a relief. It wouldn’t be my proudest way of winning it, but it’s job done,” added the 37-year-old, who finished fifth in the gravel rally.
Evans had started the rally – the ⁠final round after Saudi Arabia’s finale was cancelled due to conflict in the region – ​17 points clear of Finland’s Pajari, ​also in a Toyota, and 21 clear ​of Solberg.
after newsletter promotion
The Swede took control of the rally on Saturday, knowing he had nothing ​to lose and all to ‌gain, and started ​the final day 33.6 seconds ​clear of the field and the momentum swinging his way.
That feeling was reinforced when Evans lost time changing a wheel on Sunday’s penultimate stage, leaving the championship outcome hanging on the short final stage and the title going to which of the pair finished ahead of the other.
Toyota had already won the manufacturers’ championship.

articles.title_orig: Gavin Newsom on His Life in the Wine World
articles.title_zh: Gavin Newsom on His Life in the Wine World
articles.content_orig:
This story is from an installment of The Oeno Files , our weekly insider newsletter to the world of fine wine. Sign up here.
Long before setting his sights on Sacramento, Governor Gavin Newsom had one aspiration: to make fine wine more accessible. A lifelong wine lover who first connected with the fruit of the vine through his father, the San Francisco native cofounded PlumpJack wine shop there in 1992 with a group of partners that included family friend, oil heir, and composer Gordon Getty. Named for a Shakespeare character, the PlumpJack Group has since grown to include PlumpJack, Cade, and Odette wineries in Napa, and its leadership team includes general manager John Conover and Newsom’s sister, Hilary.
Elected mayor of San Francisco in 2003, Newsom’s interest in politics was piqued when the city’s department of health required him to install a mop sink in his carpeted wine shop. He began his career in government with a role in the San Francisco Parking and Traffic Commission before earning a spot on the city’s Board of Supervisors and then moved through the ranks of political office. Newsom placed his ownership interest in PlumpJack Group’s wineries, hotels, and restaurants into a blind trust when he was elected governor in 2018. Throughout his entire career, he continues to enjoy fine wine, especially bottles from Napa, Burgundy, Chablis, and Italy.
How did you first become interested in wine? Wine was one of the things I could connect with my dad about. Food, wine, and travel were a big part of his life. Because he could sometimes be emotionally hard to reach, wine became a kind of shared language between us—a way to sit together, talk, learn, and connect without having to force the conversation.
What was your journey toward opening the PlumpJack wine shop in 1992? It really started over dinner at the Balboa Cafe with my father and Pat Kelley, who had previously owned a wine store nearby. I became fixated on this idea of making fine wine more accessible—a store that wasn’t the discount rack but also wasn’t some precious place for the initiated, where people could discover great wine at an accessible price. I was 24, raised $174,000 from 15 friends and family, quit my job, and spent nearly two years fighting through permits and scraping the business together.
What is the origin of the name PlumpJack? PlumpJack is Sir John Falstaff, Shakespeare’s irreverent, larger-than-life character, and the inspiration for Gordon Getty’s opera. I loved that Falstaff mocked stuffiness and celebrated the absurdity of life. That was precisely the attitude we wanted to bring to wine.
How did you go from having a wine shop to opening wineries? The store worked, and two years later we opened PlumpJack Cafe with the same philosophy: exceptional wines without the extraordinary restaurant markup, including great Cabernets, Pinots, and Zinfandels by the glass. I’d always had an affinity for Oakville and Napa Cabernet, so when the opportunity came in 1995 to acquire a winery there, we jumped at it and eventually expanded to four wineries.
What are some of your favorite wines? I’ve always loved Oakville Cabernet. Groth and Silver Oak were two early favorites, but my tastes have always ranged beyond Napa, including Burgundy, Chablis, Pinot Noir, and Italian whites.
Do you consider yourself a wine drinker or collector? I’ve always been more interested in drinking and sharing wine than displaying it.
Under your leadership, in what ways has the state of California addressed the glut of wine grapes in the state that caused growers to rip out a reported 40,000 acres of vines in the past year and allow 100,000 tons of grapes to remain unharvested? Government cannot manufacture consumer demand or wave a wand and correct an oversupply that developed over many years. Across the agriculture industry, we’ve supported California growers through research, pest prevention, water resilience, and market development, but I’ve also gone out of my way throughout my public career to ensure my personal history in the wine business never influences state policy. And right now, one of the worst things Washington could do is make a difficult market even harder. President Trump’s trade war with Canada has helped trigger retaliation and restrictions on American wine in what has been our largest export market. It’s exactly the opposite of what California growers need.
There is a perception that vineyards and wineries are owned by rich people who don’t need help from the government to survive. How much truth is there to that perception? The industry is incredibly diverse. Yes, there are wealthy vineyard owners, but there are also thousands of farmers, small and multigenerational wineries, farmworkers, cellar workers, truck drivers, restaurant and hotel employees whose livelihoods depend on this industry. California wine alone supports more than 422,000 jobs in our state. That’s why Trump’s tariffs are so harmful.
Why did you title your book Young Man In A Hurry ? It actually came from a 2009 Economist article about me—not exactly a compliment at the time—and years later I realized how much truth there was in it. I came to see it less as somebody else’s critique than as a self-critique: the impatience, ambition, insecurity, and constant need to keep moving that have shaped so much of my life.
If readers of your book come away with one impression, what do you hope it to be? That people are more complicated than their caricatures, including me. Writing this book forced me to scrutinize rather than sanitize my life, to understand my parents and my family differently, and ultimately to discover things about myself that I hadn’t fully understood before.
Completely theoretical, of course … but what wines would you like to see served at a White House dinner? For now, my answer is anything but Trump Wine.

articles.title_orig: EMU Theatre to present mythical world of 'Metamorphoses'
articles.title_zh: EMU Theatre to present mythical world of 'Metamorphoses'
articles.content_orig:
Eastern Michigan University Theatre is about to perform its upcoming production "Metamorphoses " by Mary Zimmerman. The production, which was directed and choreographed by Jennifer Felts, brings to life the myths of renowned characters King Midas, Aphrodite, Poseidon, Orpheus, Eurydice and many others.
"Metamorphoses" will be at the Sponberg Theatre on Oct. 8, 9 and 10 at 7 p.m. and October 10 and 11 at 2 p.m. The show is recommended for ages 13 and older and is open to the public.
The EMU Theatre page said that "Metamorphoses" explores this myriad of stories in an imaginative and captivating series of vignettes, weaving together tales that are passionate, funny, heartbreaking, whimsical and resonant; stories that touch upon the beauty and ugliness of human nature, the mystery of the divine and the theme of transformation.
"This production is a love letter to the CAS reorganization and to our newly formed School of Performing Arts. It is truly a year of 'Metamorphoses,'" Felts said. "These beautiful myths are brought to life with water as a central element. To create this world, we have engineered a pool into the set, designed by Kristin Ellert-Sakowski and built by technical director Dustin Miller alongside our talented student staff."
There will be a pool of water onstage that is meant to help with shifting from one world to another, being able to represent the metaphorical and the literal. Audiences should be aware that some splashing from the pool may impact the first few center rows during the show.
"There's a lot of taking care of things, whether it's people or props or the actual space we're in because of the pool. And so it's not just making sure that actors are feeling safe on stage, but also that they are physically safe on stage and they're not slipping and that they're not freezing cold. It's a lot of just protecting the space and protecting the props and making sure that we're putting in extra care and effort into the show," Lily Ban, the assistant stage manager, said.
Levi Greunke, the scene shop worker and cast member, said that the pool brings some fun challenges for the show.
Dustin Miller, the technical director, said that working on this production has been an incredible learning and teaching experience as a technical director.
"With the added element of the pool in the Scenic Design by Kristin Ellert-Sakowski we’ve been able to dive into the world of plumbing, waterproofing and safety that will be invaluable to the students as they enter the workforce," Miller said.
Felts described the show as a story of hope, love and resilience. She said that it is an exciting, moving and poignant piece of theater.
"Our students have worked incredibly hard to bring this production to life," she said. "We are so proud of their creativity, dedication, and artistry, and we can’t wait to share this extraordinary production with our audience."
Grace Gil, the assistant stage manager, said that people should come to see "Metamorphoses" because of how much work everyone involved put into the production.
"It's gonna be sick as hell and you should come see it," Gil said. "If you are a student, you get a discount."
Ban told The Echo that this show brings accessible language to the audience to help them comprehend Greek myths.
Those who are interested can purchase tickets online which can be found on the "Metamorphoses" webpage on the EMU Communication, Media & Theatre Arts site.
Lelaina MacDonald is a copy editor at The Eastern Echo .

articles.title_orig: Trump names national intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new AI czar
articles.title_zh: Trump names national intelligence chief Jay Clayton as new AI czar
articles.content_orig:
Jay Clayton testifies during a Senate Intelligence Committee confirmation hearing to be the next Director of National Intelligence on Capitol Hill, Wednesday, July 15, 2026, in Washington. Mariam Zuhaib/AP hide caption
Director of national intelligence Jay Clayton is the new White House AI czar, President Trump said on Sunday.
Trump wrote on Truth Social that Clayton will lead the White House's new "Super Intelligence Force," a group that will "ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence."
Trump prefers the term "super intelligence" to "artificial intelligence." He said his "Super Intelligence Force" will "coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies."
Before being confirmed earlier this year to lead national intelligence, Clayton was United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, and chairman of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
Trump's announcement follows various statements of alarm from tech leaders over risks in the rapid development of AI, including that it could go rogue. Trump has largely brushed aside the warnings and attempted to reframe concerns around AI.
On Tuesday, Trump met with AI executives at the White House, and said afterwards that leaders of several artificial intelligence companies had signed a voluntary accord that will include internal and external reviews of their work.
Meanwhile, the White House also launched a revamped government website this week, America.gov , which says it is sourced via artificial intelligence from "official government sources."
In his social media post, Trump also named other members of his "Super Intelligence Force". He said it will include: Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, and Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael.
It is unclear what Clayton's appointment as AI czar means for the AI industry, as current artificial intelligence regulation by the U.S. government is limited. Congress has not passed federal law broadly regulating the use or development of AI. Some states, including California, have enacted measures about AI, including requiring entities to be transparent when it is used .
During an interview with CNBC last month, Clayton called super intelligence a "national security issue." He also pushed back against calls for a "pause" in developing the technology, pointing out that other countries around the world are continuing to develop AI. "I don't think any American should think that that's a good strategy," he said.
In December 2024, president-elect Trump announced he would appoint David Sacks, a Silicon Valley investor, as an AI and crypto czar , with a brief to advise the administration on policies surrounding AI.
Earlier this year, Sacks stepped down from his role and became co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. He has backed AI leaders Sam Altman and Dario Amodei's warnings about the technology, and the idea of a "slow down" in AI development. Last month, Sacks wrote on social media that the tech leaders should "stop pretending you need anyone else's permission" to make such moves.

articles.title_orig: Delivering Remote Audio Production Over IP
articles.title_zh: Delivering Remote Audio Production Over IP
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › Tech and Gear › Tech Tips
Distributed workflows are fast becoming the norm for radio. What does it mean for you? This is one in a series of articles.
The author is VP Sales, Americas, for Tieline .
Tieline has delivered wired and wireless IP solutions for over two decades, so it’s not a new concept for us. However, it took quite a long time for many engineers to shift to using IP, as they felt it was safer to use a wired solution like ISDN. It had always “just worked.”
When the pandemic hit in 2020, it showed everyone that we have the tools to broadcast remotely from anywhere. Since then, centralization has accelerated and new studios have become physically smaller and more flexible to stream live shows, perform audio production, create podcasts and social media videos.
Downsizing was made possible because it is common for radio show hosts, sports commentators, news readers, traffic reporters and syndicated talent and guests to broadcast partially, or entirely, from home.
As an example, Tieline users Don McDonald and Tom Cock are hosts often out on the road away from their flagship studio producing the “Talking Real Money” show. They use a ViA when on the road together, or Tom will use a Tieline codec at his home studio, and Don will use another Tieline codec at his home/mobile studio.
Both hosts can simply dial into the studio (or each other’s codec) for low-latency bidirectional links. Listeners dial into the flagship studio with questions and their audio from phone hybrids is routed to Don and Tom in real-time as a mix-minus.
Nowadays, broadcasting over IP is an accepted practice for radio and television networks around the world. Reliability is enhanced through multiple layers of redundancy with fully automated backup. Tieline employs SmartStream Plus hitless packet switching over multiple wired or wireless IP network interfaces; this technology has set a high standard for resilient IP streaming over the public internet over many years. Technology such as this, along with FEC, RIST and bonded IP, is the gold standard for broadcasting in 2026.
The ViA audio codec has become an industry standard remote codec preferred by major broadcasters on every continent.
Flexibility is paramount and that’s why Tieline’s newest product, the ViA Duo, provides even greater adaptability for a range of new use cases and workflows.
It’s driven by increasing demand for flexible platforms with professional, broadcast-quality connections for critical broadcasts. We see demand for a traditional IP codec, as well as opportunities for more flexible equipment supporting AoIP protocols including AES67, ST 2110-30, Ravenna, Dante, Livewire and NMOS. This allows the same unit to be an audio codec and provide commentary solutions by acting as an AoIP node on a network at a sports venue, or over a managed or dark fiber WAN connection back to a station in a remote integration (REMI) workflow.
More stations are expanding remote production, given how easy it is to route multiple production signals in and out of the studio. A single Tieline codec at a station can support 32 mono (or 16 stereo) signals in/out of their studio.
As an example, I was recently at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway with the group from Radio One Indianapolis. For the month of May, they weren’t just going live from the track but also producing prerecorded shows remotely for later use. I had the pleasure of seeing them deploy remote gear all over the 2.5-mile track at multiple different locations.
Radio One could handle so many live broadcasts and remote productions simultaneously because they have a large fleet of IP audio codecs back at their home studio. Each remote codec could simply dial back to the studio and be routed straight on-air, or be sent to a production room for recording and editing purposes.
Without their codec network, Radio One wouldn’t have been able to broadcast live from the track and their remote production would not have delivered a real-time solution. Felix Rosenqvist wasn’t the only Indy 500 winner, it was also Radio One’s engineering team and codec network running full speed during the entire month of May!
Audio codecs have been used for remote off-tube commentary of major events for several years. By integrating video into an audio codec like the ViA Duo, it means broadcasters can send a live gameday video feed to remote talent directly and commentators can call any event remotely from anywhere in the world.
We have all heard about new technologies merging from software-based services that allow for broadcasting anywhere using nothing more than a laptop and microphone.
However, I believe this isn’t always the most reliable or consistent experience for remote broadcast production. Laptops are truly 100% customizable by the operator and engineer, which isn’t a bad thing, but can lead to issues if not checked.
If installed software is out of place or not updated, services may become unreliable and not connect. In addition, if you are a PC user, regular updates have been known to “accidentally” disturb network and audio drivers, so a simple software update could impact your entire remote.
Of course, one can bypass this issue by either declining to update, changing registry or even opting for a “Long Term Service” edition of Windows.
Ideally, you shouldn’t have to monitor critical software updates to maintain your remote production capabilities. It makes more sense to use purpose-built hardware for which the manufacturer maintains functionality and security updates for you.
With this said, I do believe there is a time and place for software-based solutions, and Tieline itself has the Report-IT Enterprise app for reporting and similar applications. However, for reliability, nothing beats a dedicated hardware solution with multiple layers of built-in redundancy, compared to a cobbled-together PC/software solution requiring more effort to maintain.
With teams of announcers and commentators working remotely, it is critical that engineers can remote control their equipment. This helps maintain quality control and provides confidence that if issues occur at a remote site, they can be managed effectively.
For example, tools like Tieline’s built-in Toolbox Web-GUI or the optional Cloud Codec Controller are designed for comprehensive network management, configuration and control of all IP codecs, as well as Report-IT Enterprise app users. This provides confidence that people without technical knowledge can use IP codec technology and stay connected.
Read more on this topic in the Radio World ebook “Audio Production (From Anywhere).”

articles.title_orig: ‘His grace is for all,’ President Oaks declares during October 2026 general conference
articles.title_zh: ‘His grace is for all,’ President Oaks declares during October 2026 general conference
articles.content_orig:
As was foretold in the scriptures, today is a moment in history when individuals around the world are looking for God and for his eternal truths, Church President Dallin H. Oaks taught during the Sunday morning session of October 2026 general conference .
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is home to the Savior’s restored doctrine and authority, President Oaks said. In it, God’s children learn about the nature of the Godhead and the significance of the Savior’s Atonement in Heavenly Father’s plan.
“God the Father, the great Elohim, is the Father of our spirits, the framer of heaven and earth, and the author of the plan of our salvation. (See Moses 1:31–33 ; 2:1–2 ; Doctrine and Covenants 20:17–21 .) Jesus Christ is His Only Begotten Son, Jehovah, and the Messiah, ‘the God of the whole earth’ ( 3 Nephi 11:14 ),” he said.
Members of the Church both obey the invitation of the Book of Mormon prophet Amaleki and invite all others to “come unto Christ” ( Omni 1:26 ).
“As your President, I pray for what our Heavenly Father wants for each of us — to be active members of the Church of Jesus Christ, proceeding forward on the covenant path into the eternities. We need one another’s prayers.”
Each individual on the earth is a work in progress with personal trials and challenges to work through and help others to work through, he said.
“We all have present or future concerns or struggles we are trying to overcome. These may include questions or doubts. Whatever they are, the way to overcome them is to get closer to our Savior, Jesus Christ.”
Those challenges of mortality have the purpose of providing opportunities for individuals to develop faith in Heavenly Father and His Son, Jesus Christ.
“Strong faith requires more than strong desire. It means daily trying, one step at a time, with prayer and scriptural learning,” he said.
In that process of personal development, individuals need to have patience with themselves and others, President Oaks said. That patience includes allowing time for increased understanding by one’s self or a loved one. It also includes being patient with the progress of scientific understanding and the “sometimes-incomplete teachings of religion,” he said.
Reconciling the conflicts that may exist between science and religion can take time. This process may also help build faith and humility. That same faith and humility compels obedience to the Lord’s commandments to repent and be baptized.
“A major concern to your prophet leaders are those members of diminishing faith in Jesus Christ. We love you. ... So does the Lord God. He is relentless in His loving pursuit of each of you,” President Oaks said.
The Prophet invited individuals to maintain momentum in the building of their faith by keeping the commandments, keeping their covenants and avoiding the artificial limits of secular learning.
The Sunday morning general conference address was President Oaks’ second in such a conference since being sustained as Church President in a general conference solemn assembly on April 4. In the April 2026 general conference , President Oaks invited individuals to act as peacemakers at home and in all relationships.
Six months later, President Oaks invited continued learning and the study of the Book of Mormon.
President Oaks taught there are two ways to earn the necessary knowledge of life.
“There is no ultimate conflict between knowledge obtained by these different methods because God, our omnipotent Father, knows all truth and expects us to learn by both methods.”
President Oaks also invited individuals to maintain humility as they seek and obtain learning by these two methods. He referenced then-Elder Spencer W. Kimball’s 1963 address at BYU in which the member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and future President of the Church referred to humility as “teachableness.”
“Teachableness is an ability to realize that all virtues and abilities are not concentrated in one’s self. … [Humility] is forgiving others in the realization that there may be errors of the same kind or worse [that we ourselves commit],” Elder Kimball taught.
One way members of the Church can strengthen their humility is through the weekly participation in the ordinance of the sacrament and living up to the promises made in that covenant each week. For those who have made additional covenants in the temple, President Oaks invited them to attend the house of the Lord regularly.
“These simple practices will protect and strengthen you,” he said.
President Oaks also shared teachings from the Book of Mormon that can strengthen testimonies of the Savior, Jesus Christ.
First, he said the Book of Mormon teaches that Jesus, as the Creator, died “for all men, that all men might become subject unto him” ( 2 Nephi 9:5 ).
“This means that if our sins are to be forgiven through His Atonement, we must comply with the conditions He has prescribed, including faith, repentance and baptism,” President Oaks said.
Those conditions will not and cannot be compelled by the Savior or Heavenly Father, President Oaks taught. Their execution must arise from individuals’ desires, choices and actions.
Second, President Oaks taught that the Book of Mormon illustrates how the resurrected Savior ministered to some of those who did not have the chance to learn from Him during His mortal ministry in Jerusalem.
When the Savior appeared to the Nephites on the American continent, He said He was fulfilling Heavenly Father’s commandment to visit “other sheep” than those who had witnessed His teachings in and around Jerusalem (see 3 Nephi 16:1 ; John 10:16 ). The Savior was also clear in the Book of Mormon that the Nephites were not exclusively those “other sheep” to whom He would minister.
Third, the Book of Mormon includes teachings that show God loves everyone, President Oaks said.
From 2 Nephi 29:7 , President Oaks read, “Know ye not that I, the Lord your God, have created all men, and that I remember those who are upon the isles of the sea; and that I rule in the heavens above and in the earth beneath; and I bring forth my word unto the children of men, yea, even upon all the nations of the earth?”
Fourth, President Oaks said the Book of Mormon serves to correct the “erroneous assertion that the grace of God saves only a chosen few.”
The Book of Mormon prophet Nephi taught in 2 Nephi 26 that the Savior will receive everyone to Him regardless of their differences.
“His grace is for all,” President Oaks reiterated. And everyone who lives on this earth will have the opportunity to receive a manifestation of Christ’s reality through the power of the Holy Ghost, he said.
President Oaks said that millions of people have had personal experiences and can testify that that promise has been fulfilled in their lives.
“I invite all to believe them,” President Oaks said of those promises contained in the Book of Mormon.
The book’s purpose, as stated in its title page , is to help everyone “know of the covenants of the Lord” and “that Jesus is the Christ, the Eternal God, manifesting himself unto all nations.”
President Oaks concluded his message by inviting individuals to live the truths of the Book of Mormon and to share them with others. Doing so will allow all to “draw closer to Jesus Christ our Savior,” he said.

articles.title_orig: OPEC+ holds output targets steady as Middle East conflict tightens supply
articles.title_zh: OPEC+ holds output targets steady as Middle East conflict tightens supply
articles.content_orig:
OPEC+ agreed to keep oil production targets steady for November at a meeting on Sunday, the producer group said, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year.
Seven core members of the group comprising the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia made the decision for November in a brief online meeting on Sunday. The core members are Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman.
Gulf OPEC+ producers have been pumping well below output targets in the face of continuing export disruptions from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran , with exports fluctuating at 60% to 80% of normal levels in recent months.
"The OPEC+ group of seven kept their production ceilings unchanged, in line with market expectations. That said, despite rising flows through the Strait of Hormuz, their output levels remain well below quota," said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo.
"Consequently, the oil market remains tight."
Oil prices had dropped on Friday after European leaders agreed to U.S. President Donald Trump's request to release diesel reserves. Crude oil prices settled lower after the Group of Seven nations announced the release of diesel and crude stocks to ease surging fuel prices.
International benchmark Brent crude futures slipped 6 cents to close at $102.25 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude slid $1.76 to $91.11 a barrel.
The G7 will release 100 million barrels of reserves over the next four months "with a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days," the group's leaders said in a joint statement. The G7 includes France, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the U.S.
Despite the G7 announcement, Brent crude remains above $100 a barrel, up from about $73 before the Iran war started in late February.
The Iran war has also delayed the group's output capacity review — crucial to determine members' 2027 output quotas — because it has thrown estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, industry sources told Reuters last week.
OPEC+ has been raising output targets for much of 2026 after years of production cuts, but most of the increases stayed on paper because of the Middle East conflict.
The seven core OPEC+ members pumped 25 million barrels per day in August, up 630,000 bpd from July, yet still roughly 5 million bpd below prewar levels in February, OPEC data shows.
The seven will meet next on Nov. 1.
OPEC+ still has about 2 million bpd of output cuts in place covering most members. It needs the result of the capacity review to decide how to distribute increases, and any changes to output are unlikely before 2027, sources have said.
A separate OPEC+ ministerial group, the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee, which does not set policy, also met on Sunday to review the market.
— CNBC contributed to this report .

articles.title_orig: Oat of this world: cooks descend on Scotland for ultimate porridge making contest
articles.title_zh: Oat of this world: cooks descend on Scotland for ultimate porridge making contest
articles.content_orig:
Technical mishaps and plenty of whisky as competitors from as far afield as US and Australia vie for Golden Spurtle
T here are many varieties of spurtle. The traditional Scottish cooking implement, designed for stirring porridge without forming lumps, comes in a range of sizes, can be formed from cherry wood, beech, or maple, and might be topped with a decorative finial or smoothed out at its end for a more modern finish. But on Saturday in Carrbridge, in the Scottish Highlands, only one spurtle mattered: the Golden Spurtle, awarded annually to the winner of the World Porridge Making championship, which have been hosted here since 1994.
The sun shone on the picturesque village as almost 40 competitors lined up in the village hall for six heats across the day. Tasked with producing a traditional porridge – made only from untreated oatmeal, water and salt – and a speciality dish where additional ingredients and flourishes were permitted, entrants had travelled from across Scotland and as far afield as Australia and the US for a shot at the Golden Spurtle.
As the first heat kicked off, technical difficulties beset some contestants when the provided induction hobs, new this year after a long tradition of gas, failed to heat. But the reigning champion, Norway’s Sven Seljom, was unaffected, serenely stirring Norwegian mutton into oats and filtered water he had brought with him especially for the competition. He had planned to bring Norwegian cheese, too, he said, but import rules meant he had to make do with something more local. A sizeable entourage watched on in traditional Scandinavian dress as he measured, stirred and tasted, boisterous chants of “SVEN, SVEN, SVEN” breaking out at each mention of his name.
The first of the day’s many whisky breaks came 10 minutes into proceedings at 10.40am, with shots of a lowland malt distributed throughout the exuberant crowd as competitors did well to retain their focus. The drams’ effects meant nobody seemed to mind too much when the crucial timer was accidentally reset just moments from the heat’s tense final countdown.
Any initial teething problems were quickly ironed out as the day settled into a well-oiled rhythm. In a separate “judging chamber”, a trio of judges from Scotland’s culinary scene blind-tasted each batch, assessing primarily for taste, texture and colour. Among the speciality porridges on offer throughout the day were a “Granola Espanola”, a porridge cannoli from the Australian national champion, Robert Reid , and a recipe featuring soft-boiled quail eggs.
“The first thing I did was burn my oats,” lamented Switzerland’s Jeremy McTeague after a heat that didn’t quite go to plan. But he remained upbeat: “It gave them a distinctive toastiness – maybe the judges will like it.”
Hundreds of spectators showed up for the day’s spectacle, from Carrbridge residents who turn out each year to support the community-powered event, to tourists such as Joe, 43, and Tina, 39, who were visiting from England and had overheard a conversation about the championship in a local pub the previous night.
“We looked it up and decided straight away we’d be here,” said Joe. “It’s Scotland, it’s porridge, someone said there would be whisky … it was a no-brainer.” The pair said they were making a beeline for the tasting room to sample the produce left over from judging.
The event proved so popular that the village hall had to operate a one-in, one-out policy. Those who couldn’t fit inside were decanted into a merch tent bursting with oats, spurtles and “always stir clockwise” tote bags, while local cafes and tourist centres screened a live stream of the competition. There was plenty of action to be found around the village, from competitors spotted calming their nerves with pints in the local hotel, to an American visitor who accidentally caused controversy by dressing as a box of Scott’s Porage Oats – rolled oats of the kind not allowed in competition, and a rival to the event’s sponsors, Hamlyns.
By the afternoon, the hall was full of cooking aromas and the crowd full of whisky and porridge as they took their seats once more to see who would walk away victorious. There was a minor upset when the reigning champion, Seljom, missed out on the final, but a surprise win for McTeague saw him through to the cook-off despite his earlier woes.
Once the top six had taken to the hob one last time, though, it was the Netherlands national champion, Gina Saarberg, who emerged victorious in the traditional competition, with the speciality prize going to Reid for his cannoli.
“I’m at a loss for words,” Saarberg said as she clutched her Golden Spurtle. “To be here was already such a win in the first place. This is a beautiful community, so of course I’m very happy I won, but it’s also just a pleasure to be here.”

articles.title_orig: Cornell rape accuser faces threats demanding she drop her lawsuit, attorney says
articles.title_zh: Cornell rape accuser faces threats demanding she drop her lawsuit, attorney says
articles.content_orig:
The woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted by Cornell University fraternity members has received threats pressuring her to drop her lawsuit, her attorney said Sunday.
Thomas Giuffra told CNN’s “State of the Union” that people attempting to unmask his client’s identity had also targeted at least three women mistakenly identified as her. The former Cornell student is identified as Jane Doe in court documents.
“She’s received multiple threats, and women who aren’t even Jane Doe receive threats,” Giuffra said. He added that he had received a threat Sunday morning.
Giuffra did not identify those responsible or say whether the threats had been reported to law enforcement. He did not immediately respond to NBC News’ request for more information about the threats.
Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month against Cornell and seven Chi Phi fraternity members, alleging she was sexually assaulted over the course of hours on Oct. 19-20, 2024, while she was under the influence of ketamine, alcohol and marijuana.
The allegations have sparked renewed scrutiny of the university’s and local authorities’ handling of the allegations. Gov. Kathy Hochul last week appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to consider whether criminal charges are appropriate.
NBC News reported Friday that Cornell police interviewed witnesses and received anonymous tips during their investigation in 2024, but Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten did not review that additional information before deciding not to pursue charges at the time. He has defended his decision, saying that Jane Doe’s initial six-page statement to police did not allege criminality.
Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said Saturday that the university must do better and that its board of trustees would announce an independent review of its handling of the case next week.
Maggie McCabe is a desk assistant at NBC News Washington.

articles.title_orig: Bosnia votes in one of world’s most complicated general elections
articles.title_zh: Bosnia votes in one of world’s most complicated general elections
articles.content_orig:
The party of banned Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik has retained its grip on power in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s predominantly Serb Republika Srpska entity, with his ally set to keep the Serb seat in the country’s three-member presidency.
Preliminary results from Sunday’s general election showed Zeljka Cvijanovic of the right-wing Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD), led by Dodik, ahead in the presidential race.
The result reinforced Dodik’s political influence despite his conviction and ban from public office, leaving a party that has repeatedly challenged state institutions in a strong position.
Dodik was not on the ballot after being convicted last year of defying decisions by the international envoy charged with overseeing the 1995 peace agreement that ended the Bosnian War.
Speaking to supporters late on Sunday, he said his party would not alter course.
“No one should ask us to change our politics,” Dodik said, while also praising United States President Donald Trump’s 2024 election victory and thanking Russian President Vladimir Putin, a longtime ally.
Nationalist figures Cvijanovic and Darijana Filipovic, as well as leftist moderate Denis Becirovic, were leading the race as the Central Election Commission released preliminary results shortly after polls closed.
Becirovic, representing the Social Democratic Party (SDP-BiH), led the contest for the Bosniak seat. Cvijanovic of the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) led the race for the Serb seat. The Croatian Democratic Union’s (HDZ-BiH) Filipovic led the field for the Croat seat.
About 3.4 million people were eligible to vote in Sunday’s election to choose the three members of the country’s multiethnic presidency, legislators for the national Parliament and heads of institutions for the country’s two entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (FBiH) and Republika Srpska.
Bosnia’s complex web of governing institutions was created by a US-brokered peace agreement in 1995 to manage the ethnic divisions between Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats that gave rise to the 1992-95 war.
The major parties’ repeated focus on war-era rhetoric, and the division was frustrating for some voters, activist Adi Selman of the Karton Revolucija protest group told the AFP news agency.
“I don’t think these new elections in Bosnia will change anything,” the 34-year-old said in the northern Bosnian town of Tuzla ahead of the vote.
“The choice is limited to political parties that have already been around for 30 years and basically pick up votes by harping on about war, tensions, divisions and the past.”
“Bosnia and Herzegovina is dead; it is an impossible country,” Republika Srpska’s former President Dodik told the final rally of the SNSD in the entity’s capital, Banja Luka, late on Friday.
In the FBiH, Bosniak parties are pushing for a stronger central state, with incumbent Bosniak presidency member Becirovic pledging a renewed path to the EU and NATO.
The European Union granted Bosnia candidate status in December 2022, but accession negotiations scheduled for 2024 were delayed as Brussels demanded the country pass stronger anticorruption laws and reform its judicial system.
Croat nationalist parties are also pushing for electoral reform, demanding a greater say in choosing the Croat member of the presidency in the entity they share with the more numerous Bosniaks.
Meanwhile, Russia is accused of slowing down the country’s path towards joining the EU, while also holding close ties with the SNSD, which favours secession for Republika Srpska, dominated by ethnic Serbs.
This general election is the first in the country to use new electronic tools to scan ballot papers and biometric fingerprint verification to reduce fraud.

articles.title_orig: Even 'Bond King' Bill Gross warns 'don’t own bonds' as long-term debt enters a new ear of volatility
articles.title_zh: Even 'Bond King' Bill Gross warns 'don’t own bonds' as long-term debt enters a new ear of volatility
articles.content_orig:
PIMCO cofounder Bill Gross, who revolutionized bond investing with active trading strategies, warned the overall credit landscape has become unbalanced and cautioned against holding longer-term debt.
In a Financial Times op-ed on Wednesday, he pointed out that government, mortgage and corporate credit now totals about $84 trillion.
“Too much debt can lead to too much risk and too much equity can lead to less earnings per share growth under certain underperforming productivity cycles,” Gross wrote. “Move them both at the same pace consistent with industry standards and economic growth more than likely expands as well.”
But balance sheets have grown too lopsided, putting growth at risk, he said. The AI sector’s debt boom is an anomaly by historical standards, and federal debt has already hit peak levels for peacetime, now at 100% of GDP.
While all that debt is fueling growth now, it has led to higher inflation today and will likely slow growth in the future, Gross added.
“In such an environment, my view is: don’t own bonds, with the exception of one-year Treasury bills, which are now at 4.55%,” he said. “Be cautious with stocks at record levels as higher yields over time will contract profit margins. Be prepared for the end of ‘what you are used to’ stock markets and higher volatility in prices for the benchmark 10-year Treasury bonds.”
His admonition is notable given his career in bond investing, which earned him the moniker “Bond King .” For decades, he dominated a corner of financial markets that was considered sleepy before he arrived on the scene.
Rather than simply buying bonds and holding them to maturity to collect interest, his investment strategies generated returns well beyond what “clipping coupons” provided.
But in recent years, the market has experienced its own transformation as well. Central banks around the world no longer reliably buy and hold Treasury debt as they seek to diversify their reserves. At the same time, price-sensitive hedge funds have emerged as bigger players in the bond market and are quicker to sell.
The so-called basis trade that’s become popular among hedge funds, where they profit from small price differences between Treasury bonds and the Treasury futures, has made the market more volatile.
In fact, the basis trade has grown so much that hedge funds’ share of total Treasury holdings has almost doubled since 2023 to 8.5%, exceeding the portion that depository institutions and mutual funds command.
The new era of volatility has been on display this year, as 10-year Treasury yields have soared more than 100 basis points since the Iran war started and recently hit the highest levels in 24 years.
While hedge funds are a key source of liquidity in the market, they may weaken bonds’ reputation as a safe-haven asset, Joe Maher, markets economist at Capital Economics, said in a note in August.
“In a risk-off environment, safe-haven flows into sovereign bonds may be offset by hedge funds unwinding their leveraged trading positions as funding conditions tighten,” he wrote. “And given they have no obligation to act as market makers, the more likely it is that liquidity dries up in these markets in times of stress.”
On top of that, hedge funds could transmit stress across different assets, Maher warned. For example, a stock market selloff could force hedge funds to dump bond positions to cover their losses in equities.
For his part, Gross said he is suspicious of AI hyperscalers, unless they have price-to-earnings ratios of less than 20. And while stocks like Verizon and AT&T have decent yields, their mobile phone businesses are threatened by SpaceX’s Starlink.
Some income funds that are trading at a discount to net asset values may offer some opportunities, but they would suffer if short-term interest rates rise higher than expected, he added.
“Preserve and protect is my current investment motto,” Gross wrote.
Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune , where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

articles.title_orig: Sybiha on bridge attacks: World must make it clear to Russia that it must stop escalation
articles.title_zh: Sybiha on bridge attacks: World must make it clear to Russia that it must stop escalation
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called on partners to respond decisively to Russian terror, strengthen Ukraine's air defense and impose effective sanctions on Russia's defense industry.
He said this in a post on X , according to Ukrinform.
The foreign minister said that this week marked a new chapter in Russia's campaign of all-day terror against civilians and that after targeting food depots, retail chains, pharmacy warehouses, and vital databases, Russia is now going after bridges.
"They are important lifelines that keep the country functioning, connect communities, allow people to get to work and access essential services," Sybiha said.
The minister recalled that over the past few days, Russia had struck two bridges in Kyiv six times, right when civilian traffic was using them and metro trains were crossing.
"The world cannot simply watch and wait – we urge strong reactions by our partners. Both in words and deeds. Make clear to Moscow that it must stop its escalation and terror – and engage in diplomacy and peace efforts," Sybiha said.
He also called on allies to strengthen Ukraine's air defense, impose effective sanctions on Russia's military-industrial complex, and add to sanctions lists the individuals and organizations that enable the regime to continue committing its crimes.
As reported, two people were injured in a Russian strike on Kyiv's Northern Bridge on October 4.
